teile.einleitung: A lithium-ion battery is a rechargeable battery. It is found in mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars. Its invention was so important that three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 2019.
wichtigste: A lithium-ion battery stores electrical energy and can be recharged many times.
Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019 for this invention.
At 97, John Goodenough was the oldest Nobel Prize winner so far.
Sony brought the first lithium-ion battery onto the market in 1991.
The negative electrode is usually made of graphite.
When charging, the lithium ions move to the negative electrode and lodge there.
A typical cell with a cobalt cathode has about 3.6 to 3.7 volts.
A damaged battery can catch fire through thermal runaway.

abschnitte.text: A **rechargeable battery**, or accumulator, is an energy store that can take in electricity and give it out again later. Unlike an ordinary battery, it can be recharged hundreds of times. Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy for little weight. That is why smartphones today are so thin and light. **Lithium** is the lightest of all metals, which is ideal for a light battery.

A battery has two **electrodes**: a negative one, the anode, and a positive one, the cathode. Between them is a liquid or a gel, the electrolyte, through which lithium ions can move. When charging, the ions move to the negative electrode made of graphite and lodge there between the layers of carbon. When discharging, they move back to the cathode, and at the same time electrons flow through the device as an electric current. You can imagine it like a rocking chair, with the ions swinging back and forth.

In the 1970s Stanley Whittingham built the first lithium battery, but it was still dangerous. In 1980 John Goodenough introduced **lithium cobalt oxide** as the cathode, which greatly increased the voltage. In 1985 Akira Yoshino developed an anode made of carbon, which made the battery much safer. The company Sony brought the first lithium-ion battery onto the market in 1991. In 2019 the three researchers jointly received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Lithium-ion batteries are found in mobile phones, tablets, laptops, headphones and cordless drills. In Switzerland many people ride e-bikes, whose batteries are also based on this technology. Electric cars have large battery packs made of thousands of single cells. Homeowners also use them to store electricity from their **solar panels** for the night. A single cell with a cobalt cathode supplies about 3.6 to 3.7 volts.

If a battery is damaged, overcharged or strongly heated, it can keep on getting hotter and hotter. This dangerous chain reaction is called **thermal runaway** and can lead to fires. That is why you should no longer use swollen or broken batteries and should take them to a collection point. In Switzerland you can return batteries free of charge wherever they are sold. Recycling recovers valuable materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A store for electrical energy that can be charged again and again.
A particle that has an electric charge.
A part of the battery where the electric current goes in or out.
A substance between the electrodes through which ions can move.
The unit of electrical voltage.

gewusst: John Goodenough kept working into old age and died in 2023 at the age of 100.
Batteries like neither great heat nor severe cold, so it is better not to leave a mobile phone in a hot car.
An electric car battery can weigh several hundred kilograms.

teile.einleitung: Ichthyosaurs were marine reptiles that lived in the oceans at the time of the dinosaurs. With their streamlined bodies they looked like today's dolphins. Their name means “fish lizard”.
wichtigste: The name “ichthyosaur” means fish lizard.
Ichthyosaurs were not dinosaurs but marine reptiles.
In their body shape they resembled today's dolphins.
They breathed with lungs and had to surface to do so.
They mainly ate fish and squid.
At the beginning of the 19th century, Mary Anning and her brother found one of the first known skeletons.
In Holzmaden in Baden-Württemberg, especially many, often complete, ichthyosaurs were found in shale.

abschnitte.text: Ichthyosaurs had a spindle-shaped body, a long, narrow snout and many pointed teeth. Their legs had turned into **flippers**, and at the end of the body was an upright tail fin like a shark's. Many species also had a dorsal fin. Especially striking were their **very large eyes**, which in some species reached more than 20 centimetres across. The smallest species were about one metre long, the largest over 15 metres.

Although they lived at the same time, ichthyosaurs were **not dinosaurs**. Dinosaurs lived on land, whereas ichthyosaurs lived only in the sea. They were reptiles whose ancestors had returned from land to the water. Like whales and dolphins, they had to come to the surface to breathe, because they had **lungs** and not gills. The fact that ichthyosaurs and dolphins look similar despite completely different origins is called **convergent evolution**.

Ichthyosaurs were fast swimmers and hunters. They fed mainly on **fish and squid**. In fossilised stomach contents, tiny hooks from the tentacles of prehistoric squid have often been found. Their large eyes helped them to see prey even in dark, deep water. Unlike most reptiles, they did not lay eggs but gave birth to live young in the water.

The first ichthyosaurs appeared in the early **Triassic**, around 250 million years ago. They had their heyday in the Triassic and the Jurassic. In the Cretaceous they became rarer and died out about 90 million years ago. That was long before the great extinction of the dinosaurs. Why exactly they disappeared is not yet fully understood.

At the beginning of the 19th century, the English fossil collector **Mary Anning** and her brother Joseph found one of the first known ichthyosaur skeletons on the coast at Lyme Regis. In **Holzmaden** in Baden-Württemberg, especially many, often complete, skeletons were found in the Posidonia Shale from the Jurassic. Some even show the outline of the skin. There are finds in Switzerland too: on **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, ichthyosaurs from the Triassic were discovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cold-blooded vertebrate with scales, such as lizards, snakes and crocodiles.
A petrified remain or trace of a living thing from prehistoric times.
When unrelated animals develop in a similar way because of a similar way of life.
A geological period about 252 to 201 million years ago.

gewusst: The eyes of some ichthyosaurs were among the largest any animal has ever had.
At the Hauff Museum in Holzmaden you can admire numerous fossilised ichthyosaurs.
Mary Anning was still a child when the first ichthyosaur skeleton was found.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer and mathematician who lived from 1571 to 1630. He found out the rules by which the planets move around the Sun. His three laws of planetary motion still apply today and even help in steering space probes.
wichtigste: Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt in Württemberg.
From 1600 he worked in Prague as an assistant to the astronomer Tycho Brahe.
In 1601 he became imperial mathematician at the court in Prague.
From Brahe's observations of the orbit of Mars he derived Kepler's laws.
According to the second law, a planet is fastest when it is closest to the Sun.
He proposed a telescope made of two convex lenses, the Keplerian telescope.
A NASA space telescope that searched for planets around other stars bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Johannes Kepler was born on 27 December 1571 in **Weil der Stadt**. His family was poor, and as a child he was often ill. Because he was very gifted, he was allowed to attend monastery schools and study at the University of **Tübingen**. There he learned about the world view of Nicolaus Copernicus, according to which the Sun is at the centre. From 1594 he taught mathematics in Graz.

In 1600 Kepler moved to Prague and became an assistant to **Tycho Brahe**. Brahe had collected the most precise observations of the sky of his time, still without a telescope. When Brahe died in 1601, Kepler succeeded him as **imperial mathematician** to Emperor Rudolf II. This allowed him to continue analysing the valuable measurements.

For years Kepler worked on calculating the orbit of **Mars**, because it would not fit a circle. Finally he realised: the planets travel on **ellipses**, that is, oval orbits, with the Sun at one focus. The second law states that a planet is faster when it is near the Sun than when it is far from it. The first two laws appeared in 1609 in the book “Astronomia nova”, the third law in 1619. It links a planet's orbital period with its distance from the Sun.

Kepler also studied light and lenses. He explained how an image forms on the retina in the eye. In 1611 he described an **astronomical telescope** made of two convex lenses. Although it shows the image upside down, it gives a larger field of view. Almost all later lens telescopes for astronomy followed this principle.

Kepler's life was marked by war and religious disputes. From 1615 his mother Katharina was accused of **witchcraft**. Kepler defended her in court himself, and in 1621 she was released. He also wrote the story **“Somnium”**, which is about a journey to the Moon. Kepler died in Regensburg in 1630.

With Kepler's laws, planetary orbits could be calculated much more accurately than before. Isaac Newton later used **gravity** to explain why these laws hold. From 2009 NASA's **Kepler** space telescope searched for planets around other stars and discovered thousands of them. A lunar crater and an asteroid are also named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A closed, oval curve, like a stretched-out circle.
The path that one heavenly body travels around another.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and focuses light rays, like a magnifying glass.
A person who studies stars, planets and the universe.

gewusst: Kepler earned part of his living with horoscopes, even though he himself doubted astrology.
For the orbit of Mars, Kepler filled hundreds of pages with calculations, without any calculator.
Kepler is regarded as one of the first people to write a kind of science-fiction story about a journey to the Moon.

teile.einleitung: The CH2018 climate scenarios are a major report on how the climate in Switzerland could change by the end of the 21st century. It was produced mainly by MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich and published in November 2018. The scenarios show what would happen without climate protection and how much can be avoided with climate protection.
wichtigste: The CH2018 climate scenarios were produced under the lead of MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich.
Without climate protection, summers in Switzerland will become drier and hotter.
Heavy precipitation will become more frequent and more intense.
Winters will have less snow, with more rain instead of snow.
The freezing level will continue to rise.
The RCP8.5 scenario stands for a development without climate protection.
With consistent climate protection, a large part of the changes can be avoided.

abschnitte.text: **CH2018** is the name of the climate scenarios for Switzerland that were published in 2018. The lead was taken by **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, and **ETH Zurich**. Other universities and specialist bodies helped too. The results are intended for authorities, companies, farmers and the whole population.

A **scenario** is not a forecast but a possible development under certain assumptions. CH2018 mainly compares what happens if a lot or a little greenhouse gas is emitted worldwide. The **RCP8.5** scenario stands for a world without climate protection. Other scenarios such as RCP2.6 assume consistent climate protection. The calculations are based on many climate models.

Without climate protection, summers in Switzerland will become considerably **drier and hotter**. There will be less rain in summer, and the soil will dry out more. There will be many more **hot days**, that is, days with at least 30 °C. Especially in cities and low-lying areas such as Ticino, Geneva or Basel, the heat will become a burden for people and nature.

**Heavy precipitation** will become more frequent and more violent, which increases the risk of floods and debris flows. In winter, more precipitation will fall as rain instead of snow. The **freezing level** will continue to rise, and winters will have less snow. This affects ski resorts, but also the glaciers and the water supply in summer.

The scenarios clearly show that a large part of the changes can be avoided through consistent **climate protection**. The less greenhouse gas humanity emits, the smaller the warming. Switzerland has therefore set itself targets to reduce its emissions. At the same time, it must adapt to the changes that can no longer be prevented.

Since measurements began in the 19th century, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average. One reason is that land areas warm up faster than the oceans. The Alps, with their glaciers, snow and permafrost, react especially sensitively. That is why accurate climate scenarios for Switzerland are very important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A possible development in the future that is based on certain assumptions.
A day on which the maximum temperature reaches at least 30 °C.
The altitude above which the air temperature is below zero degrees.
A great deal of rain or snow in a short time.
A computer program that calculates the Earth's climate.

gewusst: Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average.
A scenario is not a weather forecast, but shows what could happen under certain conditions.
With more rain instead of snow in winter, the meltwater from the mountains is missing in summer.

teile.einleitung: An isotope is a version of a chemical element with a different number of neutrons in its atomic nucleus. Isotopes of the same element behave almost the same chemically, but they have different weights. Some are stable, others radioactive.
wichtigste: An isotope is a version of an element with a different number of neutrons.
The number of protons determines which element it is.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Isotopes are named by their mass number, for example carbon-14.
Some isotopes are stable, others decay radioactively.
Hydrogen has three natural isotopes: protium, deuterium and tritium.
Isotopes are used in medicine, research and nuclear power stations.

abschnitte.text: Every atom has a nucleus made of **protons** and **neutrons**. The number of protons determines which element it is; carbon, for example, always has 6 protons. But the number of neutrons can vary. Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called **isotopes**.

Protons and neutrons together give the **mass number**. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. That is why carbon-14 is slightly heavier. Chemically both behave almost the same, because the electron shell is built in the same way.

Normal hydrogen has only one proton and no neutron; it is called protium. **Deuterium** has an extra neutron and is also called heavy hydrogen. Water made with deuterium is called **heavy water**. The third isotope, tritium, has two neutrons and is radioactive.

Many isotopes are stable and never change. Others have too many or too few neutrons and decay over time. These are called **radioisotopes**. Uranium-235 is split in nuclear power stations, and carbon-14 is used to work out the age of finds.

The British chemist **Frederick Soddy** coined the term isotope in 1913. The word comes from Greek and means “same place”, because isotopes stand in the same place in the **periodic table**. In medicine, weakly radioactive isotopes are injected to make organs visible. Researchers also use isotopes to work out where water, food or old bones come from.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A particle in the atomic nucleus with no electric charge.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atomic nucleus.
A table in which all the chemical elements are arranged.

gewusst: Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element.
In 1921 Frederick Soddy received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his research on isotopes.
Heavy water looks exactly like normal water, but it is about 10 per cent heavier.

teile.einleitung: The competitive exclusion principle is a rule from ecology. It states that two species with exactly the same requirements for food and habitat cannot live together in the same place in the long term. Over time the stronger species pushes out the weaker one.
wichtigste: Two species with exactly the same requirements cannot exist side by side in the long term.
After its discoverer, the principle is also called Gause's principle.
Georgy Gause demonstrated it in the 1930s with paramecia.
At its centre is competition between different species, interspecific competition.
Similar species can still live together through niche differentiation.
In 1961 Joseph Connell showed displacement in two species of barnacle in Scotland.
The paradox of the plankton seems to contradict the principle.

abschnitte.text: Every species has an **ecological niche**, that is, a particular way of living: what it eats, where it lives and when it is active. If two species want exactly the same scarce things, **interspecific competition** arises, competition between different species. The competitive exclusion principle says that one species will then push out the other in the long run. The American ecologist Garrett Hardin summed it up briefly in 1960: complete competitors cannot coexist.

In the 1930s the Russian biologist **Georgy Gause** grew two species of **paramecia** in glass vessels. Each species on its own grew well. When he kept both in the same vessel with the same food, only one species survived after a while. That is why the rule is also called **Gause's principle**.

In 1961 the ecologist **Joseph Connell** studied two species of barnacle on the Scottish coast. One species lived high up in the tidal zone, the other further down. When he removed the lower species, the upper one could also grow further down. So the stronger species pushed the other out of the lower zone, while the weaker one survived higher up because it copes better with drying out.

In nature, many similar species often live in the same area. This works because they divide up their niches; this is called **niche differentiation**. Here, for example, different species of tit look for their food in different parts of the trees. Where two related species occur together, they sometimes differ more than elsewhere, for example in the shape of their beak; this is called **character displacement**.

In 1961 the ecologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson puzzled over the plankton in lakes and seas. A great many species of algae live together in the water there, although almost all of them need the same things: light and a few nutrients. This **paradox of the plankton** seems to contradict the principle. One possible explanation is that conditions in the water are constantly changing, so that no species has an advantage for long enough to push out all the others.

The principle helps to understand why introduced species can push out native ones. In Great Britain and northern Italy, for example, the **grey squirrel** brought in from North America has pushed out the native red squirrel in many places. Conservation experts therefore watch closely whether such species are also spreading in Switzerland. The principle is also an important basis for research on biodiversity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the relationships of living things with each other and with their environment.
The particular way of life of a species: food, habitat and time of activity.
Competition between different species for the same scarce things.
When similar species use food or habitat in different ways.
Tiny living things that float in the water and are carried by the current.

gewusst: Gause did his famous experiments as a young researcher in Moscow, in his early twenties.
Darwin's finches on the Galápagos Islands are considered a prime example of how related species share out their food.
A single drop of lake water can contain dozens of different species of algae.

teile.einleitung: The La Tène culture is the culture of the Celts in the later Iron Age, from about 450 BC until Roman times. It is named after a site on Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland. It is known for skilfully made jewellery, weapons and the first towns north of the Alps.
wichtigste: The La Tène culture lasted from about 450 BC until Roman times.
Before it came the Hallstatt culture of the earlier Iron Age.
The name comes from the site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel.
A typical feature is an art style with curving tendrils and spirals.
In the late La Tène period, the Celts built fortified, town-like settlements, the oppida.
The priests and scholars of the Celts were called druids.
The first Celtic gold coins imitated gold staters of Philip II of Macedon.
The name Yverdon-les-Bains goes back to the Celtic word “dunum”.

abschnitte.text: The La Tène culture followed the **Hallstatt culture** of the earlier Iron Age around 450 BC. It was widespread across large parts of Europe, from France through Switzerland and southern Germany to Bohemia and Hungary. It was carried by Celtic peoples, in the area of present-day Switzerland above all the **Helvetii**. It ended when the Romans conquered these areas in the 1st century BC.

La Tène lies at the north-eastern end of **Lake Neuchâtel** near Marin in the canton of Neuchâtel. From 1857, hundreds of finds were discovered there in the shallow water, including swords, spearheads, shields, brooches and tools. When the Jura water correction later lowered the level of the lake, even more finds came to light. Because of this wealth of finds, the place gave its name to a whole era. Today the Laténium museum in Hauterive shows many of the finds.

Celtic craftsmen were masters at forging iron and working bronze and gold. Typical of the **La Tène style** are curving tendrils, spirals, swirls and intertwined faces of animals and people. It is found on neck rings, the **torcs**, on clothing brooches and sword sheaths. The Celts also invented new things, such as coloured glass bracelets and iron tyres for cart wheels.

In the late La Tène period, large fortified settlements called **oppida** were built. They had mighty walls, craftsmen's quarters and markets. In Switzerland there were such places, for example, on the Enge peninsula in Bern and on Mont Vully. At the same time the Celts began to mint coins, using gold staters of Philip II of Macedon as a model. There were also cast **potin coins** made of copper, tin and lead.

Celtic society consisted of tribes with nobles, warriors, farmers and craftsmen. The **druids**, who were priests, judges and scholars, had a special position. They passed on their knowledge by word of mouth, which is why there are hardly any writings by the Celts themselves. We know a lot from the reports of Roman and Greek authors, for example Julius Caesar. Offerings were often placed in lakes, rivers and bogs, perhaps also at La Tène.

In 58 BC the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to Gaul but were defeated by Caesar near **Bibracte**. After that they came under Roman rule. Celtic traces live on in many place names: Yverdon goes back to Eburodunum, with the word “dunum” for a fortified place. The names Thun, Solothurn and Winterthur also have Celtic roots. The Latin name for Switzerland, Helvetia, is also a reminder of the Helvetii.

begriffe.erklaerung: A period in which people made tools and weapons mainly from iron.
A group of related peoples who lived in large parts of Europe during the Iron Age.
A large, fortified Celtic settlement; the plural is oppida.
A Celtic priest, judge and scholar.
A heavy, often decorated Celtic neck ring.

gewusst: Some of the finds from La Tène only came to light because the Jura water correction lowered Lake Neuchâtel by several metres.
The word “La Tène” is also used as a technical term for the whole later Iron Age in central Europe.
The Celts wore trousers, which the Romans, who wore tunics, found strange.

teile.einleitung: Lateralisation means that the two halves of the brain are specialised in some tasks. In most people, language sits mainly on the left, while recognising faces happens more on the right. Even so, the two halves almost always work closely together.
wichtigste: Lateralisation means that the halves of the brain are specialised in some tasks.
In the vast majority of right-handed people, the most important language centres are in the left half of the brain.
When recognising faces, the right half of the brain is usually more involved.
About 90 per cent of people prefer their right hand.
Roger Sperry received the Nobel Prize in 1981 for research on people whose brain halves had been separated.
The idea of “left-brained” and “right-brained” people is a myth with no evidence.
Creative thinking uses both halves of the brain.

abschnitte.text: The cerebrum consists of two halves, the left and the right **hemisphere**. They look almost the same, but partly take on different tasks. This division of labour is called **lateralisation**, from the Latin word “latus” for side. The two halves are connected by the **corpus callosum**, a thick bundle of about 200 million nerve fibres.

Each half of the brain mainly controls the opposite side of the body. So the left half moves the right hand, and the right half moves the left hand. About 90 per cent of people are **right-handed**, and about 10 per cent are left-handed. Being left-handed is completely normal, and today children in Switzerland no longer have to switch to their right hand.

abschnitte.titel: Language on the left, faces on the right
abschnitte.text: In 1861 the French doctor **Paul Broca** discovered that damage to an area in the left half of the brain disturbs speech. This area is now called Broca's area. A few years later Carl Wernicke described another language centre, also on the left. In the vast majority of right-handers, and in many left-handers too, language is mainly on the left. When recognising faces and perceiving space, on the other hand, the right half is usually more involved.

In some people with severe **epilepsy**, doctors cut through the corpus callosum to ease the seizures. The seizures could then no longer spread from one half to the other. The American researcher **Roger Sperry** studied these so-called split-brain patients. He showed that each half has its own abilities, for example that only the left half could name an object. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1981.

abschnitte.titel: The myth of left and right
abschnitte.text: You often hear that there are logical “left-brained” and creative “right-brained” people. But there is no scientific evidence for this. Large studies with brain scans found no people who use one half clearly more than the other. Creative thinking, arithmetic and reading use both halves of the brain together. Lateralisation only concerns certain parts of tasks.

Lateralisation is not only found in humans. Many parrots prefer to grab food with one particular foot. In songbirds, control of the song is often mainly in one half of the brain. Researchers suspect that the division of labour makes the brain more **efficient**, because both halves do not have to do the same thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two halves of the cerebrum.
A broad bundle of nerve fibres that connects the two halves of the brain.
An area in the left half of the brain that is important for speaking.
An illness in which sudden seizures occur in the brain.
A condition in which the connection between the two halves of the brain has been cut.

gewusst: People with a cut corpus callosum usually seem completely normal in everyday life; the differences only show up in special tests.
In 1981 Roger Sperry shared the Nobel Prize with David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel, who researched vision.
Because the nerves cross over, an image that you see only on the left arrives first in the right half of the brain.

teile.einleitung: Ibn al-Haytham was an Arab scholar who lived around 1000 years ago. He studied light and vision and tested his ideas with experiments. In Europe he was known by the name Alhazen.
wichtigste: Ibn al-Haytham was born around 965 in Basra in what is now Iraq.
He spent most of his later life in Cairo.
In Europe he was known by the Latin name Alhazen.
His most famous work is the Book of Optics, which consists of seven books.
He showed that light falls from objects into the eye.
He described the camera obscura, which casts an upside-down image into a dark room.
Because he tested assumptions with experiments, he is regarded as a pioneer of modern science.

abschnitte.text: Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham was born around 965 in **Basra** and died around 1040 in **Cairo**. He lived in the so-called Golden Age of Islam, when scholars in cities such as Baghdad and Cairo collected and developed a great deal of knowledge. He wrote about mathematics, astronomy and above all about light. Altogether around a hundred writings are attributed to him.

A well-known story tells that he promised the caliph al-Hakim in Cairo to control the flooding of the **Nile**. When he realised that this was impossible with the means of his time, he is said to have pretended to be mad. He then lived in seclusion until the caliph died. During this time he is said to have carried out a large part of his research.

Many ancient scholars believed that the eyes send out rays of sight. Ibn al-Haytham showed that it is the other way round: **light** falls from objects into the eye. He investigated how light travels in straight lines, how it is reflected and how it is refracted. He collected these findings in the **Book of Optics** in seven parts.

Ibn al-Haytham described exactly what happens in a **camera obscura**. When light falls through a small hole into a dark room, an upside-down image of the outside world appears on the wall. He used this to show that light moves in straight lines. This principle is still found in every camera today.

His way of working was especially important. He did not simply rely on old books, but tested **assumptions** with careful **experiments** and precise observations. He also explained that the Moon only seems bigger on the horizon because our perception deceives us. That is why he is regarded as one of the pioneers of the scientific method.

Around 1200 the Book of Optics was translated into Latin and widely read in Europe. Scholars such as Roger Bacon and later Johannes Kepler built on his ideas. A crater on the Moon bears the name Alhazen. In the International Year of Light 2015, UNESCO commemorated his work on optics, which is around 1000 years old.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of light and vision.
A dark room or box with a small hole in which an upside-down image appears.
A deliberate test with which you check a guess.
The change in direction of light when it passes, for example, from air into water.

gewusst: The word camera comes from the Latin camera obscura, which means dark chamber.
Ibn al-Haytham is pictured on an Iraqi banknote.
You can test the Moon illusion that he explained yourself: seen through a tube, the Moon on the horizon suddenly looks smaller.

teile.einleitung: Louis Agassiz was a Swiss naturalist who studied fish, fossils and glaciers in the 19th century. He became famous for the ice age theory, according to which large parts of Europe once lay under ice. Later he worked in the USA, but today he is strongly criticised for his racist views.
wichtigste: Louis Agassiz was born in the canton of Fribourg in 1807.
From 1832 he was a professor in Neuchâtel.
In a large work on fossils he studied mainly fish.
He became famous for the ice age theory.
His research shelter, the “Hôtel des Neuchâtelois”, stood on the Unteraar Glacier.
With stakes in the ice he measured how fast a glacier moves.
In 1846 he emigrated to the USA.
Today he is strongly criticised for his racist views.

abschnitte.text: Jean Louis Rodolphe Agassiz was born in 1807 in Môtier on Lake Murten in the canton of **Fribourg**. His father was a pastor. Agassiz studied medicine and natural sciences in Zurich, Heidelberg and Munich. In Paris he learned from the famous naturalist Georges Cuvier, who inspired him to study fossils. From 1832 he taught as a professor in **Neuchâtel**.

Agassiz studied fossilised fish from all over Europe. In his large work on fossil fish he described hundreds of species that lived millions of years ago. For this he had the **fossils** drawn precisely and sorted them by their scales. The work appeared in several parts between 1833 and 1843. This made him famous among experts while he was still a young man.

Other Swiss researchers such as Ignaz Venetz and Jean de Charpentier had noticed that glaciers must once have been much bigger. Agassiz took up this idea and in 1837 presented the theory of a great **ice age**. In this way he explained the huge erratic boulders in the Central Plateau and the polished rocks in the Jura. On the **Unteraar Glacier** in the Bernese Oberland, he and his helpers built a simple hut, the “Hôtel des Neuchâtelois”. There he drove stakes into the ice and measured how fast the glacier moves.

In 1846 Agassiz travelled to the USA and stayed there for the rest of his life. He became a professor at Harvard University in Cambridge near Boston. There in 1859 he founded the **Museum of Comparative Zoology**, a large natural history museum. He was one of the best-known scientists in America and supported many young researchers. However, he rejected Charles Darwin's theory of evolution all his life. Agassiz died in Cambridge in 1873.

Agassiz held the false view that people of different origins are worth different amounts. He had photographs taken of enslaved people to support his opinion. Such **racist** ideas were later used to justify injustice. That is why in Switzerland there is discussion about whether places such as the Agassizhorn in the Bernese Alps should be renamed. His achievements in glacier research, however, are still considered important.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long period when it was much colder and glaciers covered wide areas.
A large stone that a glacier has carried far away from where it came from.
A trace or remain of a living thing from earlier times that has turned to stone.
The false opinion that people are worth less because of their origin or skin colour.

gewusst: In North America, a huge ice-age lake that disappeared long ago is named after Agassiz: Lake Agassiz.
The “Hôtel des Neuchâtelois” was not a real hotel but a shelter under a large boulder on the glacier.
Agassiz had his measuring stakes on the glacier observed for years and was able to show that the middle of a glacier flows faster than its edge.

teile.einleitung: A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without itself being changed or used up. Catalysts are found in cars, in factories and even in our own bodies. Without them, many important processes would happen far too slowly.
wichtigste: A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction.
It is not changed itself and is not used up.
Catalysts lower the energy that a reaction needs to get started.
In the body, enzymes act as catalysts, for example in digestion.
A car's catalytic converter makes poisonous exhaust gases less harmful.
The term was coined in 1835 by the Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius.
A large share of all industrial products is made with the help of catalysts.

abschnitte.text: A **catalyst** is a substance that makes a chemical reaction happen faster. At the end of the reaction it is there again unchanged and can be used again. That is why small amounts of it are often enough. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “dissolving”. The process is called **catalysis**.

For a reaction to start, it needs a push of energy, the **activation energy**. You can picture this as a hill that the substances first have to climb over. A catalyst, so to speak, builds a tunnel through this hill. This way the substances react faster or at a lower temperature. The catalyst briefly joins with the substances and then releases them again.

In the exhaust of many cars there is a **catalytic converter**, often just called a “cat”. It contains small amounts of the precious metals platinum, palladium and rhodium. These turn poisonous exhaust gases such as carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides into less harmful substances, such as carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen. In Switzerland, from 1987 strict exhaust rules applied to new petrol cars that could practically only be met with a catalytic converter. As a result the air in towns became much cleaner.

There are also catalysts in our bodies; they are called **enzymes**. Enzymes in saliva, for example, start breaking down starch from bread into sugar while it is still in the mouth. Without enzymes, digestion would take far too long. Enzymes from yeast also help in baking and brewing beer. In washing powders, enzymes remove stains of protein or fat.

In factories, catalysts are used to make substances faster and with less energy. A famous example is the **Haber-Bosch process**, in which ammonia for fertiliser is made with an iron catalyst. This fertiliser helps to grow food for billions of people. Plastics and medicines are also often made with catalysts. Because they save energy, they are also important for protecting the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which a catalyst speeds up a reaction.
The energy needed for a chemical reaction to begin at all.
A protein in living things that acts as a catalyst, for example in digestion.
A valuable metal such as gold or platinum that hardly rusts or reacts with other substances.

gewusst: Without enzymes, digesting a single meal would take a very, very long time.
A car's catalytic converter contains only a few grams of precious metal, but it is so valuable that thieves sometimes steal catalytic converters from parked cars.

teile.einleitung: A light-emitting diode, LED for short, is a tiny electronic component that gives off light when electricity flows through it. Today LEDs are found in lamps, mobile phones, televisions, bike lights and traffic lights. They are economical, long-lasting and have changed lighting all over the world.
wichtigste: An LED shines because of an effect called electroluminescence.
It consists of a semiconductor, a special material between a conductor and an insulator.
The first LEDs that shone visibly, from 1962, gave off red light.
Akasaki, Amano and Nakamura received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for the blue LED.
Only with the blue LED could efficient white LED light be produced.
In white LED lamps, a blue LED usually excites a yellow-glowing phosphor.
LEDs need much less electricity than light bulbs for the same brightness.

abschnitte.text: LED is the abbreviation for Light Emitting Diode. A **diode** is a component that lets electricity through in only one direction. The heart of the LED is a tiny crystal made of a **semiconductor**, which is often smaller than a grain of sand. It sits in a plastic casing that focuses the light.

In the semiconductor, two differently treated layers meet. When electricity flows, electric charges move to the boundary layer and join together there. Energy is released directly as light; this is called **electroluminescence**. The colour of the light depends on the material of the semiconductor. That is why there are red, green, yellow and blue LEDs.

abschnitte.titel: The story of the blue LED
abschnitte.text: In 1962 the American Nick Holonyak built the first LED that gave off visible red light. Yellow and green LEDs soon followed, but a bright blue LED could not be made for a long time. Only around 1990 did the Japanese researchers Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura succeed, using the material **gallium nitride**. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014. A blue-violet laser made of the same material also reads **Blu-ray discs** today.

White light is a mixture of many colours. In most white LED lamps, a blue LED shines onto a yellow **phosphor**. Part of the blue light is turned into yellow light, and together it looks white to our eyes. So without the blue LED there would be no economical LED lamps for homes and streets.

An old **light bulb** turns most of its energy into heat and only a small part into light. An LED lamp needs only about a fifth to a tenth of the electricity for the same brightness. It also lasts for many years. That is why traditional light bulbs were gradually taken off the market in Switzerland and the EU from 2009.

You can find LEDs in torches, car headlights, Christmas lights and traffic signals. Big screens in stadiums are made of thousands of coloured LEDs. Many mobile phones and televisions use **OLEDs**, a variant made of organic substances. The little indicator lights on devices are usually light-emitting diodes too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that conducts electricity only under certain conditions, for example silicon or gallium nitride.
An electronic component that lets electricity flow in only one direction.
The glowing of a material when an electric current flows through it.
A substance that takes in light of one colour and gives off light of another colour.

gewusst: Good LED lamps can shine for several tens of thousands of hours, which is many years with daily use.
LEDs hardly get hot when shining, so they can even be sewn into clothes.
Remote controls send their signals with an LED whose light is invisible to our eyes.

teile.einleitung: Lamarckism is an early theory about how living things develop. The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck believed that animals pass on to their offspring characteristics they acquire during their lives. Today we know that this is not true, but Lamarck was an important pioneer of research into evolution.
wichtigste: Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck came from France.
His main work “Philosophie zoologique” was published in 1809.
He believed that characteristics acquired during life are inherited.
According to Lamarck, organs that are used a lot become stronger, and this is inherited.
He explained the giraffe's long neck by constant stretching towards high leaves.
August Weismann disproved the idea, among other ways with mice whose tails he cut off.
Darwin, on the other hand, explained change through the selection of random differences.

abschnitte.text: **Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck** lived in France from 1744 to 1829. He was first a soldier, then a botanist and later a professor at the natural history museum in Paris. He studied above all animals without a backbone and introduced the term **invertebrates** for them. Lamarck was also one of the first to use the word biology.

Lamarck was convinced that living things change slowly and that species do not stay the same for ever. At the time this was a bold idea. As an example he gave the giraffe: its ancestors, he said, constantly stretched for high leaves, and so their necks became a little longer. They passed this small lengthening on to their young. Over many generations, he said, the long giraffe neck developed in this way.

Lamarck presented his ideas in 1809 in the book **Philosophie zoologique**. He had two basic ideas. First, organs that are used often become stronger, and those that are not needed waste away. Second, such **acquired characteristics** were supposed to be passed on to the offspring. Today this idea is called Lamarckism.

The German zoologist **August Weismann** tested the idea in the 1880s. He cut off the tails of mice over many generations. Even so, all the new mice were born with tails of normal length. In this way Weismann showed that changes to the body do not simply get into the genes. A person who does a lot of sport does not pass on their muscles to their children either.

In 1859 Charles Darwin published his theory of **natural selection**. According to Darwin, in every generation there are small random differences between living things. Giraffes with slightly longer necks found more food and survived more often. They passed on this characteristic, not because they had stretched, but because they were born with it. Darwin's explanation is considered correct today.

Lamarck was wrong about his idea of inheritance, but he was one of the first to put forward a complete theory of how species develop. Today **epigenetics** studies how environmental influences affect which genes are switched on or off. Some of these traces can be passed on to a limited extent. But that is something different from Lamarck's idea of the stretched giraffe neck.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gradual change of living things over many generations.
A feature that a living thing only gets during its life, such as strong muscles.
The passing on of features from parents to their offspring.
Animals without a backbone, such as insects, snails and worms.
Research into how genes are switched on and off by environmental influences.

gewusst: Lamarck died poor and almost blind; his achievements were only appreciated later.
Darwin, too, still thought the inheritance of acquired characteristics was possible.
The term invertebrates, which Lamarck coined, covers about 95 per cent of all animal species.

teile.einleitung: Johannes Gutenberg was a goldsmith and inventor from Mainz in Germany. Around 1450 he invented printing with movable metal type. This meant that books could be produced much faster and more cheaply, which changed the world.
wichtigste: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type.
He was born in Mainz around 1400 and died in 1468.
His type consisted of individual metal letters that could be put together again and again.
He also developed a casting instrument, a special printing ink and a printing press.
His most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible from the mid-1450s.
Printing spread knowledge quickly throughout Europe.
In Switzerland, Basel soon became an important printing city.

abschnitte.text: Johannes Gensfleisch zum Gutenberg was born in **Mainz** around 1400. His exact year of birth is not known. He worked with metals and knew all about casting. For a time he lived in **Strasbourg** before returning to Mainz, where he died in 1468.

Before Gutenberg, monks copied books laboriously by hand. Gutenberg cast individual letters out of metal, the **type**. These were put together into words and pages, printed, and could then be reused for new pages. With a **hand mould** he produced the type quickly and all at the same height.

For printing, Gutenberg used a **printing press**, similar to a wine press. He mixed an oil-based printing ink that stuck well to the metal letters. The type was made of a mixture of lead, tin and antimony. It was the combination of all these inventions that made his success.

His main work is the **Gutenberg Bible**, printed in the mid-1450s. It has about 1280 pages in Latin. Around 180 copies were made, some on parchment, most on paper. Today 49 copies survive in whole or in part, and they are among the most valuable books in the world.

Printing spread rapidly throughout Europe. In Switzerland, **Basel** soon became a centre of printing, where the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam also had books printed. Through printed writings, the ideas of the **Reformation** and new knowledge spread much faster. Many experts regard printing as one of the most important inventions of the second millennium.

begriffe.erklaerung: Individual cast metal letters for printing.
A machine that presses paper firmly onto the inked letters.
A writing material made from specially prepared animal skin.
A book printed in the first decades of printing, before 1501.

gewusst: Long before Gutenberg there was already movable type in China and Korea, for example made of clay or metal.
In Mainz there is a Gutenberg Museum where you can see original pages of his Bible.
There is no picture of Gutenberg from his own time; all portraits were made up later.

teile.einleitung: The cerebellum is a part of the brain that lies at the back of the head below the cerebrum. It makes sure that our movements are smooth and precise and that we keep our balance. Although it is small, it contains more than half of all the nerve cells in the brain.
wichtigste: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement and balance.
It lies at the back of the head below the cerebrum.
Its Latin name, cerebellum, means “little brain”.
The cerebellum contains more than half of all the nerve cells in the brain.
It is especially involved when practising movements such as cycling.
Alcohol disturbs the cerebellum, which is why drunk people often walk unsteadily.
The large, branched nerve cells of the cerebellar cortex are called Purkinje cells.

abschnitte.text: The **cerebellum**, Latin for “little brain”, lies at the back of the head below the cerebrum and behind the brainstem. It makes up only about a tenth of the size of the brain. It consists of two halves, joined by a narrow middle part called the vermis, or worm. Its surface is folded into many fine folds that look like the leaves of a tree.

The cerebellum **coordinates** movements. It constantly compares what we want to do with what our muscles are actually doing, and corrects small mistakes. To do this it receives messages from the muscles, joints, eyes and the organ of balance in the ear. This lets us catch a ball, stand on one leg or lift a cup to our mouth without thinking.

The cerebellum is especially important when we **practise** new movements, for example cycling, skiing or playing the piano. At first the movements are wobbly and need a lot of attention. With practice, the cerebellum stores the right sequences. At some point they happen almost automatically.

Although the cerebellum is small, it contains more than half of all the **nerve cells** in the brain. The vast majority of them are tiny granule cells. Especially striking are the large, highly branched **Purkinje cells**. They are named after the Czech researcher Jan Evangelista Purkyně, who described them in the 19th century.

If the cerebellum is injured or diseased, movements become unsteady, imprecise and shaky; this is called **ataxia**. Those affected sway as they walk and often miss when reaching for things. Alcohol also disturbs the cerebellum, which is why drunk people walk unsteadily. Doctors test the cerebellum, for example, with the finger-to-nose test, in which you have to touch the tip of your nose with your eyes closed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cell that passes on and processes electrical signals in the body.
The precise interplay of many muscles in a movement.
An organ in the inner ear that reports how the head is positioned and moving.
A disorder in which movements become unsteady and imprecise.

gewusst: A Purkinje cell can be connected to more than a hundred thousand other nerve cells.
You cannot tickle yourself, partly because the cerebellum calculates your own movement in advance.
A cut through the cerebellum shows a tree-like pattern called the tree of life.

teile.einleitung: The psychology of learning is a part of psychology that studies how people and animals learn. It asks, for example, why we forget things and which learning methods really help. Many of its findings can be used directly when learning for school.
wichtigste: The psychology of learning studies how learning works and what helps it.
In 1885 Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
You forget the most shortly after learning.
Spaced repetition over several days is usually more effective than learning everything at once.
Testing yourself helps more than simply reading through several times.
In operant conditioning, you learn through rewards and punishments for behaviour.
With the Bobo doll, Albert Bandura showed that children learn by watching.

abschnitte.text: For his experiments, the German researcher **Hermann Ebbinghaus** learned lists of meaningless syllables by heart. Then he tested how much he still knew after hours and days. In 1885 he described the **forgetting curve**: you forget the most shortly after learning, and later forgetting slows down. If you repeat something before it is completely gone, you keep it much longer.

Around 1900 the Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov discovered that dogs produced saliva at the mere sound of a signal if food always came afterwards. This is called **classical conditioning**: one stimulus becomes linked with another. People learn like this too, for example when you already get an uneasy feeling at the sound of the dentist's drill. Such links often form without any intention.

Edward Thorndike put cats in **puzzle boxes**, from which they had to find a way out by trial and error. They got faster with each attempt, because successful behaviour was reinforced. Burrhus F. Skinner studied learning in rats and pigeons in his **Skinner box**, where they were given food for particular actions. Learning through reward and punishment is called **operant conditioning**.

In the 1960s Albert Bandura showed children a film in which an adult hit an inflatable **Bobo doll**. Afterwards many children treated the doll in exactly the same way. This shows that children learn by **watching** and copying. That is why role models in the family, at school and in the media are so important.

The Austrian researcher **Konrad Lorenz** studied greylag geese. Freshly hatched goslings follow the first moving creature they see, and with his geese that was Lorenz himself. This special form of learning within a short time span is called **imprinting**. In 1973 Lorenz received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with two colleagues.

Spreading learning over several days is usually more effective than cramming everything the evening before the test. Testing yourself, for example with **flashcards**, helps more than reading the text through several times. Enough sleep is important, because the brain strengthens what you have learned while you sleep. The Swiss researcher **Jean Piaget** from Neuchâtel also showed that children think and learn in different ways at different ages.

begriffe.erklaerung: Learning by linking stimuli or through the consequences of behaviour.
A curve that shows how quickly you forget what you have learned without repetition.
Rapid learning during a short, special phase of life, for example in goslings.
Learning by watching and copying others.
Repeating material in several short sessions spread over days.

gewusst: In his famous memory experiments, Ebbinghaus was both the researcher and the only test subject.
Skinner taught pigeons to play games similar to table tennis.
If you explain what you have learned to someone else, you often understand and remember it better.

teile.einleitung: A jet stream is a narrow band of very strong wind high up in the atmosphere. It blows at a height of around 8 to 12 kilometres and can reach speeds of several hundred kilometres per hour. It is very important for our weather in Europe and for air traffic.
wichtigste: Jet streams are bands of strong wind at great heights.
The polar front jet stream blows at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres.
In the mid-latitudes it blows mainly from west to east.
It arises from the temperature difference between cold polar air and warm subtropical air.
The polar front jet stream has the strongest influence on the weather in Central Europe.
Aircraft flying east use it as a tailwind.
It became known through pilots in the Second World War who encountered very strong headwinds.

abschnitte.text: A jet stream is a **band of strong wind** that winds its way around the Earth like a long, snaking river of air. It is often several thousand kilometres long, but only a few hundred kilometres wide and a few kilometres thick. The wind speed is often over 200 kilometres per hour. It blows just below the **tropopause**, the boundary between the lowest layer of air and the layer above it.

At the equator it is warm, at the poles cold. Where cold polar air and warm subtropical air meet, there is a large **temperature contrast**. This creates strong pressure differences at height, and therefore wind. Because the Earth is rotating, the wind is deflected and so blows from **west to east**.

In each hemisphere there are two important jet streams. The **polar front jet stream** blows in the mid-latitudes at a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres. The subtropical jet stream lies closer to the equator and somewhat higher still. In winter, when the temperature difference is greatest, the jet streams are usually at their strongest.

The polar front jet stream does not run straight but in large waves. Under it, **low-pressure areas** form, which bring rain and wind to Europe. If it bends strongly and stays put, the same weather can last for weeks. Such a blocking situation, in which it curves around a high like the Greek letter omega, is called an **omega block**; it can bring heatwaves or long periods of rain.

In the Second World War, pilots of long-range bombers flying at high altitude encountered surprisingly strong headwinds, and this is how the jet stream became known. Today airlines plan their routes so that they make use of it. A flight from New York to Zurich therefore often takes less time than in the opposite direction, because the jet stream provides a **tailwind**. This saves time and fuel, but it can also cause turbulence.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
The boundary between the lowest layer of air, where the weather happens, and the layer above it.
An area of low air pressure that often brings clouds and rain.
A weather situation in which a high stays in one place for a long time because the jet stream curves around it.
Unsettled, swirling air that shakes an aircraft about.

gewusst: As early as the 1920s, the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi used weather balloons to measure very strong high-altitude winds over Japan.
Thanks to the jet stream, an aircraft over the Atlantic can be more than an hour faster than in the opposite direction.
The jet stream is invisible to the eye, but sometimes long, fast-moving bands of cloud give it away.

teile.einleitung: Karl Popper was an Austrian-British philosopher who lived from 1902 to 1994. He asked how science actually works and when a theory is scientific. His answer was: a good theory must be testable against reality and could, in principle, be refuted.
wichtigste: Karl Popper was born in Vienna in 1902.
His work “The Logic of Scientific Discovery” from 1934 founded his philosophy of science.
His position is called critical rationalism: all knowledge is provisional and grows through criticism.
In 1937 he emigrated to New Zealand to escape National Socialism.
In 1945 “The Open Society and Its Enemies” appeared.
From 1946 he taught at the London School of Economics.
In 1965 he was knighted in Great Britain.

abschnitte.text: Karl Raimund Popper was born on 28 July 1902 in **Vienna**. At first he worked as an apprentice cabinet-maker and as a social worker with children. Later he studied mathematics, physics and psychology and became a teacher. In 1934 his first great book, **“The Logic of Scientific Discovery”**, appeared. Because his family was of Jewish origin, he was in increasing danger in Austria.

In 1937 Popper fled from **National Socialism** to **New Zealand**, where he taught philosophy at a college in Christchurch. There he wrote two important books during the Second World War. In 1946 he moved to England and taught at the **London School of Economics** until he retired. In 1965 he was knighted and could call himself Sir Karl Popper. He died in London in 1994.

Popper believed that a general theory can never be finally proved. A famous example: even after a thousand white swans, you do not know for certain that all swans are white. But a single black swan refutes the statement at once. A scientific theory must therefore be worded in such a way that it could be **refuted**. This idea is called **falsification**.

Popper's philosophy is called **critical rationalism**. According to it, all knowledge is only provisional. We learn by putting forward bold guesses and then testing them strictly. Mistakes are not a bad thing, but the path to progress. With his **three worlds theory** he distinguished between the physical world, the world of consciousness and the world of mental contents such as theories and stories.

In **“The Open Society and Its Enemies”** from 1945, Popper defended democracy. In an open society, people may criticise, and governments can be voted out peacefully. In **“The Poverty of Historicism”** he criticised the idea that history follows fixed laws that can be predicted. He thought such ideas were dangerous because they could be used to justify dictatorships.

begriffe.erklaerung: Refuting a claim through an observation that contradicts it.
A branch of philosophy that asks how science works.
Leaving your own country, often because of persecution.
A guess that you test with observations or experiments.

gewusst: Popper had also trained as a cabinet-maker.
His idea of the open society later even gave foundations and organisations their names.

teile.einleitung: Lise Meitner was an Austrian physicist who was born in Vienna in 1878. Together with her nephew Otto Robert Frisch, she was the first to explain what happens in nuclear fission. Although she was one of the most important researchers of her time, she did not receive a Nobel Prize for it.
wichtigste: Lise Meitner was born in Vienna in 1878 and died in Cambridge in England in 1968.
For about 30 years she worked in Berlin with the chemist Otto Hahn.
Around 1917/18 Meitner and Hahn discovered the element protactinium.
In 1938 she fled from the Nazis to Sweden.
In 1938/39 she explained nuclear fission with Otto Robert Frisch.
She was left out of the Nobel Prize for the discovery of nuclear fission.
The element meitnerium was named in her honour.

abschnitte.text: Lise Meitner grew up in a large family in **Vienna**. At that time girls in Austria were not yet allowed to go to grammar school, so she prepared privately for the school-leaving exam. In 1906 she became one of the first women to complete a doctorate in **physics** at the University of Vienna. A year later she moved to Berlin to continue her research there.

In Berlin, Meitner began working with the chemist **Otto Hahn**, a partnership that lasted about 30 years. At the beginning, as a woman, she was only allowed to enter the laboratories through a side entrance and worked in a converted carpentry workshop. Around 1917/18 the two discovered the element **protactinium**. In 1926 Meitner became a professor in Berlin, the first woman in Germany in the subject of physics.

Lise Meitner came from a Jewish family. After Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938, she was in great danger. With the help of friends she fled via the Netherlands to **Sweden** in the summer of 1938. In Stockholm she continued to work, but had far fewer opportunities than in Berlin.

At the end of 1938, in experiments with uranium in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann surprisingly found the much lighter element barium. Hahn wrote to Meitner about it because he could not explain it. On a walk in the snow, Meitner and her nephew **Otto Robert Frisch** realised that the uranium nucleus had broken into two parts. They also calculated the huge energy released in the process and called it **nuclear fission**.

In 1945 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of nuclear fission went to Otto Hahn alone; Lise Meitner was not included. Today this is considered a great injustice. She refused to work on building the **atomic bomb** because she did not want to build weapons. Albert Einstein is said to have once called her “our Madame Curie”. Since 1997 the chemical element 109 has borne her name: **meitnerium**.

Lise Meitner is an important role model for women in science. Many schools, streets and prizes are named after her. Her gravestone in England says, in essence, that she was a physicist who never lost her humanity. Her explanation of nuclear fission is still the basis for nuclear power stations today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus into two smaller nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy.
The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
A radioactive chemical element that Meitner and Hahn discovered.
An artificially made element with the atomic number 109, named after Lise Meitner.

gewusst: Lise Meitner was nominated for a Nobel Prize almost 50 times but never received one.
Meitner and Frisch had the decisive idea about nuclear fission while sitting on a tree trunk during a winter walk.
Meitnerium is one of only a few chemical elements named after a woman.

teile.einleitung: An air conditioner is a device that cools the air in a room, dries it and often cleans it too. It works like a fridge in reverse: it takes the heat out of the room and gives it off outside. One of the first modern air conditioning systems was built by the American engineer Willis Carrier in 1902.
wichtigste: In 1902 Willis Carrier developed one of the first modern air conditioning systems.
An air conditioner carries heat from the room to the outside.
For this it needs a unit outside the room.
It needs electricity, because heat does not flow by itself from cold to warm.
The water that drips from an air conditioner comes from the humidity in the air.
A reversible air conditioner can heat as a heat pump in winter.
In a split unit, pipes containing refrigerant connect the indoor and outdoor units.

abschnitte.text: The American engineer **Willis Carrier** developed one of the first modern air conditioning systems in 1902. He built it for a printing works in New York, because damp summer air made the paper wavy. His system was meant above all to control the **humidity**. Soon air conditioning was also being used in factories, cinemas and offices.

In an air conditioner, a **refrigerant** flows in a closed circuit. In the indoor unit it evaporates and takes in heat from the room air. A compressor squeezes the vapour together, making it hot. In the outdoor unit the refrigerant gives off the heat to the outside air and becomes liquid again. Because heat does not flow by itself from cold to warm, the compressor needs electrical energy.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the water come from?
abschnitte.text: When the air conditioner cools the air, the air can hold less water vapour. Part of the **humidity** turns into water droplets, similar to what happens on a cold bottle in summer. This water drips out of the unit or is drained away through a hose. That is why the air conditioning in a car also helps against misted-up windows: it dries the air.

Many modern units can reverse the circuit. They then work as a **heat pump** and bring heat from the outside air into the house in winter. In a **split unit**, the indoor and outdoor units are separate and connected by pipes containing refrigerant. You can often hear the outdoor unit with its fan humming.

Compared with countries further south, only a few homes in Switzerland have air conditioning. Because summers are getting hotter, however, it is being bought more often. Air conditioners use a lot of electricity, and some refrigerants harm the climate if they escape. In many cantons a permit is needed for permanently installed units.

You can often keep a flat cool even without air conditioning. During the day, close the windows and **blinds** so that the sun does not shine in. At night and early in the morning, air the rooms thoroughly when the air outside is cooler. A fan moves the air so that you feel cooler, and it uses much less electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that takes in and gives off heat in cooling appliances.
A machine that squeezes a gas together.
A device that moves heat from a cooler place to a warmer one in order to heat.
The amount of water vapour in the air.

gewusst: The first modern air conditioning system was not meant to cool people, but to protect paper in a printing works.
A fridge and an air conditioner work on the same principle.
The heat that an air conditioner takes out of a room ends up outside and makes the air there a little warmer still.

teile.einleitung: Plastic recycling means collecting used plastics such as PET bottles and making new material from them. This saves oil and energy, and less plastic ends up in the environment. Switzerland is especially successful at collecting PET bottles.
wichtigste: In plastic recycling, plastic waste is turned back into a raw material.
PET stands for polyethylene terephthalate and has the number 1 in the recycling code.
According to the FOEN, about 85 per cent of PET drinks bottles in Switzerland were recycled (as of 2024).
Modern sorting plants recognise the type of plastic with near-infrared light.
PET bottles are shredded into small pieces called flakes.
In chemical recycling, plastics are broken down into their basic building blocks.
In energy recovery, plastic is burned and the energy is used.

abschnitte.text: Plastics are mostly made from **crude oil** and last a very long time. That is exactly the problem, because plastic thrown away in nature only breaks down after decades or even centuries. In **recycling**, used plastics are collected, sorted and processed into new material. According to the OECD, only a small part of plastic waste worldwide is recycled, about 9 per cent (as of 2019).

Not all plastic is the same. An international **recycling code** in a small triangle shows which type it is. Number 1 stands for PET, 2 for hard polyethylene (HDPE), 5 for polypropylene (PP) and 6 for polystyrene (PS). Plastics of a single type are much easier to recycle than a mixture, which is why **sorting** is so important.

Modern sorting plants shine **near-infrared light** on the waste on a conveyor belt. Each type of plastic reflects the light a little differently, and small air jets blow the pieces into the right container. PET bottles are then washed and shredded into small pieces, the **flakes**. These are melted and made into pellets or directly into new bottles.

In **mechanical recycling**, the plastic stays as it is and is only reshaped. If this produces a product of lower quality, it is called **downcycling**, for example when bottles become fibres for fleece jumpers. In **chemical recycling**, plastics are broken down into their basic building blocks, from which new plastic can be made. What cannot be recycled is burned in waste incineration plants in Switzerland, and the energy is used as electricity and district heating.

In Switzerland there are collection bins for PET bottles at almost every railway station and in many shops. The organisation PET-Recycling Schweiz organises the collection, paid for by a small advance recycling fee when you buy a bottle. Many bottles are made back into new drinks bottles, which is called **bottle-to-bottle**. Many municipalities now also have collection bags for mixed household plastics, which you have to pay for.

It is best to put bottles into the PET collection empty and with their lids on. Other plastic bottles, for example for shampoo or cooking oil, do not belong in the PET collection but in the plastics collection or the rubbish. Even better than recycling is **avoiding waste**, for example by using a reusable water bottle. Reusable bags instead of single-use bags also help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Polyethylene terephthalate, a clear, light plastic used for drinks bottles.
Small pieces of shredded PET bottles.
Recycling that produces a product of lower quality.
A number in a triangle that shows the type of plastic.
Burning waste in order to use the energy.

gewusst: Fibres from several recycled PET bottles can be used for one fleece jumper.
Recycled PET needs much less energy than new PET made from crude oil.
The recycling triangle with its number only tells you which plastic it is, not whether it is really recycled.

teile.einleitung: Mental arithmetic means calculating only in your head, without a calculator, paper or fingers. It helps when shopping, when estimating and everywhere in everyday life. With a few simple tricks, mental arithmetic gets faster and is even fun.
wichtigste: In mental arithmetic you calculate only in your head, without any aids.
7 plus 8 makes 15, and 15 minus 6 makes 9.
48 divided by 6 makes 8.
You can easily add nine by adding 10 and then taking away 1.
Double 35 is 70, and half of 90 is 45.
Four pieces of chewing gum at 50 centimes each cost 2 francs altogether.
Regular practice makes mental arithmetic faster and more reliable.

abschnitte.text: In **mental arithmetic** you solve sums using only your memory. For this you need to know the **times tables** and the additions up to 20 by heart. Bigger sums are broken down into small, simple steps. In Switzerland children practise mental arithmetic from the first year of school. It also trains memory and concentration.

For 7 plus 8 you can first fill up to 10: 7 plus 3 makes 10, then add 5 more, which makes 15. The easiest way to add nine is to do **plus 10** and then take away 1. For 100 minus 37 you first do 100 minus 30, which makes 70, then minus 7 more, which makes 63. And 15 minus 6 is 9, because 9 plus 6 makes 15 again. In this way you can check every subtraction with an **addition**.

For multiplying and dividing, the **times tables** are especially important. 48 divided by 6 is 8, because 6 times 8 makes exactly 48. 25 plus 25 plus 25 is the same as 3 times 25, so 75. When **doubling**, you work out the tens and units separately: double 35 is 60 plus 10, so 70. **Halving** works the other way round: half of 90 is 45.

When shopping, mental arithmetic helps you add up prices and check your change. A piece of chewing gum costs 50 centimes, two cost 1 franc, so four cost **2 francs**. You also work out how much time is left before a train leaves. Often a **rough estimate** with round numbers is enough. That way you quickly notice whether a result can be right.

In the past there were no calculators, so mental arithmetic was very important for traders and craftsmen. Aids such as the **abacus** or counting boards were used centuries ago. Today there are even world championships in mental arithmetic. There the best calculators solve huge problems in an astonishingly short time. Many of them practised on the abacus as children.

begriffe.erklaerung: The multiplications of the numbers from 1 to 10, which you learn by heart.
A rough calculation with rounded numbers to estimate a result.
Adding a number to itself, that is, multiplying by 2.
A counting frame with beads that can be moved.

gewusst: People who have practised on the abacus often picture the frame in their head when doing mental arithmetic and move the beads in their thoughts.
With the trick “plus 10, minus 1” you can also quickly add 19, 29 or 99.

teile.einleitung: Cooking means preparing food with heat, usually in hot water or steam. A lot of physics and chemistry happens in the process: water evaporates, pasta swells and proteins change. If you understand what happens in the saucepan, you can save energy and cook more safely.
wichtigste: At sea level, water boils at about 100 °C.
On a high mountain, water boils at a lower temperature.
The large bubbles in boiling water consist of water vapour.
The white cloud above the pan consists of tiny water droplets.
With a lid, the water boils faster.
In a pressure cooker it gets hotter than usual, so the food cooks faster.
For safety reasons, you turn the handle of a pan inwards.

abschnitte.text: When you heat water, its particles move faster and faster. At about 100 °C, **steam bubbles** form at the bottom, rise and burst at the surface. These bubbles are not air but **water vapour**, that is, water in the form of a gas. The white cloud above the pan is vapour that has already cooled again, made of tiny **water droplets**. Real water vapour is in fact invisible.

The **boiling point** of water depends on air pressure. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there at a lower temperature. On the Jungfraujoch, at around 3500 metres, it boils at about 88 °C. That is why pasta or eggs take longer to cook in a mountain hut.

A **lid** on the pan keeps in heat and steam, so the water boils faster and you save energy. For water for tea, a **kettle** is the most economical, because it heats the water directly. In a **pressure cooker** the pressure rises, and the water gets considerably hotter than 100 °C. That is why potatoes or beans become soft much faster in it.

Food changes when it is cooked. **Pasta** and rice absorb water and become soft as a result. Egg white becomes firm when heated, as you can see with a boiled egg. When frying in a pan, high heat produces browning and fine roasted flavours, for example with rösti. Heat also kills many germs and makes some foods digestible in the first place.

Pan handles are often made of **plastic** or wood, because these materials conduct heat poorly and hardly get hot. You turn the handle of a pan inwards so that nobody catches on it and hot food falls down. You must never put out burning oil with water; instead you cover the pan with a lid. Children should always cook at the stove together with adults.

People have been cooking their food over **fire** for a very long time. Cooked food is easier to chew and digest. Later came clay pots, wood-fired stoves and finally gas and electric cookers. Today many Swiss households cook with an **induction hob**, which heats the pan directly by means of a magnetic field.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil.
Water in the form of a gas, which is invisible.
The weight of the air pressing down on everything from above.
A tightly sealed pan in which pressure builds up and the water gets hotter than 100 °C.

gewusst: On the summit of Mount Everest, water boils at only about 70 °C.
Salt in the cooking water raises the boiling point so little that you hardly notice it.

teile.einleitung: James Cook was a British captain and one of the most famous explorers of all time. On three great voyages in the 18th century he sailed through the Pacific and charted coasts so accurately that his maps were used for a long time. He went further into the cold south than anyone before him.
wichtigste: James Cook lived from 1728 to 1779 and came from England.
He was a captain in the British Navy and an outstanding map-maker.
He made three great voyages of discovery into the Pacific.
In 1770 he landed on the east coast of Australia.
He sailed around New Zealand and charted its coast precisely.
In 1773 he was the first to cross the Antarctic Circle with a ship.
With sauerkraut he protected his sailors from the disease scurvy.
In 1779 he was killed in Hawaii during a dispute with local people.

abschnitte.text: James Cook was born on 27 October 1728 in the village of **Marton** in northern England. His father was a farm labourer, and the family was not rich. As a teenager Cook worked on coal ships that sailed from the port of **Whitby**. There he learned seamanship, mathematics and navigation. In 1755 he joined the British Navy.
