In Canada, Cook surveyed the coasts around **Newfoundland** and the St Lawrence River. His maps were so accurate that the Navy took notice of him. He could use instruments to work out a ship's position at sea. That is why in 1768 he was given the task of leading a great research voyage.

With the ship **Endeavour**, Cook sailed to Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus across the Sun there in 1769. After that he sailed around New Zealand and showed that it consists of two large islands. In 1770 he reached the east coast of Australia and landed at **Botany Bay**. On board was the naturalist Joseph Banks, who collected many unknown plants.

On the second voyage, Cook searched with the ships **Resolution** and Adventure for a great southern continent. In January 1773 he became the first seafarer to cross the Antarctic Circle. But pack ice and icebergs blocked his way to Antarctica, which he never saw. He did, however, prove that there was no huge, habitable continent in the south.

From 1776 Cook searched for a sea route between the Pacific and the Atlantic north of America, the **Northwest Passage**. On the way, in 1778, he became the first European to reach the islands of **Hawaii**. In February 1779 a dispute broke out there over a stolen boat. Cook was killed on 14 February 1779 in Kealakekua Bay.

On long sea voyages in the past, many sailors fell ill with **scurvy** because they lacked vitamin C. Cook had his crew eat sauerkraut and fresh greens and made sure the ship was kept clean. As a result, far fewer sailors died of this disease on his voyages. Today Cook's voyages are also viewed critically, because for many peoples of the Pacific they marked the start of a difficult time under foreign rule.

begriffe.erklaerung: A disease caused by a lack of vitamin C, in which the gums bleed and wounds heal poorly.
An imaginary line on the Earth beyond which there is at least one day a year on which the sun does not set or does not rise.
Working out where a ship is and how it can reach its destination.
A specialist who draws maps and surveys coasts.

gewusst: The Cook Islands in the Pacific and Cook Strait between New Zealand's two main islands are named after James Cook.
On his second voyage Cook tested a new, very accurate ship's clock, with which a position at sea could be worked out much better.
In 1934 the house of Cook's parents was taken down in England and rebuilt in Melbourne in Australia.

teile.einleitung: Carbon nanotubes are tiny tubes made of carbon atoms that can be only about one nanometre thick. You can imagine them as a rolled-up layer of carbon just one atom thick. They are extremely strong, conduct heat very well and, depending on their structure, can conduct electricity.
wichtigste: The Japanese researcher Sumio Iijima made carbon nanotubes known worldwide in 1991.
He found them in the arc discharge between graphite electrodes.
Single-walled nanotubes have a diameter of around 1 nanometre.
Whether a tube conducts like a metal or is a semiconductor depends on the angle at which it is rolled up.
They have very high tensile strength combined with low density.
Today they are often made by chemical vapour deposition.
In industry they are used, for example, as an additive in composite materials for sports equipment.

abschnitte.text: **Carbon nanotubes** consist only of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons, like a honeycomb. A single such layer is called **graphene**. If you roll it into a tube, you get a nanotube. Single-walled tubes have a diameter of about one **nanometre**, which is around a hundred thousand times thinner than a hair. But they can be a thousand times longer than they are thick.

There are **single-walled** nanotubes, which consist of a single tube. In **multi-walled** nanotubes, several tubes sit inside one another like a telescope. The way the graphene lattice is rolled up is called **chirality**. This determines whether a tube conducts electricity like a metal or is a semiconductor.

Nanotubes have an enormously high **tensile strength**; they are much more tear-resistant than steel and very light at the same time. Along their axis they conduct heat better than almost any other material. Some conduct electricity excellently. This combination makes them exciting for many technical applications.

In 1991 **Sumio Iijima** of the Japanese company NEC was studying soot from an **arc discharge** between graphite electrodes. Under the electron microscope he discovered tiny tubes in it. His publication made nanotubes known worldwide. Similar structures had been observed earlier, but had hardly been noticed.

Today nanotubes are mostly made by **chemical vapour deposition**, in which gases containing carbon break down on hot metal particles. In industry they are used as an additive in **composite materials**, for example for bicycle frames, tennis rackets or hockey sticks. In batteries, too, they improve conductivity. Researchers are testing them for tiny transistors, sensors and transparent conductive layers.

Because nanotubes are so small, scientists are investigating carefully whether they can be harmful when breathed in. Long, stiff fibres could have a similar effect to asbestos, which is why strict **safety measures** apply in the laboratory. At the same time there are bold ideas for the future, such as a **space elevator** made of an extremely long nanotube cable. Whether something like this can ever be built is, however, very uncertain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A billionth of a metre, so unimaginably small.
A layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern, only one atom thick.
A substance that conducts electricity only under certain conditions, important for computer chips.
How hard you can pull on a material before it tears.

gewusst: Researchers found signs of nanotube-like structures in an old Damascus sabre blade.
One gram of nanotubes can have a surface area larger than a tennis court.

teile.einleitung: Germination is the moment when a young plant begins to grow from a seed. For this, the seed needs above all water, warmth and air. With simple experiments, for example with beans on cotton wool, you can watch germination at home.
wichtigste: During germination, a seedling grows out of a seed.
To germinate, a seed needs water, warmth and oxygen.
Beans on dry cotton wool do not germinate, but on damp cotton wool they do.
In a warm room, seeds germinate faster than in the fridge.
When germinating, the seed soaks up water and swells, and the seed coat bursts.
Light germinators need light, while many other seeds such as beans also germinate in the dark.
A germination test is used to check whether seeds can still germinate.

abschnitte.text: A seed contains a tiny **embryo plant** and a store of nutrients. It can stay in a kind of resting state for a long time without growing. During **germination** it wakes up: first the root grows out, then the shoot with the first leaves. These first leaves are called **seed leaves**; a bean has two of them, maize only one.

The most important thing is **water**. The dry seed soaks itself full and swells until the seed coat bursts, and only then do the life processes inside begin. It also needs **warmth**: beans in a warm room germinate much faster than in the fridge. Oxygen from the air is also needed, which is why seeds germinate poorly in very wet, airless soil.

Many seeds also germinate in the dark soil, for example beans. They have enough stored food to grow up to the surface. **Light germinators** such as basil, on the other hand, need light and should only be covered very thinly with soil. Dark germinators such as the pumpkin germinate better when they are pushed deeper into the soil.

Put beans on dry and on damp cotton wool in two dishes: only the damp ones germinate. If you put one damp dish in the fridge and one in a warm room, you can see how important warmth is. Gardeners carry out a **germination test**: for example, they put ten seeds on damp paper and count how many germinate. That way they know whether old seeds are still worth sowing.

abschnitte.titel: Seeds that survive for a very long time
abschnitte.text: Some seeds can still germinate after many years. In Israel, a tree was grown again from a **date palm** seed around 2000 years old from the fortress of Masada. On the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen, seeds from all over the world are stored in a seed vault in the permafrost. In this way crop plants are to be preserved even after disasters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny plant inside the seed, from which the new plant grows.
The first leaves of a plant, which are often already formed inside the seed.
Seeds that need light in order to germinate.
A test in which a few seeds are left to germinate to check their quality.

gewusst: The date palm grown from the 2000-year-old seed was nicknamed “Methuselah”.
Cress germinates so quickly that you can often see the first little roots after just one day.
Some seeds only germinate after a forest fire or the frost of winter has triggered them.

teile.einleitung: Jost Bürgi was a Swiss clockmaker, instrument maker and mathematician from the Toggenburg. He lived from 1552 to 1632 and built elaborate clocks and celestial globes for princes and the emperor. He also invented logarithms, independently of the Scotsman John Napier.
wichtigste: Jost Bürgi came from Lichtensteig in the Toggenburg.
He was originally a clockmaker and never went to university.
From 1579 he worked as court clockmaker at the princely court in Kassel.
Later he worked in Prague for Emperor Rudolf II and together with Johannes Kepler.
His clocks showed seconds at an early date.
He developed logarithms as an aid to calculation, independently of John Napier.
He built mechanical celestial globes and improved the proportional compass.

abschnitte.text: Jost Bürgi was born on 28 February 1552 in **Lichtensteig**, in what is now the canton of St Gallen. Little is known about his youth. He probably learned the trade of a **clockmaker**, perhaps during years of travelling as a journeyman in southern Germany. He did not attend a higher school, and he hardly knew Latin, the language of scholars.

From 1579 Bürgi worked at the court of Landgrave William IV in **Kassel**. The landgrave ran his own observatory there. Bürgi built very accurate clocks for him, which were among the first to show **seconds** as well. Accurate clocks were needed to measure the positions of the stars. Bürgi also helped with the observations of the sky himself.

Bürgi built magnificent mechanical **celestial globes**. A clockwork mechanism turned the sphere so that the stars moved as in the real sky. Such globes were valuable works of art and scientific instruments at the same time. He also improved the **proportional compass**, a drawing and measuring instrument with which surveyors could transfer distances in the correct proportion.

From 1604 Bürgi worked in Prague for Emperor **Rudolf II**, who loved art and science. There he met **Johannes Kepler**, with whom he worked. Kepler greatly valued Bürgi's skill at calculating. Only around 1631 did Bürgi return to Kassel, where he died in 1632.

Bürgi's most important mathematical achievement is **logarithms**. With them, difficult multiplications can be turned into simple additions. This helped astronomers enormously, as they had to calculate with huge numbers. Bürgi worked out his tables independently of the Scotsman **John Napier**, but only published them in 1620, six years after Napier. That is why Napier is better known today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of calculation that tells you how many times you have to multiply a base number by itself to get a particular number.
A sphere on which the stars and constellations of the sky are shown.
A pair of compasses with an adjustable pivot, used to transfer distances at a larger or smaller scale.
A clockmaker who works in the service of a prince or king.

gewusst: Bürgi was one of the few great mathematicians of his time who had never studied at a university.
Today a memorial plaque in Lichtensteig commemorates the little town's famous son.

teile.einleitung: A habitat is the place where a living thing lives and finds everything it needs to survive. This includes food, shelter, water and the right climate. Every animal and every plant is specially adapted to its habitat.
wichtigste: Every animal needs food and shelter in its habitat.
Another word for habitat is biotope.
The marmot lives in the mountains, and the ibex climbs on steep rocks in the Alps.
The beaver builds its lodge by the water.
The woodpecker lives in the forest.
The polar bear lives on the ice in the Arctic.
The camel is well adapted to life in the desert.

abschnitte.text: A **habitat** is an area with particular conditions such as temperature, light, water and soil. Experts also say **biotope**, from the Greek for “place of life”. The living space of one particular species is called its **habitat** in the narrower sense. A biotope can be large, like a forest, or small, like a pond or a piece of dead wood.

Every animal needs food, water and shelter in its habitat. On top of that come protected places for raising its young. The **beaver** lives by the water, fells trees and builds dams and lodges. The woodpecker carves holes in tree trunks and finds insects under the bark in the forest. If one important part is missing, a species cannot survive in an area.

The **polar bear** lives on the sea ice in the Arctic and has thick fur and a thick layer of fat. The **camel** can go a long time without drinking in the desert and has broad feet that do not sink into the sand. Its humps store fat as a reserve, not water. Such features are called **adaptations**; they developed over many generations.

Switzerland has very different habitats in a small space, from the chestnut forests of Ticino to the glaciers. In the Alps live **marmots**, which spend a long winter hibernating in burrows. The ibex climbs safely on steep rocks; it had died out in Switzerland until it was reintroduced from 1911. Other important habitats are lakes, rivers, moors, dry meadows and forests, which cover about a third of the country.

When people build roads and houses, drain moors or straighten rivers, habitats disappear. Many animals then become rare or die out in an area. Climate change also alters habitats, for example when glaciers melt. In Switzerland, moors have been specially protected since the Rothenthurm Initiative was accepted in 1987. The loss of habitats is considered one of the main causes of the decline in **biodiversity**.

Nature reserves and the Swiss National Park in the Engadine protect valuable habitats. Restored streams and hedges give animals space again. You can also help in your own garden or on your balcony, for example with native flowers, a pile of branches or a small pond. Such **small structures** are important stepping stones for insects, hedgehogs and birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A habitat with particular conditions, for example a pond or a hedge.
The typical living space of a particular species of animal or plant.
A feature that helps a living thing to survive in its habitat.
The variety of different species of animals and plants in an area.

gewusst: The beaver died out in Switzerland in the 19th century and now lives again on many rivers and lakes.
All the ibex in Switzerland are descended from animals that came from the Gran Paradiso area in Italy.
A single old tree can be home to hundreds of different animal species.

teile.einleitung: Justus von Liebig was a German chemist who lived from 1803 to 1873. He studied what plants need in order to grow and so laid the foundation for modern mineral fertiliser. With his teaching laboratory in Giessen he also changed how chemistry is taught at universities.
wichtigste: From 1824 Liebig set up a pioneering teaching laboratory at the University of Giessen.
He showed that plants take up mineral salts and so contradicted the humus theory.
The law of the minimum for plant growth is linked to his name.
From 1865 his meat extract was produced industrially in Uruguay.
The Liebig condenser bears his name, even though he did not invent it.
In 1845 he was made a baron and from then on was called “von Liebig”.
In 1852 he moved to Munich.

abschnitte.text: Justus Liebig was born on 12 May 1803 in **Darmstadt**. His father traded in paints and chemicals, and even as a child Justus experimented with them. He studied chemistry and learned from famous researchers in **Paris**. In 1824, at only 21, he became a professor in **Giessen**. He died in Munich in 1873.

In Giessen, Liebig set up a **teaching laboratory** in which students carried out experiments themselves. This was new at the time, because before then chemistry was learned mainly from lectures. Students came to him from all over Europe and America. His teaching model was adopted by many universities. With his **potash apparatus** he could also determine exactly how much carbon a substance contains.

People used to believe that plants feed on **humus**, that is, rotted material in the soil. Liebig showed that they mainly take up **mineral salts** such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. This gave rise to the idea of mineral fertiliser. According to the **law of the minimum**, the scarcest nutrient determines how well a plant grows. It is compared to a barrel that can only hold as much water as the height of its shortest stave.

Liebig looked for ways to preserve the nutrients in meat. This led to **Liebig's Extract of Meat**, a dark, thickened paste. From 1865 it was produced industrially in **Uruguay**, where there were a great many cattle. The product was sold worldwide and advertised with popular collectable picture cards.

In 1831 Liebig discovered **chloroform**, at about the same time as other chemists. The **Liebig condenser**, a glass tube with a cooling jacket for cooling vapours, bears his name. But he did not invent it; he only made it well known. Today such condensers are found in almost every chemistry laboratory, including in Swiss schools.

In 1845 Liebig was raised to the rank of **baron**. In 1852 he accepted a post at the University of **Munich**. The university in Giessen is now called Justus Liebig University. His former laboratory in Giessen houses a museum.

begriffe.erklaerung: Nutrients from the soil, such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, that plants need to grow.
A substance that adds nutrients to the soil so that plants grow better.
The dark, fertile layer of soil made of decomposed plant and animal remains.
A glass laboratory instrument that cools hot vapours with flowing water.

gewusst: As a child, Liebig lived through the hunger year of 1816, when there was hardly any harvest because of a volcanic eruption.
Liebig became a professor at only 21, which was very unusual even at that time.

teile.einleitung: A confidence interval is a range in which an unknown true value lies with great certainty. Statisticians need it because you usually cannot measure all people or things, only a sample. The interval shows how precise an estimate is.
wichtigste: A confidence interval gives a range instead of just a single number.
With a 95 % interval, 95 % of the intervals contain the true value over many repetitions.
The usual 95 % interval extends about 1.96 standard errors to the left and right of the mean.
If you quadruple the sample, the interval becomes roughly half as wide.
A 99 % interval is wider than a 95 % interval from the same data.
In a survey of 1000 people, the margin of error is about 3 percentage points.
Jerzy Neyman formally introduced the confidence interval into statistics in 1937.

abschnitte.text: If you want to know how tall Swiss teenagers are on average, you cannot measure them all. So you measure a **sample**, for example 500 teenagers, and calculate the mean. This value is only an estimate and differs a little from the true value. The **confidence interval** gives a range that very probably includes the true value. It is also called a confidence range.

For a 95 % interval, you take the mean and go about 1.96 **standard errors** down and up. If the mean is 50 and the standard error is 2, the interval therefore runs from about 46.08 to 53.92. The standard error gets smaller as the sample gets larger. Because it shrinks with the square root of the sample size, a sample four times larger roughly halves the width. If you want more certainty, say 99 %, the interval becomes wider.

A 95 % interval does not mean that the true value lies in exactly this one interval with 95 % probability. What it means is: if you repeated the study very many times, about 95 out of 100 intervals would hit the true value. You can imagine it like a game of ring toss, where the ring usually falls around the peg. The figure 95 % is called the **confidence level**.

Before votes in Switzerland, surveys are often published. If 50 % of 1000 people asked say yes, the true proportion lies roughly between 47 and 53 %. This **margin of error** of about 3 percentage points is often mentioned in the small print. So if two camps are only 2 percentage points apart, the race is still open.

Confidence intervals also help with comparisons, for example between two medicines. If the interval for a difference contains zero, for example from minus 1.5 to 4.2, the difference is not **significant** at the 5 % level. For ratios such as relative risk, 1 is the neutral value. So an interval from 0.8 to 1.3 shows no proven difference.

The Polish-American statistician **Jerzy Neyman** described the confidence interval in 1937 in a fundamental paper. He lived from 1894 to 1981 and later worked at the University of California, Berkeley. Today confidence intervals are part of almost every scientific study in medicine, biology and the social sciences.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small selection from a large group that is studied more closely.
A number that indicates how much an estimated mean can vary.
The chosen certainty, for example 95 or 99 per cent.
Half the width of the interval, that is, how far you can be out upwards and downwards.
A result that very probably did not come about by chance alone.

gewusst: To reduce the margin of error of a survey from 3 to 1.5 percentage points, you need about four times as many people.
Whether you survey 1000 people in Switzerland or in a much larger country hardly changes the margin of error.
The value 1.96 for the 95 % interval comes from the Gaussian bell curve.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Edwin Brandenberger was a Swiss chemist who invented cellophane. This transparent, shiny film is still used for packaging today. Yet he actually wanted to invent something completely different: a tablecloth that would not get dirty.
wichtigste: Jacques Edwin Brandenberger was born in Zurich in 1872.
He invented the transparent material cellophane.
Cellophane is made from cellulose.
The name is made up of “cellulose” and the French word “diaphane” for translucent.
Brandenberger originally wanted to make a dirt-repellent tablecloth.
He was working in France when he developed cellophane.
Cellophane is still used today mainly as packaging film.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Edwin Brandenberger was born in **1872** in **Zurich**. He studied chemistry and became an expert in textiles and dyes. Later he worked in **France** for a large bleaching and dyeing works in Thaon-les-Vosges. There he dealt with the treatment of fabrics. He died in Zurich in 1954.

According to legend, Brandenberger watched in a restaurant as **wine spilled onto a tablecloth**. The stain was hard to remove. That gave him the idea of a **dirt-repellent tablecloth**. He wanted to coat fabric with a thin, waterproof layer. But the layer was too stiff and peeled away from the fabric.

Brandenberger noticed that the peeled-off layer could be used as a transparent film in its own right. This film was made of **cellulose**, the substance that plant fibres and wood are also made of. Over the following years he developed a machine to produce the film in large quantities. He called it **cellophane**, from “cellulose” and the French word “diaphane” for translucent. In 1913 a company was founded in France to produce it.

Cellophane became famous above all as **packaging film**. Sweets, cigarettes, flowers and food were wrapped in it. Because the film is transparent, people could see the goods without touching them. This greatly changed selling in shops. The American company DuPont bought the rights for the USA and made the film very successful there after making it waterproof.

Today many kinds of packaging are made of plastics such as polypropylene, which look similar. In everyday language such films are often still called cellophane. Real cellophane is also known in German as **Zellglas**, cellulose glass. Because it is made of cellulose, it can break down in nature. That is why it is becoming interesting again today for more environmentally friendly packaging.

begriffe.erklaerung: The main building block of the walls of plant cells, for example in wood and cotton.
An expert who studies substances and how they change.
The German word for real cellophane, meaning cellulose glass.
Letting light pass through.

gewusst: A failed tablecloth led to one of the best-known packaging films in the world.
The name cellophane became so well known that today it is often used for completely different films.

teile.einleitung: A refrigerant is a substance that carries heat from one place to another in fridges, air conditioners and heat pumps. It takes in heat inside the appliance and gives it off again outside. Without refrigerants there would be no cold drinks from the fridge and no ice cream from the freezer.
wichtigste: Refrigerants carry heat by evaporating and becoming liquid again.
When a substance evaporates, it takes in a lot of heat from its surroundings.
CFCs, which damage the ozone layer, used to be widely used.
The Montreal Protocol of 1987 governs the worldwide phase-out of CFCs.
Many household fridges in Europe today contain the natural refrigerant isobutane.
Ammonia, propane and carbon dioxide are also used as refrigerants.
Some of the substitutes for CFCs are powerful greenhouse gases and are also being restricted.

abschnitte.text: A **refrigerant** is a liquid or gas that circulates in a closed system of pipes. It is chosen so that it boils at low temperatures. When it evaporates, it takes heat away from its surroundings. You know this from sweating: when sweat evaporates on your skin, it cools the body.

Inside a fridge a **refrigeration cycle** runs with four important parts. In the **evaporator** inside, the refrigerant evaporates and takes in heat from the fridge. A **compressor** squeezes the gas together, and it becomes hot. At the back, in the condenser, the gas gives off the heat to the kitchen and becomes liquid again. Then it flows through a narrow point back to the evaporator, and everything starts again.

From the 1930s, **CFCs** (chlorofluorocarbons) became very popular because they do not burn and are not poisonous. Later, researchers found out that high up in the atmosphere they destroy the **ozone layer**. This layer protects us from the sun's dangerous UV radiation. As a result, a so-called ozone hole formed over Antarctica every spring. With the **Montreal Protocol** of 1987, countries agreed to ban CFCs step by step.

Today **natural refrigerants**, which occur in nature, are used more and more. Household fridges in Europe mostly contain **isobutane**, a gas that is also found in lighters. Large cold stores and ice rinks often work with ammonia. Propane and carbon dioxide are also used, for example in heat pumps and supermarket refrigeration. These substances do not harm the ozone layer and hardly contribute to global warming.

Many of the substitutes for CFCs, the so-called **HFCs**, do not harm the ozone layer, but they are very powerful greenhouse gases. That is why the Montreal Protocol was extended in 2016 in Kigali (Rwanda) so that they are reduced too. Natural refrigerants have other disadvantages instead: isobutane and propane are flammable, and ammonia is poisonous. That is why refrigeration appliances are built carefully, and old appliances must be disposed of properly. In Switzerland you can return old fridges to specialist shops free of charge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that takes in heat in refrigeration appliances and gives it off again somewhere else.
Refrigerants used in the past that destroy the protective ozone layer.
A pump that squeezes a gas together so that it becomes hot.
A layer high up in the air that protects us from UV radiation.
A natural gas that is used as a refrigerant in many fridges today.

gewusst: The warm air behind your fridge is the heat that was previously in the food.
The Montreal Protocol has been signed by all UN member states and is regarded as one of the most successful environmental agreements.
A heat pump works like a fridge in reverse: it brings heat from outside into the house.

teile.einleitung: Dragonflies are fast, elegant flying insects with four transparent wings and huge eyes. They are among the oldest insects on Earth and existed even before the dinosaurs. In summer in Switzerland you often see them by ponds and lakes.
wichtigste: Dragonflies are predatory insects with four wings.
They existed even before the dinosaurs.
They can hover in the air and even fly backwards.
Their very large eyes are made of thousands of single eyes.
Dragonflies have no sting and cannot sting people.
Their larvae live in water and grab prey with their mask.
When it emerges, the dragonfly leaves behind an empty larval skin.

abschnitte.text: Dragonflies have a long, slender abdomen and four strong, transparent wings. The head is almost completely filled by two large **compound eyes**. With them they can see almost all the way round and spot movements in a flash. Many species shimmer in blue, green, red or gold. A distinction is made between the sturdy **true dragonflies** and the delicate damselflies, which fold their wings together when resting.

Dragonflies can move each of their four wings separately. This lets them hover in the air, change direction in a flash and even **fly backwards**. Large species reach high speeds and are among the fastest insects. They catch their prey, for example midges and flies, directly in flight with their legs, which they shape like a basket.

Dragonflies spend most of their lives as a **larva** in the water, often for one to several years. The larva hunts tadpoles, midge larvae and small water creatures. For this it has a **mask**, a kind of grabbing arm under its head, which it shoots forward in a flash. When it is fully grown, it climbs out of the water up a plant stem.

On the stem, the larva's skin splits open on its back, and the adult dragonfly squeezes out. At first the wings and body are soft and crumpled. The dragonfly pumps liquid into the veins of its wings until the wings are large and hard. What remains is an empty skin, the **exuvia**, which you can find on reeds and grasses in summer.

Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, long before the dinosaurs. In the **Carboniferous** period there were giant dragonfly-like insects such as Meganeura, with a wingspan of about 70 centimetres. Their imprints are known from fossils. Today over 5000 dragonfly species are known worldwide.

Several dozen dragonfly species live in Switzerland, for example the **southern hawker** and the banded demoiselle. They need clean ponds, streams, moors and lake shores with lots of plants. Because many wetlands have been drained, some species have become rare. If you make a small wildlife pond in your garden, you can offer dragonflies a new home.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made up of a great many small single eyes.
The young form of an animal, which looks different from the adult.
A fold-out grabbing arm on the head of a dragonfly larva, with which it seizes prey.
The empty skin that an insect leaves behind after emerging.

gewusst: A dragonfly eye can consist of up to 30,000 single eyes.
Dragonfly larvae breathe with gills in their rear gut and can shoot forward in a flash by pushing out water.
When hunting, dragonflies catch the vast majority of the prey they fly at.

teile.einleitung: A vaccination prepares the body to defend itself against certain pathogens. The body's defences get to know a germ without you becoming really ill. Vaccinations are among the most important inventions in medicine.
wichtigste: In a vaccination, the body learns to fight off certain germs.
Usually you get a vaccination with an injection.
After the vaccination the body forms defence substances called antibodies.
In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner vaccinated a boy against smallpox using cowpox.
The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.
Thanks to vaccinations, smallpox no longer exists anywhere in the world.
In Switzerland, vaccinations are entered in a vaccination record.

abschnitte.text: In a vaccination you are given a **vaccine**, usually with an injection in the upper arm. Some vaccines are swallowed. The vaccine contains weakened or killed pathogens, only parts of them, or a blueprint for such parts. It cannot make you seriously ill, but the body recognises it as foreign.

The **immune system** is the body's defence. It examines the vaccine and forms matching **antibodies** that fit exactly this pathogen. In addition, special defence cells remember the enemy; this is called immunological memory. If the real pathogen comes later, the body can react much faster. Some vaccinations have to be boosted after a few years.

In the past, **smallpox** was a feared disease from which a great many people died. The English country doctor **Edward Jenner** noticed that milkmaids who had had harmless cowpox did not get smallpox. In 1796 he gave a boy cowpox and showed that the boy was then protected. The terms vaccine and vaccination come from the Latin word “vacca” for cow.

Thanks to worldwide vaccination programmes, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. Polio has also disappeared in most countries. In 1885 the French researcher **Louis Pasteur** developed a vaccine against rabies. Today vaccinations protect against measles, tetanus, whooping cough and flu, among others.

In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health publishes a **vaccination schedule** every year, with recommendations on which vaccinations make sense at which age. Vaccinations here are voluntary in principle. All the vaccinations you have had are entered in your **vaccination record**, so that you keep track. After a vaccination you may have a sore arm or a slight temperature, which usually goes away after one or two days.

When many people are vaccinated, a pathogen finds it harder to spread. This also benefits people who cannot be vaccinated themselves, such as very young babies or people who are ill. This effect is called **herd protection** or community protection. How many people need to be vaccinated for this depends on the disease.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance given in a vaccination that prepares the body for a pathogen.
The body's defence substances, which attach to particular pathogens and make them harmless.
The body's defence system against pathogens.
A tiny germ such as a virus or bacterium that causes disease.
Protection of a whole group, because a pathogen can hardly spread when many people are vaccinated.

gewusst: Even before Jenner, people in China, India and the Ottoman Empire tried to protect themselves with small amounts of real smallpox.
Smallpox is the first and so far only human disease to have been completely eradicated.
Some vaccines are swallowed, such as the former oral polio vaccine on a sugar lump.

teile.einleitung: Ichnology is the science of traces left by living things. It studies tracks, burrows and feeding traces that animals left in the ground long ago. Such trace fossils reveal how prehistoric creatures moved, fed and lived.
wichtigste: Ichnology deals with trace fossils such as tracks, burrows and feeding traces.
According to Adolf Seilacher, typical communities of traces, the ichnofacies, indicate depositional environments such as water depth.
Tracks of predatory dinosaurs are usually three-toed and narrow, with claw marks.
The trace genus Chirotherium from the Triassic resembles human hands.
Burrowing trilobites typically left traces called Cruziana.
The trace fossil Treptichnus pedum marks the lower boundary of the Cambrian.
The churning up of sediment by living things is called bioturbation.

abschnitte.text: **Trace fossils** are fossilised traces of living things, not their bodies. They include footprints, crawling traces, dwelling tubes, bite marks and feeding tunnels. The name ichnology comes from the Greek word ichnos for trace. Because traces stay where they were made, they show where an animal really lived. Bones, on the other hand, can be washed a long way after death.

A lot can be read from tracks: an animal's size, its way of walking and even its speed. Predatory dinosaurs, the **theropods**, left three-toed, narrow prints with claw marks. Large plant-eaters such as sauropods, on the other hand, made round, elephant-like footprints. There are famous tracks in Switzerland too, for example in the quarry at **Lommiswil** in the canton of Solothurn. When the A16 motorway was built in the canton of Jura, thousands of dinosaur footprints also came to light.

The trace genus **Chirotherium** comes from the Triassic, the period about 250 to 200 million years ago. Its name means hand animal, because the prints resemble human hands. They probably come from relatives of crocodiles. The traces called **Cruziana** are plait-like grooves that burrowing trilobites left on the sea floor. In 2010, tracks of four-legged animals about 395 million years old from Zachełmie in Poland caused a stir, because they are older than known transitional forms such as Tiktaalik.

The German palaeontologist **Adolf Seilacher** developed the concept of **ichnofacies**. According to it, certain types of trace typically occur together in certain habitats. In shallow, moving water you often find vertical dwelling tubes. In calm, deep water, on the other hand, flat feeding traces with intricate patterns are more likely. In this way geologists can tell from traces how deep a prehistoric sea was.

Some trace fossils serve as time markers. The trace fossil **Treptichnus pedum** officially marks the lower boundary of the **Cambrian**, about 539 million years ago. It shows that animals at that time began to burrow through the ground in a new way. By churning up the sediment, called **bioturbation**, living things changed the sea floor permanently. Today earthworms mix our soils in a similar way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the traces that living things leave behind.
A fossilised trace of life, for example a footprint.
A row of footprints of an animal.
The churning and mixing of soil or sediment by living things.
The group of two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs.

gewusst: A single animal can leave many traces during its life, but only one skeleton, which is why trace fossils are often more common than bone finds.
From the distance between the footprints you can calculate how fast a dinosaur was moving.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, AI for short, is a branch of computer science in which computers learn to solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking. AI can translate languages, recognise images or answer questions in a chatbot. It was developed by people and can also make mistakes.
wichtigste: AI is meant to let computers solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.
Many AI programs learn from very large numbers of examples, for example from many pictures of cats.
The term “artificial intelligence” was coined by John McCarthy and became known at the Dartmouth Conference in 1956.
In 2016 the program AlphaGo beat one of the best Go players in the world.
A chatbot is a program you can have a conversation with in text messages.
AI can make mistakes, so you should check its answers.
In 2024 the EU passed the AI Act, a law that regulates AI according to its risk.

abschnitte.text: **Artificial intelligence** means that computers can do things that look like thinking: recognising, understanding, planning and deciding. But an AI has no consciousness and no feelings like a human. Most of today's systems are **weak AI**, which is good at only one particular task, such as playing chess or recognising faces. A strong AI that can do everything as flexibly as a human does not exist so far. People developed AI and decide what it is used for.

Many AI programs use **machine learning**. Instead of programming every rule one by one, you show the computer a great many examples. If an AI is to recognise cats in photos, it first needs thousands of pictures of cats. In doing so, it learns by itself which features matter, such as ears, whiskers and fur patterns. Often **neural networks** are used for this, which are loosely inspired by the structure of the brain.

In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing asked whether machines can think. At the **Dartmouth Conference** in the USA in 1956, the term coined by John McCarthy became known. In 1997 the chess computer Deep Blue beat the world champion Garry Kasparov. In 2011 IBM's system Watson won the quiz show “Jeopardy!” against two record winners. In 2016 AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the difficult board game Go, and from the end of 2022 chatbots such as ChatGPT became known worldwide.

We often come across AI without noticing it. It is found in translation programs, voice assistants on mobile phones and in sat navs that steer around traffic jams. Streaming services use AI to suggest films and music. In medicine, AI helps to analyse X-ray images. A **chatbot** can answer questions, write texts or help with learning.

AI can be wrong and sometimes makes up things that are false but sound convincing. That is why you should always check answers and not simply replace your own thinking. AI can also be used to make fake pictures and videos, known as **deepfakes**. For this reason the European Union passed the **AI Act** in 2024, which sorts AI applications according to their risk. Switzerland is also discussing how it wants to regulate the use of AI.

Switzerland is an important location for AI research. **Lugano** is home to the well-known research institute **IDSIA**, where important foundations for learning neural networks were developed. ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne also do intensive research on AI and robotics. Several large technology companies have research labs in Zurich. Swiss researchers work, for example, on AI for weather forecasting and medicine, and on robots.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact step-by-step set of instructions that a computer follows.
Computers learn from many examples instead of having every rule programmed in.
A computing model made of many connected units, loosely inspired by the brain.
A program you can have a conversation with in text messages.
A picture, video or sound recording faked with AI.

gewusst: The game of Go has more possible positions than there are atoms in the visible universe.
The name of the Turing test recalls Alan Turing, who suggested that a machine should count as intelligent if you cannot tell it apart from a human in conversation.
AI programs often need huge data centres to learn, and these use a great deal of electricity.

teile.einleitung: A laser is a device that produces a very concentrated and even beam of light. Laser light is so special that it can be used to cut metal, operate on eyes and even measure the distance to the Moon. The first laser shone in 1960.
wichtigste: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
Albert Einstein described stimulated emission as early as 1917.
The first laser had a ruby crystal as its active medium.
A laser needs a population inversion in the active medium.
Two mirrors form a resonator, in which the light travels back and forth and is amplified.
Laser light is coherent: the waves vibrate in step.
The forerunner of the laser worked with microwaves and is called a maser.
Lidar measures distances with laser pulses and creates 3D maps.

abschnitte.text: The word **LASER** is an abbreviation from English: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Laser light usually has exactly one colour and travels as a narrow beam that hardly spreads out. It is also **coherent**, which means that all the light waves vibrate in step. A light bulb, on the other hand, sends out a jumble of many waves in all directions.

Inside there is an **active medium**, such as a crystal, a gas or a semiconductor. Energy is pumped into it, for example with flashes of light or electricity. As a result, more atoms are in the excited state than in the ground state, which is called **population inversion**. When a particle of light hits an excited atom, the atom sends out an exactly identical particle of light: this is stimulated emission. Two mirrors at the ends form a **resonator**, in which the light runs back and forth and gets stronger and stronger, until part of it leaves through a half-silvered mirror.

**Albert Einstein** described the basis as early as 1917 in a theoretical paper. In 1954 the American Charles Townes and his colleagues built the **maser**, which worked with microwaves instead of visible light. In 1960 Theodore Maiman in California made the first laser shine. Its active medium was a small ruby crystal, and the laser produced red light. At the time it was jokingly called a solution looking for a problem.

Today lasers are found in many devices. Tills in the supermarket use them to read barcodes, and CD, DVD and Blu-ray players read the data with a laser beam. Fibre-optic cables carry internet data over thousands of kilometres with laser light. In industry, powerful lasers cut and weld metal, and in medicine eye doctors use them to correct poor eyesight.

With laser pulses you can measure distances very accurately, because you measure how long the light takes to go there and back. This method for landscapes is called **lidar**. Aircraft and drones scan the ground in this way and create accurate 3D maps, including for the Swiss national survey. Astronauts on the Apollo missions placed mirrors on the Moon. Since then, laser beams from Earth have measured the distance to the Moon to within a few centimetres.

Laser light is so concentrated that it can seriously damage the retina in the eye. You must never look into a laser beam and never point a laser pointer at people, animals or aircraft. Lasers are therefore divided into **laser classes**, from harmless to very dangerous. In Switzerland, powerful laser pointers are banned for private individuals.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the light waves vibrate in the same rhythm, like soldiers marching in step.
A particle of light makes an excited atom send out an identical particle of light.
An arrangement of two mirrors between which the light travels back and forth.
The forerunner of the laser, which amplifies microwaves instead of light.
A measuring method that determines distances with laser pulses.

gewusst: A laser beam sent to the Moon is several kilometres wide when it gets there, despite being concentrated.
Lasers can produce light in pulses that last less than a trillionth of a second.
You can only see laser light in the air if dust, smoke or fog scatter it sideways.

teile.einleitung: Mapping the sea floor means surveying the mountains, valleys and plains that lie hidden under the sea. Because light only reaches a little way into the water, sound, lasers and satellites are needed for this. For a long time the sea floor was less well known than the surface of the Moon.
wichtigste: Measuring and showing the depths of seas and lakes is called bathymetry.
Today research ships map the sea floor in wide strips with multibeam echo sounders.
Shallow coastal waters are surveyed from aircraft with green laser light, using bathymetric lidar.
Satellites detect seamounts because their gravity slightly raises the sea surface.
In the 1950s the cartographer Marie Tharp drew the rift in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
The Seabed 2030 project aims to map the whole sea floor accurately by 2030.
In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the deepest point of the oceans in the Trieste.

abschnitte.text: **Bathymetry** measures how deep seas and lakes are at every point. From many measuring points a map is made, similar to a land map with contour lines. Such maps show underwater mountains, trenches and plains. The sea floor covers around seven tenths of the Earth's surface, but it has still not been surveyed precisely everywhere.

In the past, sailors let a rope with a weight, a **sounding line**, sink to the bottom. Today people use the **echo sounder**: it sends a pulse of sound downwards and measures how long the echo takes to come back. A **multibeam echo sounder** sends out many beams in a fan shape and so surveys a wide strip at once. Side-scan sonar produces picture-like images that can be used, for example, to find shipwrecks.

In shallow water near the coast, aircraft fly with **bathymetric lidar**. Green laser light penetrates the water and is reflected by the bottom. Satellites measure the height of the sea surface very precisely. Above a seamount the water bulges up slightly because of the mountain's gravity, so large structures can be detected even from space.

In the 1950s the American cartographer **Marie Tharp** analysed depth measurements from the Atlantic. Together with Bruce Heezen she drew maps of the sea floor. In doing so she discovered a deep rift in the middle of the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**. This discovery helped to prove that the continents are slowly moving apart.

In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived in the submersible **Trieste** into the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench. There the sea is almost 11,000 metres deep. Jacques Piccard had built the Trieste together with his father Auguste Piccard; both were Swiss. Today the deep sea is often explored by unmanned underwater robots.

The international project **Seabed 2030** aims to map the entire sea floor at high resolution by the year 2030. It was launched in 2017 and collects measurement data from ships from many countries. By around 2024 about a quarter of the sea floor had been mapped accurately. Accurate maps help with shipping, laying cables, tsunami warnings and protecting the seas.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measuring the water depth of seas and lakes.
A device that measures water depth with sound.
A method that locates things under water with sound waves.
A measuring method using laser light.

gewusst: The surface of Mars has been mapped more precisely than large parts of the sea floor.
The submersible Trieste, which reached the deepest point of the oceans, was developed by two Swiss men.
Swiss lakes are also surveyed with echo sounders so that their depths are known precisely.

teile.einleitung: Jean Piaget was a Swiss researcher who studied how children learn to think. He found that children do not simply know less than adults, but think in a completely different way of their own. His stages of mental development are still well known today in schools and psychology.
wichtigste: Jean Piaget was born in Neuchâtel in 1896 and died in Geneva in 1980.
Even as a teenager he studied molluscs such as snails and mussels.
He divided children's mental development into four main stages.
The first stage is called the sensorimotor stage and lasts from birth to about two years.
According to Piaget, from about 11 or 12 young people can think abstractly and hypothetically.
According to Piaget, children learn through assimilation and accommodation.
With the three mountains experiment he showed that young children find it hard to imagine how others see things.

abschnitte.text: Jean Piaget was born on 9 August 1896 in **Neuchâtel**. At about eleven he wrote a short report on a white sparrow, and as a teenager he published work on **molluscs**. He studied natural sciences and wrote his doctoral thesis on snails. After that he turned to psychology and worked for a long time in **Geneva**, where he died in 1980.

In Paris, Piaget helped with intelligence tests for children and noticed something fascinating. Children of the same age often made the **same mistakes**. From this he concluded that children have their own logic, which develops step by step. He observed children closely, asked them questions and had them solve small tasks.

In the **sensorimotor stage**, up to about two years, a child learns by grasping and moving and acquires **object permanence**. In the **preoperational stage**, from about two to seven years, the child thinks in pictures and words but often pays attention to only one striking feature. In the **concrete operational stage**, from about seven to eleven years, the child thinks logically about things it can see and touch. In the formal operational stage, from about 11 or 12, the young person can think abstractly and hypothetically.

If you pour water from a wide glass into a tall, narrow one, younger children believe there is now more water. They have not yet understood the **conservation of quantity** and only pay attention to the height, which Piaget called **centration**. In the **three mountains experiment**, children were asked to say what a doll could see from another side of a model of mountains. Younger children usually described their own view; Piaget called this characteristic egocentrism.

According to Piaget, every person has **schemas**, patterns of thought with which they put the world in order. If a new experience fits into a schema, it is slotted in; this is called **assimilation**. If it does not fit, the schema has to be changed; this is called **accommodation**. A child who calls every four-legged animal a “dog” learns in this way, over time, to tell cats and cows apart.

In 1955 Piaget founded an international centre in Geneva for the study of thinking. His ideas have changed teaching: children should try things out for themselves and **learn by discovery**. Today we know that children can do some things earlier than Piaget thought. Even so, he is one of the most influential psychologists of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: Knowing that an object still exists even when you cannot see it.
Slotting new experiences into a familiar pattern of thought.
Adapting a pattern of thought to new experiences.
Only being able to see the world from your own point of view.

gewusst: Piaget was already publishing scientific articles on snails while he was still at school.
Piaget made many of his observations on his own three children.
If you hide a toy under a cloth in front of a baby a few months old, it often does not look for it at all.

teile.einleitung: In nuclear fusion, light atomic nuclei fuse to form a heavier nucleus, and an enormous amount of energy is released. This is how the Sun and every other star shine. Researchers all over the world are trying to make this source of energy usable on Earth too.
wichtigste: In nuclear fusion atomic nuclei fuse together; in nuclear fission they are split.
The Sun gets its energy from the nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
Fusion requires extremely high temperatures and pressures.
On Earth this needs plasma hotter than 100 million degrees.
Fusion power stations do not exist yet; they are still being researched.
The fuel for fusion comes partly from water.
The large experimental reactor ITER is being built in France.

abschnitte.text: Everything is made of atoms, and at the centre of every atom is a tiny **atomic nucleus**. In **nuclear fusion**, two light nuclei collide so violently that they fuse into a heavier nucleus. The new nucleus is a tiny bit lighter than the two original nuclei together. This missing mass is released as energy, as Albert Einstein described with E=mc². In nuclear fission it is the other way round: there a heavy nucleus such as uranium is split into pieces.

abschnitte.titel: The Sun as a power station
abschnitte.text: Inside the Sun it is about 15 million degrees hot, and the pressure is enormous. There **hydrogen nuclei** constantly fuse into helium. In this way the Sun converts around 600 million tonnes of hydrogen every second. The energy released reaches us as light and heat. So without nuclear fusion there would be no life on Earth.

On Earth the pressure is much lower than in the Sun, so even higher temperatures of over 100 million degrees are needed. At this heat the fuel becomes **plasma**, an extremely hot, electrically charged gas. No material can withstand this, so the plasma is held suspended with strong magnetic fields in machines called **tokamaks**. The fuel is deuterium and tritium, two heavy forms of hydrogen. Deuterium can be obtained from ordinary seawater.

In southern France, many countries are jointly building the huge experimental reactor **ITER**. It is meant to show that a fusion reactor can deliver more energy than is put into it. At the end of 2022 in the USA, a laser experiment for the first time produced more fusion energy than the lasers delivered to the target. Research is also being done in Switzerland: the Swiss Plasma Center at EPFL in Lausanne has its own tokamak. But it will probably still be decades before fusion power stations deliver electricity.

Nuclear fusion would have great advantages: it emits no carbon dioxide, and the fuel is available in almost unlimited amounts. It produces much less long-lived radioactive waste than **nuclear fission**. An accident such as a meltdown is not possible, because the reaction stops immediately if something goes wrong. The problem is that the technology is extremely difficult and expensive. To this day, fusion facilities still use more energy overall than they deliver.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny core at the centre of an atom, which contains almost all of its mass.
Splitting a heavy atomic nucleus, as happens in nuclear power stations.
An extremely hot gas in which the atoms are electrically charged.
A ring-shaped machine that holds plasma in place with strong magnets.
A heavy form of hydrogen that serves as fuel for fusion.

gewusst: In theory, the deuterium in a bathtub full of water could provide as much energy as many tonnes of coal.
The plasma in a tokamak is hotter than the inside of the Sun.

t1ht488z.t: Climate and Environmental Physics, University of Bern

teile.einleitung: The Division of Climate and Environmental Physics at the University of Bern is one of the world's leading groups in climate research. It became known for measuring the air of past times in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. In this way it was able to show how greenhouse gases and the climate have changed over hundreds of thousands of years.
wichtigste: Climate and Environmental Physics is a division of the Physics Institute of the University of Bern.
Its pioneer was the Bern physicist Hans Oeschger.
Oeschger developed an especially sensitive proportional counter for radiocarbon.
Around 1980, researchers from Bern and Grenoble showed that there was less CO2 in the air during the last Ice Age.
Abrupt climate swings of the Ice Age are called Dansgaard-Oeschger events.
Using the EPICA Dome C core, Bern helped to determine the course of CO2 over around 800,000 years.
The Oeschger Centre for Climate Change Research is named after Hans Oeschger.

abschnitte.text: At the **University of Bern**, physicists have been working for decades on the question of how the Earth's climate is changing. The Division of **Climate and Environmental Physics** develops its own measuring instruments and climate models for this. It belongs to the Oeschger Centre for Climate Change Research, which was founded in 2007. There experts from physics, geography, biology, history and other subjects work together.

The physicist **Hans Oeschger** lived from 1927 to 1998. He developed an especially sensitive measuring instrument, a **proportional counter**, with which very small amounts of radiocarbon can be measured. This can be used, for example, to determine the age of samples. Oeschger realised early on that ice from the polar regions is an archive of climate history.

Tiny **air bubbles** are trapped in glacier ice. They contain air from the time when the snow turned into ice. However, the air is younger than the ice around it, because the **firn** stays open for a long time and exchanges air. Around 1980, researchers from Bern and Grenoble showed that the CO2 content of the air in the last Ice Age was considerably lower than today.

To measure CO2, the ice is usually crushed dry instead of being melted. Otherwise the CO2 would dissolve in the meltwater and distort the result. Besides CO2, the researchers in Bern also measure **methane** and **nitrous oxide**. These gases show how closely greenhouse gases and temperature were linked in the past.

In the European **EPICA** project, an ice core more than three kilometres long was drilled at the Dome C site in Antarctica. The University of Bern played a major part in determining from it the course of CO2 over around 800,000 years. It shows that today's CO2 level is much higher than ever before in this long period. In Greenland ice, rapid jumps in climate were also found, the **Dansgaard-Oeschger events**, named after the Dane Willi Dansgaard and Hans Oeschger.

The results from Bern feed into the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the IPCC. Researchers from Bern have also held leading roles there, for example the climate physicist Thomas Stocker. The measurements help to test climate models and improve forecasts for the future. In this way Swiss research contributes worldwide to understanding climate change.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long cylinder of ice drilled out of a glacier or ice sheet.
Old, compacted snow that slowly turns into ice.
A kind of carbon that slowly decays and is used for dating.
A gas in the air that holds back heat, such as CO2, methane or nitrous oxide.

gewusst: An ice core from Antarctica contains air that is hundreds of thousands of years old.
The air in the ice bubbles is younger than the ice that surrounds it.
A Swiss physicist gave his name to a group of worldwide jumps in climate.

teile.einleitung: Joseph John Thomson, J. J. Thomson for short, was a British physicist. In 1897 he discovered the electron, the first known particle that is smaller than an atom. In doing so, he showed that atoms are not indivisible.
wichtigste: J. J. Thomson lived from 1856 to 1940 and was a British physicist.
In 1897 he discovered the electron as the first known subatomic particle.
To do so, he studied cathode rays in glass tubes.
He developed the plum pudding model of the atom.
In 1906 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He led the famous Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.
His son George Paget Thomson also received a Nobel Prize in Physics.

abschnitte.text: Joseph John Thomson was born in 1856 near **Manchester** in England. He studied at the University of Cambridge. At only 28 he became head of the **Cavendish Laboratory**, one of the most important physics laboratories in the world. He died in 1940 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

At the time, researchers were puzzling over mysterious rays in glass tubes with the air removed, the **cathode rays**. Thomson deflected them with magnets and electrically charged plates. From this he concluded that they consist of tiny, negatively charged particles. He was even able to calculate that these particles are much lighter than the lightest atom.

In 1897 Thomson presented his results. The tiny particles were later called **electrons**. Until then people had believed that the atom was the smallest, indivisible building block. Thomson showed that there are **subatomic particles**, that is, particles smaller than atoms.

Thomson thought about how an atom might be built. He imagined a positively charged sphere in which the electrons are stuck like raisins in a cake. This **atomic model** is called the plum pudding model. His former student **Ernest Rutherford** showed in 1911 that atoms have a tiny, heavy nucleus, and so improved the model.

For his research, Thomson received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 1906. Many of his students and colleagues were also awarded the Nobel Prize. Without knowledge of electrons there would be no **electronics**, no computers and no mobile phones. Later Thomson also found the first clues to isotopes in the noble gas neon.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of every atom.
Smaller than an atom, that is, a building block of an atom.
Streams of electrons in a glass tube with the air removed.
A simplified idea of how an atom is built.

gewusst: The father discovered that the electron is a particle, and his son George received the Nobel Prize in 1937 for showing that it also behaves like a wave.
Old cathode-ray televisions worked with electron beams, similar to those in Thomson's experiments.
An electron is about 1800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom.

teile.einleitung: A correlation describes a relationship between two characteristics, for example between height and shoe size. When one changes, the other usually changes too. But it is important to remember: a correlation does not prove that one is the cause of the other.
wichtigste: A correlation describes a relationship between two characteristics.
With a positive correlation, one value rises when the other rises.
With a negative correlation, one value falls when the other rises.
Height and shoe size are typically positively correlated.
In the Alps, altitude and air temperature are negatively correlated.
The correlation coefficient always lies between minus 1 and 1.
A correlation does not automatically mean that one thing is the cause of the other.

abschnitte.text: A **correlation** shows whether two quantities occur together or change together. With a **positive correlation**, both get bigger at the same time, for example height and shoe size. With a **negative correlation**, one gets bigger while the other gets smaller. An example from the Alps: the higher you climb, the colder it gets. If there is no relationship, this is called no correlation.

How strong a relationship is, is measured by the **correlation coefficient**. It always lies between minus 1 and 1. A value close to 1 means a strong positive relationship, a value close to minus 1 a strong negative one. At 0 there is no linear relationship. The best-known formula goes back to the English statistician **Karl Pearson**, building on ideas by Francis Galton.

The best way to show a relationship is with a **scatter plot**. Each point stands for a person or measurement, with one value on the horizontal axis and one on the vertical axis. If the points lie roughly along a rising line, the correlation is positive. If the cloud of points falls, it is negative. If it is wildly scattered, there is hardly any relationship.

In summer, ice cream sales and the number of sunburns rise at the same time. Yet nobody gets sunburnt from eating ice cream. Both depend on sunny, warm **weather**, a so-called **third variable**. That is why experts say: correlation is not **causation**. To prove a cause, you also need well-planned experiments.

Correlations are looked for in medicine, economics, climate research and sports analysis. They help to find hunches, which are then checked more closely. A famous example comes from the Swiss doctor Franz Messerli. In 2012 he showed, as a joke, that countries with high **chocolate consumption** have more Nobel Prize winners, and Switzerland was well up at the top. This shows how easily you can draw the wrong conclusions from correlations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A relationship between two characteristics that change together.
A cause and effect relationship in which one thing brings about the other.
A diagram made of points that shows two measurements at the same time.
A hidden third quantity that influences two others at the same time.

gewusst: There are collections of crazy chance correlations, for example between cheese consumption and quite different things, which match purely by chance.
Even a very strong correlation can arise completely by chance if you only have a little data.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Piccard was a Swiss oceanographer and engineer who dived to the deepest point of the world's oceans. On 23 January 1960, with Don Walsh in the submersible Trieste, he reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench. Down there it was pitch dark and cold, and the pressure was unimaginably high.
wichtigste: Jacques Piccard was born in Brussels in 1922 and was Swiss.
His father was the famous researcher Auguste Piccard.
In 1960 he dived into the Mariana Trench with Don Walsh.
The two reached a depth of almost 11 kilometres.
The Trieste stayed at the deepest point for about 20 minutes.
At the bottom of the Mariana Trench it is pitch dark and cold.
For Expo 64 he built the world's first tourist submarine.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Piccard was born on 28 July 1922 in **Brussels**, where his father taught at the university. The family came from Switzerland. In 1931 his father, **Auguste Piccard**, had been one of the first people to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon. Jacques studied economics in Geneva, but then worked with his father on submersibles.

Father and son built a **bathyscaphe**, a deep-sea submersible that works like an underwater balloon. It was called **Trieste**, after the Italian city of Trieste, which helped with its construction. A large float was filled with petrol, which is lighter than water. Beneath it hung a small, thick steel sphere in which the researchers sat, and heavy iron balls served as ballast.

On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and the American naval officer **Don Walsh** dived into the **Mariana Trench** in the Pacific. The descent took almost five hours. They reached a depth of almost 11,000 metres and stayed on the bottom for about 20 minutes. There it is pitch dark and only a few degrees warm, and the water presses with more than a thousand times the pressure of the air.

For the **Expo 64** national exhibition in Lausanne, Piccard built the mesoscaphe “Auguste Piccard”. It was the world's first submarine for tourists. During the exhibition, tens of thousands of visitors dived with it into Lake Geneva. In 1969 he also drifted for a month through the Atlantic in the Gulf Stream in the submersible Ben Franklin.

All his life Jacques Piccard worked to protect lakes and seas. He set up a foundation for the study and preservation of waters. He died on 1 November 2008 in La Tour-de-Peilz on Lake Geneva. His son **Bertrand Piccard** also became an adventurer and flew around the world in a balloon and later in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deep-sea submersible that rises and sinks under water like a balloon.
The deepest known point of the world's oceans, in the western Pacific.
A heavy weight that can be dropped in order to rise again.
A researcher who studies the seas.

gewusst: After Piccard and Walsh, nobody reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench again until 2012, when the film director James Cameron did so.
The Piccard family travelled through air and water in three generations in a row: grandfather Auguste, son Jacques and grandson Bertrand.
Shortly before reaching the bottom, a window of the Trieste cracked, but the dive was able to continue anyway.

teile.einleitung: An ambiguous image is a picture that can be seen in two different ways. Depending on what you focus on, your perception suddenly flips from one interpretation to the other. Ambiguous images show that our brain actively works along and interprets when we see.
wichtigste: An ambiguous image can be interpreted in two different ways.
You see the two interpretations alternately, but never at the same time.
In Rubin's vase you see either a vase or two faces in profile.
Rubin's vase uses the distinction between figure and ground.
The Necker cube is named after Louis Albert Necker from Geneva.
In 1899 Joseph Jastrow described the duck-rabbit ambiguous image.
The Schröder staircase is seen once from above and once from below.

abschnitte.text: An **ambiguous image** is a drawing that allows two interpretations. As you look at it, your perception jumps from one interpretation to the other; it **flips**. You see one or the other alternately, but never both at the same time. Ambiguous images are a kind of optical illusion and are studied in the psychology of perception.

The best-known ambiguous image is **Rubin's vase**. You see either a light vase in the middle or two dark faces in profile looking at each other. The Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin described this picture around 1915. It shows the distinction between **figure and ground**: the brain decides what is foreground and what is background.

The **Necker cube** is a cube drawn only with lines. You can see it so that sometimes one face and sometimes the other is at the front. It is named after the Geneva naturalist Louis Albert Necker, who described it in 1832. The **Schröder staircase** works in a similar way; you see it once from above and once from below.

A famous ambiguous image shows a **duck or a rabbit**. What is the beak for the duck is the ears for the rabbit. The psychologist Joseph Jastrow described the picture in 1899. Another ambiguous image is called “My Wife and My Mother-in-Law” and shows either a young or an old woman, depending on how you look.

With an ambiguous image, the eyes always deliver the same picture. But the **brain** has to decide what it means. Because both interpretations fit equally well, after a while it switches back and forth between them. This shows that seeing does not work like taking a photograph, but always involves interpreting too.

You can easily draw a Necker cube yourself: two squares of the same size, slightly offset, with their corners joined. If you fix your eyes on one point, you can sometimes control the flipping on purpose. Many artists play with such effects in their pictures. Hidden second images can also be found in logos and advertising.

begriffe.erklaerung: How we take in and interpret our surroundings with our senses.
A picture in which the eye or brain sees something different from how it really is.
The distinction between what is in the foreground and the background.
A view of a face from the side.

gewusst: The Necker cube was discovered by a man from Geneva who was actually studying crystals under a microscope.
With an ambiguous image, the picture on the retina stays the same; only the brain switches its interpretation.
With an ambiguous image, some people at first see only one interpretation and only find the second after a hint.

teile.einleitung: Laughter is an inborn reaction with which we show joy, fun or relief. When we laugh, the face, the diaphragm and our breathing move in a very special way. Laughter brings people together and is even catching.
wichtigste: Laughter is inborn and known in all the cultures of the world.
Babies usually laugh out loud for the first time at about 3 to 4 months.
When everyone around you laughs, you often have to laugh along.
Tickling makes many people laugh.
You can hardly tickle yourself, because your brain knows what is coming.
Rats also make sounds when tickled, which researchers compare with laughter.
Quiet, secret laughing is called giggling, and strong laughter you cannot stop is a fit of laughter.

abschnitte.text: When we laugh, many facial muscles tighten, especially around the mouth and eyes. The **diaphragm**, a muscle below the lungs, twitches in quick jerks. This pushes air out in short bursts, making sounds like “ha ha ha”. With strong laughter, tears can come and your tummy almost hurts. That is why laughter is often written as “Haha” in comics.

You do not have to learn to laugh. Babies smile in their first weeks and usually laugh out loud for the first time at about 3 to 4 months. Even children who have been blind and deaf from birth laugh. Laughter is known all over the world and is understood in all cultures. It is one of the oldest forms of **communication**.

People laugh much more often when they are with others than when they are alone. When you hear others laugh, you often simply have to laugh along, even without knowing the joke. Researchers believe that laughter mainly has a **social** job. It shows: I am friendly, and we belong together. That is why people often laugh at things that are not especially funny at all.

Tickling the soles of the feet, under the arms or on the tummy makes many people laugh. You can hardly tickle yourself, though, because the **brain** works out your own movement in advance. It knows what is coming and so dampens the reaction. Tickling is only fun if it is voluntary and you can say stop at any time.

Great apes such as chimpanzees and gorillas also show an open play face and panting sounds when playing and being tickled. Researchers found that even **rats** make high-pitched sounds when tickled. These are in the ultrasound range and cannot be heard by humans. Afterwards the rats kept coming back to the tickling hand.

Laughter can reduce stress and ease tension. The heart briefly beats faster, and afterwards you often feel more relaxed. The science of laughter is called **gelotology**, after the Greek word for laughter. In hospitals, hospital clowns visit sick children to bring them joy. In Switzerland, for example, the Theodora Foundation does this.

begriffe.erklaerung: An important breathing muscle between the chest and the belly, which twitches when we laugh.
Quiet, often secret laughing.
Strong laughter that you cannot stop.
The science that studies laughter and its effects.

gewusst: People laugh about thirty times more often in company than when they are alone.
Most laughs in conversations do not follow jokes at all, but perfectly ordinary sentences.
Rats that are tickled give out high calls that people can only hear with special equipment.

teile.einleitung: The Large Hadron Collider, LHC for short, is the largest and most powerful particle accelerator in the world. It lies underground on the border between Switzerland and France at CERN in Geneva. There, researchers make tiny particles collide at almost the speed of light in order to study the building blocks of the world.
wichtigste: The LHC is a ring-shaped particle accelerator with a circumference of about 27 kilometres.
It belongs to the CERN research centre near Geneva and lies partly in Switzerland and partly in France.
1232 superconducting dipole magnets keep the protons on their circular path.
In 2008 proton beams circulated in the LHC for the first time.
In 2012 the Higgs boson was detected using data from the LHC.
Since Run 3 in 2022, protons have collided at 13.6 TeV.
The four big experiments are called ATLAS, CMS, ALICE and LHCb.

abschnitte.text: The ring of the LHC lies in a tunnel about 50 to 175 metres underground between Lake Geneva and the Jura. The tunnel is about **27 kilometres** long, as far as a fairly long bike ride. It was originally built for an older accelerator called LEP. The LHC is run by **CERN**, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, which was founded in 1954.

In the LHC, two beams of **protons** fly in opposite directions through two pipes. They are accelerated to almost the speed of light and go round the ring over 11,000 times a second. 1232 **superconducting magnets** force them onto the circular path.
