A set of calculation rules with which a computer program decides, for example, what to display.
Where a piece of information comes from, that is, who first published it.
A careful check of whether a claim is true.

gewusst: Studies show that false reports on social networks often spread further and faster than true reports.
There are online games in which you take on the role of a faker yourself and so learn to see through the tricks.
The term filter bubble became known in 2011 through a book by the American internet activist Eli Pariser.

teile.einleitung: Yoghurt is a dairy product that is made when certain bacteria make milk sour and thick. It has been made for thousands of years and is popular all over the world today. You can even make it yourself quite easily.
wichtigste: Yoghurt is made from milk.
Lactic acid bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid.
Yoghurt tastes sour because of the lactic acid.
When yoghurt is made, the milk becomes thick.
The milk should be about 40 degrees warm.
If you make yoghurt yourself, you add a spoonful of yoghurt to the warm milk.
The word “yoghurt” comes from Turkish.

abschnitte.text: Yoghurt is a **soured milk product** made from **milk**. Usually cow's milk is used, but sheep's, goat's or buffalo milk can be used too. Yoghurt is thicker than milk and tastes slightly sour. It comes plain or with fruit, vanilla and other flavours. Yoghurt contains a lot of protein and calcium, which is important for bones and teeth.

Yoghurt needs certain **lactic acid bacteria**, above all Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus. These tiny living things feed on the **milk sugar** in the milk. As they do so, they produce **lactic acid**, which is why yoghurt tastes sour. The acid makes the milk protein curdle, and the milk becomes thick. At the same time the acid protects the yoghurt from going off quickly.

First you warm the milk to about **40 degrees**, which is roughly as warm as a hot bath. Then you add a **spoonful of yoghurt**, because it contains the bacteria you need. The mixture must then stay warm for several hours. There are **yoghurt makers** for this, but you can also put the jar in a warm oven. After that the yoghurt goes into the fridge, where it becomes firmer.

A yellowish liquid often collects on top of yoghurt. This is **whey**, the watery part of the milk that separates from the solid part. It has not gone bad and can simply be stirred back in. Whey contains vitamins, minerals and some protein. If you let the whey drain off completely, you get an especially thick yoghurt, such as Greek yoghurt.

The word **yoghurt** comes from **Turkish**. Thousands of years ago, herding peoples in Asia and the Balkans were already making soured milk. They probably discovered by chance that milk in warm containers becomes sour and thick. At the beginning of the 20th century the Bulgarian researcher Stamen Grigorov studied the bacteria in yoghurt. In Switzerland yoghurt is very popular and is made in large quantities in dairies.

begriffe.erklaerung: An acid that bacteria make from milk sugar.
Tiny living things made of only one cell; some of them are useful.
The yellowish liquid that separates from yoghurt or cheese.
A sugar that occurs naturally in milk.

gewusst: One spoonful of yoghurt is enough to turn a whole bowl of milk into yoghurt.
Millions of bacteria live in yoghurt, and most of them are good for digestion.

teile.einleitung: Coevolution means that two species influence each other and adapt to each other in the course of evolution. This can be an arms race between predator and prey or a close partnership between flower and pollinator. Many astonishing forms in nature have come about through coevolution.
wichtigste: Coevolution is the mutual evolutionary adaptation of two species.
In 1862, because of an orchid, Darwin predicted a moth with an extremely long proboscis.
The Red Queen hypothesis states that species must constantly adapt in order to keep up with their opponents.
Some garter snakes became resistant to the poison tetrodotoxin of their prey.
Cuckoo eggs often resemble the eggs of the host birds, because these recognise and remove foreign eggs.
Figs are pollinated by fig wasps in a highly specialised partnership.
Paul Ehrlich and Peter Raven made the term coevolution well known in 1964.

abschnitte.text: In **coevolution**, two species adapt to each other over many generations. If one species changes, this has an effect on the other, and the other way round. This can happen between plants and pollinators, predators and prey, or germs and their hosts. The term was made well known in 1964 by the researchers **Paul Ehrlich** and **Peter Raven** with a study on butterflies and their food plants.

The orchid Angraecum sesquipedale from Madagascar has a spur that is around 30 centimetres long. The nectar lies right at the bottom of it. In 1862 **Charles Darwin** predicted that there must be a moth with an extremely long proboscis that pollinates the flower. Many people laughed at this, but decades later such a hawk moth was actually discovered.

In western North America live newts whose skin contains the powerful poison **tetrodotoxin**. Certain garter snakes eat these newts and have become **resistant** to the poison. In areas with especially poisonous newts, the snakes are especially resistant too. Such arms races are described by the **Red Queen hypothesis**: as in Lewis Carroll's story, you have to keep running just to stay in the same place.

The **cuckoo** lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, for example reed warblers. Many host birds have learned to recognise foreign eggs and throw them out. That is why cuckoo eggs have, over time, become closely adapted to the eggs of their hosts. Cuckoos also live in Switzerland, and their call is easy to hear in spring.

Fig trees and **fig wasps** depend on each other. The tiny wasps crawl into the fig's flower clusters and pollinate them as they do so. At the same time they use the fig as a nursery for their young. Often exactly one particular species of wasp belongs to each species of fig, so close is the partnership.

In Australia, rabbits that had been brought in had multiplied in huge numbers. Around 1950 the **myxoma virus** was released to control them. At first almost all the infected animals died. In the following years the virus became milder and the rabbits more resistant, a well-observed example of coevolution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
An animal that carries pollen from flower to flower.
The ability to withstand a poison or a germ.
A living thing that houses or feeds another living thing.

gewusst: Darwin predicted a moth that nobody had yet seen, and he was proved right.
The Red Queen hypothesis is named after a character from “Through the Looking-Glass”.
Almost every species of fig has its own tiny pollinating wasp.

teile.einleitung: Cognitive psychology studies how people perceive, think, remember and make decisions. It imagines the mind as a system that takes in, processes and stores information. With clever experiments it shows how our brain sometimes tricks us, too.
wichtigste: Cognitive psychology deals with perception, thinking and memory.
Ulric Neisser gave the subject its name in 1967 with his textbook “Cognitive Psychology”.
It regards the human mind as an information-processing system.
The multi-store model distinguishes between the sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory.
The working memory model of Baddeley and Hitch describes a central executive and a phonological loop.
The Stroop effect and the anchoring effect show how easily our thinking is influenced.
Daniel Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, partly for research on judgement heuristics.

abschnitte.text: **Cognition** is a collective word for everything in the mind that has to do with knowledge: perceiving, paying attention, learning, remembering, speaking and solving problems. Cognitive psychology studies these processes with experiments. It compares the mind to an **information-processing system**, similar to a computer. Information comes in through the senses, is processed and stored.

For a long time psychology mainly studied observable behaviour and left thinking out. In the 1950s and 1960s this changed; this is called the **cognitive revolution**. The first computers also inspired the researchers. In 1967 **Ulric Neisser** published the textbook “Cognitive Psychology”, which gave the subject its name.

The **multi-store model** of Atkinson and Shiffrin divides memory into three stages. In the sensory register, impressions last only fractions of a second. In **short-term memory** you can keep only a few things at once, such as a telephone number. What is repeated often reaches **long-term memory**. Baddeley and Hitch described short-term memory in more detail as working memory, with a central executive as the boss and a phonological loop for language.

Our **attention** is limited. If you concentrate on a task, you sometimes miss something striking; this is called **inattentional blindness**. In a famous experiment, people counted ball passes and did not notice a person in a gorilla costume walking right through the picture. With the **Stroop effect**, it takes longer to name the colour of a word if, for example, the word “red” is written in blue.

When making decisions, people often use rules of thumb, so-called **heuristics**. This is quick, but sometimes leads to mistakes. With the **anchoring effect**, a number mentioned beforehand influences later estimates, even if it has nothing to do with them. The psychologist **Daniel Kahneman** studied such thinking errors with Amos Tversky and received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002.

The findings help with **learning**, for example by revising at intervals instead of all at once. They improve the design of apps, road signs and cockpits. They are also important in medicine, for example after a stroke. In addition, cognitive psychology works closely with brain research and artificial intelligence.

begriffe.erklaerung: All mental processes such as perceiving, thinking, remembering and learning.
The part of memory that holds information briefly and works with it.
A simple rule of thumb that lets you decide quickly, but not always correctly.
A number heard beforehand unconsciously influences a later estimate.

gewusst: In the gorilla experiment, about half of the participants did not notice the gorilla.
The Stroop effect is named after John Ridley Stroop, who described it in 1935.

teile.einleitung: Informed consent means that a person only takes part in a study or treatment if they have first been given an understandable explanation and have freely agreed. It is one of the most important rules of research ethics. This rule came about because in the past people were used for experiments without their knowledge or against their will.
wichtigste: Informed consent means agreement after an understandable explanation.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time.
Anyone who wants to give valid consent themselves must have capacity of judgement.
In the Tuskegee study in the USA, sick people were denied treatment.
The cells of Henrietta Lacks were used for research without her consent.
The Belmont Report of 1979 names the basic principles of respect, beneficence and justice.
With general consent, patients in Swiss hospitals agree to research with their data and samples.

abschnitte.text: In **informed consent**, a person is first given an understandable explanation of a study or treatment. They learn what it is about, what benefit there might be and what risks exist. Then they decide freely whether they want to take part, and usually confirm this with a signature. Consent can be **withdrawn at any time** without having to give reasons. Nobody may be pressured into taking part.

For someone to give valid consent themselves, they must have **capacity of judgement**. This means they must understand the information and be able to weigh it up sensibly. With children and young people it depends on their age and maturity; often the parents must also agree. Even then, children should be listened to and their wishes taken seriously. The explanation includes the aim, the procedure, the risks and rights, but not, for example, the salary of the study leaders.

After the Second World War, doctors who had carried out cruel experiments on people in concentration camps were convicted in Nuremberg. This led in 1947 to the **Nuremberg Code**, which requires voluntary consent. In the USA, the **Tuskegee study** ran from 1932 to 1972. In it, African-American men with the infectious disease syphilis were deliberately denied effective treatment. When this became known, it led to stricter rules.

**Henrietta Lacks** was an African-American woman who fell ill with cancer and died in 1951. Doctors took cells from her without asking her or her family. These cells, called **HeLa cells**, keep multiplying in the laboratory and are still used worldwide today. They helped with many discoveries, for example in developing the vaccine against polio. Her case shows why consent is also important for samples and data.

In 1979 the **Belmont Report** from the USA named three basic principles: respect for persons, beneficence and justice. In Switzerland, the **Human Research Act** regulates research on people. Every study must first be reviewed and approved by an ethics committee. Many hospitals use **general consent** to ask their patients whether their data and samples may be used for research. You can freely say yes or no, and the treatment remains just as good.

begriffe.erklaerung: Agreement that something may be done with you.
Being able to understand a matter and decide about it sensibly.
A body that checks whether a study protects the participants and is fair.
To take back an agreement.

gewusst: The HeLa cells of Henrietta Lacks have been grown in laboratories all over the world for more than 70 years.
The Nuremberg Code of 1947 begins with the principle that the voluntary consent of the person being tested is absolutely essential.

teile.einleitung: Insects always have six legs, and these are built in astonishingly varied ways. Depending on how an insect lives, they are used for walking, jumping, digging, swimming, catching prey or even tasting. So a look at the legs reveals a lot about how an insect lives.
wichtigste: All insects have six legs, that is, three pairs of legs.
An insect's body is divided into three parts: head, thorax and abdomen.
The legs are attached to the thorax.
Spiders are not insects, because they have eight legs.
The praying mantis catches prey with its special front legs.
The mole cricket digs with broad front legs, the great diving beetle swims with flat hind legs.
Butterflies, for example, can taste with their feet.

abschnitte.text: An insect's body consists of three parts: the **head**, the **thorax** and the **abdomen**. On the thorax are the three pairs of legs and, in many species, the wings too. Spiders, on the other hand, belong to the arachnids and have eight legs. Millipedes are not insects either.

Every insect leg consists of several segments joined by joints. From the inside out these are the coxa, the trochanter, the **femur**, the **tibia** and the foot. The foot is often divided again into several small segments and ends in claws. On the outside, the legs are covered by a hard shell of **chitin**.

Ground beetles have long, slender **walking legs** with which they run fast. Grasshoppers have powerful jumping legs with thick thighs. The mole cricket has broad, shovel-like **digging legs**, with which it digs tunnels in the earth like a mole. When walking, an insect usually moves three legs at the same time; this is called the tripod gait.

The great diving beetle lives in ponds and has flat **swimming legs** covered with hairs that work like oars. The praying mantis has **raptorial legs** with spines. It snaps them shut in a flash and uses them to hold flies or grasshoppers. Honeybees have a basket on their hind legs in which they collect pollen.

Many insects have fine **sensory hairs** on their legs. Butterflies and flies use them to taste, for example, whether a leaf or flower is edible. Flies often clean their head and eyes with their front legs. Many insects also clean their antennae with their legs.

A fly can walk upside down on a smooth window pane. This is made possible by **adhesive pads** on its feet, which stick to the glass with tiny hairs and a fine liquid. Insects also use their claws to hold on to rough surfaces. Experts study such feet in order to develop new adhesive techniques.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal with six legs and a body made of head, thorax and abdomen.
A hard substance from which the outer shell of insects is made.
Soft pads on the feet with which insects hold on to smooth surfaces.
A leg that has been adapted for holding prey.

gewusst: In some butterflies, such as the peacock butterfly, the front legs are so small that it looks as if they only have four legs.
Pond skaters walk across the surface of the water thanks to water-repellent hairs on their legs.
If an insect loses a leg, it can often still walk on quite well.

teile.einleitung: The International System of Units, SI for short, lays down how we measure all over the world. Thanks to it, a metre or a second means exactly the same everywhere in the world. It is the basis for science, technology, trade and our everyday lives.
wichtigste: The International System of Units was officially introduced in 1960.
The abbreviation SI comes from French: Système international d'unités.
It has seven base units, for example the metre, the kilogram and the second.
The kilogram is the only base unit with a prefix in its name.
Since 2019 all base units have been based on fixed constants of nature.
The second is defined by the oscillations of caesium atoms.
Every year on 20 May, World Metrology Day is celebrated.

abschnitte.text: In the past almost every region had its own measures such as the ell, the foot or the fathom. This often led to arguments in trade. The **International System of Units** creates common units for everyone. It was introduced in 1960 by the General Conference on Weights and Measures and builds on the metric system from the time of the French Revolution.

The SI has seven **base units**: the metre for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time, the ampere for electric current, the kelvin for temperature, the mole for amount of substance and the candela for luminous intensity. All other units are formed from them. The newton for force, for example, is a **derived unit** made from the kilogram, the metre and the second. The watt, the volt and the pascal are also derived units.

**Prefixes** are used to make units bigger or smaller, for example kilo for a thousand and milli for a thousandth. So a kilometre is 1000 metres. The kilogram is the only base unit that already has a prefix in its name. In 2022 new prefixes such as ronna and quetta were added for huge numbers.

For a long time the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris, the **International Prototype Kilogram**. Because such an object can change very slightly, since 20 May 2019 all base units have been based on **constants of nature**. The kilogram is now determined by the Planck constant, the metre by the speed of light. The second is defined by the oscillations of caesium atoms, which are counted in **atomic clocks**.

In Switzerland, the **Federal Institute of Metrology** METAS in Bern-Wabern makes sure that measurements are correct. It realises the units very precisely and tests measuring instruments. These include, for example, scales in shops, petrol pumps at filling stations and police speed cameras. So you can rely on a kilogram of apples really being a kilogram.

Without common units, researchers could not compare their results, and parts from different countries would not fit together. In everyday life the USA still uses units such as inches and miles. In 1999 the space probe Mars Climate Orbiter was lost because two teams had used different units. **World Metrology Day** on 20 May commemorates the Metre Convention of 1875.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic unit from which other units are formed.
A quantity in nature that never changes, such as the speed of light.
The science of precise measurement.
A syllable such as kilo or milli that multiplies or divides a unit.

gewusst: One second corresponds to exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a particular radiation from caesium atoms.
A metre is the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Only very few countries in the world, including the USA, do not mainly use the metric system in everyday life.

teile.einleitung: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and one of the most important researchers in the history of medicine. He put forward the germ theory, according to which many diseases are caused by tiny living things, the microorganisms. His discoveries still save millions of lives today.
wichtigste: Louis Pasteur lived in France from 1822 to 1895.
He put forward the germ theory: microorganisms cause diseases.
He proved that living things do not simply arise out of nothing.
Pasteurisation, which makes food keep, is named after him.
He developed vaccines, among others against rabies.
In 1885 he saved a small boy with his rabies vaccine.
The Pasteur Institute in Paris bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Louis Pasteur was born on 27 December 1822 in Dole in eastern France. His father was a tanner, a craftsman who made leather. Pasteur studied **chemistry** in Paris and later became a professor. Early on he made an important discovery about crystals of tartaric acid. He died on 28 September 1895 near Paris.

In the past, people did not know where infectious diseases came from. Many believed in bad air or in an imbalance of the body's fluids. Pasteur showed that tiny **microorganisms** such as bacteria cause fermentation, rotting and diseases. This idea is called the **germ theory**. Together with the German doctor Robert Koch, who continued his work, he is considered a founder of modern microbiology.

At that time many people believed in **spontaneous generation**, the idea that tiny living things simply appear by themselves in broth or meat. Pasteur boiled a nutrient broth in a glass flask with a long, curved neck that looked like a swan's neck. Air could get in, but dust and germs got stuck in the bend. The broth stayed clear and fresh for months. In this way he proved that germs come from outside and do not arise by themselves.

Pasteur found out that wine and beer go sour because unwanted microorganisms grow in them. He suggested heating the drinks briefly to kill these germs. This method is named after him: **pasteurisation**. Today it is used above all for milk, so that it keeps longer and does not spread diseases. Fruit juices are also often pasteurised.

Pasteur developed vaccines against animal diseases such as chicken cholera and anthrax. His most famous vaccine was against **rabies**, a deadly disease passed on through animal bites. In 1885 he treated nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog. The boy survived, and Pasteur became world-famous. With donations from all over the world, the **Pasteur Institute** opened in Paris in 1888, and it still researches diseases today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing so small that you can only see it with a microscope, for example a bacterium.
The discovery that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
Briefly heating food such as milk so that germs are killed.
A treatment that prepares the body for a disease so that it can defend itself better.
The false old idea that living things arise by themselves from dead matter.

gewusst: Joseph Meister, the boy saved by Pasteur, later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.
Pasteur had a stroke at the age of 45, but still carried on researching for almost three decades.

teile.einleitung: An index fossil is a fossil that can be used to work out the age of layers of rock. Good index fossils come from living things that existed for only a short time but were widespread. If you find them, you know at once which period of Earth's history a rock comes from.
wichtigste: Index fossils are used to date layers of rock.
A good index fossil lived only for a short time but was widespread.
Trilobites are important index fossils of the Palaeozoic era.
Graptolites are important index fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian.
Tiny foraminifera often serve as index fossils in drill cores.
Around 1800 the Englishman William Smith realised that layers can be matched by their fossils.
Index fossils give a relative age, meaning older or younger.

abschnitte.text: A **fossil** is a remain or trace of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone. An **index fossil** is a special fossil that is typical of a particular section of Earth's history. It works like a date stamp in the rock. If you find the same index fossil in two places far apart, the layers are about the same age.

abschnitte.titel: What makes a good index fossil?
abschnitte.text: A good index fossil comes from a species that lived only for a short time and changed quickly. At the same time it was widespread, often in the seas of the whole world. It should be common, easily preserved and easy to recognise. Sea creatures are especially suitable, because mud is constantly being laid down on the sea floor and buries them. Land animals such as dinosaurs were preserved much more rarely and are therefore usually poorer index fossils.

**Trilobites** were arthropods with a three-part shell and are important index fossils of the Palaeozoic era. **Graptolites** were small sea creatures that formed colonies; their remains look like pencil marks on slate, and they mark the Ordovician and Silurian. For the Mesozoic era, meaning the Jurassic and Cretaceous, the **ammonites** with their spiral shells are especially important. Tiny single-celled organisms with lime shells, the foraminifera, are found in their thousands in drill cores.

Around 1800 the English surveyor **William Smith** worked on building canals. He noticed that each layer of rock contains its own typical fossils. This allowed him to match layers even in places far apart. In 1815 he published one of the first geological maps of a whole country. That is why he is also called the father of English geology.

With index fossils you can say which layer is older or younger; this is called **relative dating**. But it does not give an exact number of years. For that, absolute dating with radioactive substances in the rock is used today. The two methods together make up the geological time scale. Oil and mining companies also use index fossils to identify layers of rock in boreholes.

In the Swiss Jura you find many ammonites from the time when a warm sea lay here. The Jurassic period is even named after the Jura mountains. In the Alps there are the coin-shaped **nummulites**, single-celled organisms that are considered index fossils for the early Paleogene. Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is world-famous for its fossils from the Triassic and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone.
A layer of rock that was laid down over a long time.
Working out whether something is older or younger, without an exact date.
An extinct arthropod of the Palaeozoic era with a three-part shell.
An extinct sea creature with a spiral shell, related to squid and octopuses.

gewusst: Some ammonite species lived for only a few hundred thousand years, which makes them very precise time markers.
Trilobites were among the first animals with real eyes, which were made of lime crystals.
The name graptolite means writing stone, because the fossils look like written characters on the rock.

teile.einleitung: In autumn, green woods turn into a sea of yellow, orange and red. This change of leaf colour is no accident but a clever plan by the trees to prepare for winter. In the process they take valuable substances back out of the leaves before these fall.
wichtigste: The signal for the leaves to change colour is the shortening days.
Trees break down the green pigment chlorophyll and take back valuable nutrients.
Then yellow and orange pigments become visible, which were already in the leaf before.
Some trees make new red pigments in autumn.
A separation layer forms at the leaf stalk, and then the leaf falls.
With sunny days and cool nights, the leaves become especially colourful.
In the mountains the trees change colour earlier, because it gets cold there earlier.

abschnitte.text: In summer, leaves are green because they contain a lot of **chlorophyll**. With this pigment they use sunlight to make sugar, which is called photosynthesis. In winter this would be difficult, because it is cold and dark and the ground is often frozen. Broad leaves would also give off a lot of water, which the tree cannot replace from the frozen ground. That is why deciduous trees shed their leaves.

When the days get shorter, the tree starts to break down the chlorophyll and to take its building blocks, such as nitrogen, back into the branches and roots. Now the yellow and orange **carotenoids** become visible, which were in the leaf all year but were covered by the green. The same orange pigment is also found in carrots. Some trees, such as maples, also make new red **anthocyanins**. If a leaf lies on the ground for a long time, it usually turns brown, because tannins are left over.

At the base of the leaf stalk, the tree forms a **separation layer** of cork cells. It gradually cuts the leaf off from its water supply and seals the wound. In the end a gust of wind is enough, and the leaf falls. Young **beeches** often keep their dry brown leaves until spring, and you can hear them rustling in winter.

The leaves become especially colourful with sunny days and cool nights. Then a lot of sugar forms in the leaf, from which red pigments are made. In the mountains the trees change colour earlier than in the valley, because it gets cold there earlier. The forests in the north-east of the USA and in Canada are famous for their autumn colours, where people talk of an **Indian summer**.

Spruces and firs keep their needles in winter. The needles are narrow and protected by a layer of wax, so they lose little water. An exception is the **larch**: it turns golden yellow in autumn and sheds its needles. In the Engadine and in Valais, whole larch forests glow like gold in October.

In Switzerland the leaves in the Central Plateau usually start changing colour in October. Beeches glow copper-red, birches and maples yellow, and cherry trees often red. Autumn walks in the Jura, in Ticino or along the larch paths in the Upper Engadine are popular. The fallen leaves are important for the soil, because **soil organisms** turn them into fertile humus.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green leaf pigment with which plants use sunlight.
Yellow and orange pigments that are also found in carrots.
Red to purple pigments that some trees make new in autumn.
A layer at the leaf stalk where the leaf comes away from the twig.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.

gewusst: The yellow pigments are already in the leaf in summer; you just cannot see them because of all the green.
The larch is the only native conifer in Switzerland that loses its needles in autumn.
A large deciduous tree can shed tens of thousands of leaves in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary marks the end of the Cretaceous period about 66 million years ago. At that time a huge asteroid struck the Earth, and about three quarters of all animal and plant species died out. The dinosaurs disappeared too, except for the birds.
wichtigste: The boundary lies about 66 million years in the past.
An asteroid about 10 kilometres across struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
A lot of iridium is found in the thin layer of clay at the boundary.
Dust darkened the Sun, so many plants died.
The impact set off enormous tsunamis.
The volcanic eruptions of the Deccan Traps in India are thought to be a possible additional cause.
Birds were the only group of dinosaurs to survive.
Afterwards mammals spread widely.

abschnitte.text: Geologists divide the history of the Earth into periods. The **Cretaceous** ended about 66 million years ago, and then the **Paleogene** began. The boundary between the two can be seen in many rocks as a thin, dark layer of clay. It used to be called the K-T boundary. It marks one of the five biggest mass extinctions in the history of the Earth.

An asteroid with a diameter of about 10 kilometres hurtled towards the Earth. It struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico and left the **Chicxulub crater**, about 180 kilometres across. Today the crater lies hidden under rock and sea. The explosion was millions of times stronger than any atomic bomb. It set off earthquakes, fires and giant tsunamis.

In 1980 the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, discovered a lot of **iridium** in the boundary layer. This metal is very rare in the Earth's crust but more common in asteroids. So they suspected an impact from space. Only about ten years later was the matching crater found in Mexico.

The impact hurled huge amounts of dust, soot and sulphur into the air. These clouds darkened the Sun for months or years. Plants could hardly carry out **photosynthesis** any more and died. As a result, the plant-eaters and then the meat-eaters could no longer find food. At the same time, in India, the volcanoes of the **Deccan Traps** poured out huge amounts of lava, which put extra strain on the climate.

All dinosaurs except the birds died out, as did the pterosaurs and the large marine reptiles. The **ammonites**, sea creatures with spiral shells, disappeared too. Small animals that could hide or eat seeds and carrion had better chances. Birds are direct descendants of dinosaurs and are therefore the only ones still alive today.

After the extinction, many habitats were suddenly free. The **mammals**, which until then had mostly been small, spread quickly and developed many new forms. From them later came whales, horses, apes and finally humans. Without the impact, the animal world would probably look very different today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time when a very large number of species on Earth die out within a short period.
A rare, heavy metal that is more common in asteroids than on Earth.
A lump of rock that orbits the Sun.
The period of Earth's history that began directly after the Cretaceous.
A huge area of solidified lava in the west of India.

gewusst: A chicken is more closely related to Tyrannosaurus than a crocodile is.
The boundary layer is often only a few centimetres thick, yet it tells of one of the biggest disasters in the history of the Earth.
The name Cretaceous comes from the Latin word for chalk: white chalk cliffs formed in this period from tiny lime shells.

teile.einleitung: Ignaz Semmelweis was a doctor in the 19th century who was one of the first to realise how important clean hands are in hospital. With a simple rule about disinfecting hands, he saved many people's lives. Even so, many colleagues did not believe him during his lifetime.
wichtigste: Ignaz Semmelweis was born in 1818 in Ofen (Buda), today's Budapest.
He worked as a doctor at the General Hospital in Vienna.
In 1847 the death of his colleague Kolletschka gave him the crucial idea.
He had hands disinfected with a chlorinated lime solution.
After that the death rate in his ward fell to about 1 to 2 per cent.
He died in 1865 in a mental asylum of blood poisoning.
Later he was given the honorary title “saviour of mothers”.

abschnitte.text: Ignaz Philipp Semmelweis was born in **1818** in **Ofen**, in Hungarian Buda. Today Ofen is part of Budapest. He studied medicine in Vienna and Pest. From 1846 he worked at the large **General Hospital** in Vienna. There he was responsible for women who had just given birth.

The Vienna hospital had two wards for new mothers. In one, doctors and medical students worked; in the other, midwives. Semmelweis noticed that many more women died on the doctors' ward than on the midwives' ward. The cause was **childbed fever**, a dangerous infection. At the time nobody knew where the illness came from, because bacteria as the cause of disease were still unknown.

In 1847 Semmelweis's colleague **Jakob Kolletschka** died after cutting himself with a knife while examining a dead body. His illness looked exactly like the fever of the patients. Semmelweis concluded that tiny particles from dead bodies on the doctors' hands were passing on the disease. The doctors often came straight from the dissecting room to the patients. The midwives, on the other hand, did not examine dead bodies.

Semmelweis demanded that everyone disinfect their hands with a **chlorinated lime solution** before examining patients. Chlorinated lime kills pathogens and also gets rid of the smell of dead bodies. The effect was huge: the death rate in his ward fell to about **1 to 2 per cent**. Before, it had at times been many times higher. Later Semmelweis went back to Hungary and became a professor at the university in Pest.

Many doctors did not want to believe that they themselves were passing on diseases. Semmelweis argued fiercely with his opponents and became increasingly bitter. In 1865 he was taken to a **mental asylum** near Vienna, where he died shortly afterwards of blood poisoning. Only when Louis Pasteur and Joseph Lister proved that bacteria cause disease was his achievement recognised. Today he is called the **“saviour of mothers”**, and the medical university in Budapest bears his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Killing pathogens, for example on the hands.
A white powder that, dissolved in water, kills pathogens.
A life-threatening infection that spreads through the body via the blood.
Rejecting new findings by reflex because they contradict familiar views.

gewusst: The “Semmelweis reflex”, rejecting new findings by reflex, is named after Semmelweis.
Thorough handwashing is still regarded today as one of the most effective measures against infections in hospital.
Semmelweis's birthplace in Budapest is now a museum of the history of medicine.

teile.einleitung: Chewing gum is a sweet that you chew for a long time but do not swallow. It is made of a tough chewing base, sweeteners and flavourings. Long ago the Maya were already chewing the sap of a tree.
wichtigste: The chewing base of most chewing gums today is made of artificial plastics.
The Maya were already chewing the dried sap of the sapodilla tree.
The body cannot digest the rubbery chewing base.
Swallowed chewing gum leaves the body again after a few days.
Sugar-free chewing gum stimulates the flow of saliva and can help the teeth.
Chewed gum belongs in the bin.
In Singapore the sale of chewing gum is largely banned.

abschnitte.titel: What is chewing gum made of?
abschnitte.text: Chewing gum consists of a **chewing base**, also called gum base, plus sugar or sweeteners, flavourings and colourings. In the past the chewing base came from tree saps. Today it is usually made of artificial **plastics**, similar to plastic or rubber. This mass stays tough and elastic as you chew, while the sugar and flavour gradually dissolve.

The **Maya** in Central America were already chewing the dried milky sap of the sapodilla tree, which is called **chicle**. In northern Europe, people chewed birch tar as early as the Stone Age. In the 19th century, factory production began in the USA; one well-known name is the businessman William Wrigley. The first proper bubble gum was invented in 1928 by the American Walter Diemer.

Sugar-free chewing gum stimulates the **flow of saliva**. Saliva rinses away bits of food and helps to neutralise acids in the mouth that attack the teeth. That is why sugar-free chewing gum after eating can help the teeth. But it never replaces brushing your teeth. Many sugar-free chewing gums contain sweeteners such as xylitol, also called birch sugar.

The body cannot digest the rubbery chewing base. A piece of gum swallowed once in a while is still harmless: it travels through the gut and leaves the body again after a few days. The claim that it stays in the stomach for years is a **myth**. Small children should not swallow large amounts, though, and when doing sport or running, it is better not to have gum in your mouth.

Chewed gum belongs in the **bin**. On streets and squares it sticks fast, turns black and is hard to remove. Towns spend a lot of money cleaning it away with steam or special machines. In **Singapore**, the sale of chewing gum has been largely banned since 1992, so that streets and trains stay clean.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tough basic substance of chewing gum, which does not break down when chewed.
The dried milky sap of the sapodilla tree, which used to be the raw material for chewing gum.
The liquid in the mouth that helps with chewing and digestion.
A widespread story that is not true.

gewusst: From Stone Age birch tar with tooth marks, researchers have even been able to recover the genetic material of the people who chewed it.
The first bubble gum was pink, because that was the only colour the inventor had to hand.
In Singapore, certain dental chewing gums may still be bought in pharmacies.

teile.einleitung: Johann Jakob Scheuchzer was a doctor and naturalist from Zurich who lived from 1672 to 1733. He was one of the first to study the Alps scientifically; he drew maps, measured mountains and collected fossils. He also became famous for a big mistake: he thought a fossilised giant salamander was a human from the Great Flood.
wichtigste: Johann Jakob Scheuchzer lived from 1672 to 1733 and worked in Zurich as a doctor and naturalist.
On many journeys in the Alps he collected plants, stones, fossils and reports of dragons.
He used a barometer to work out the height of mountains on his travels.
In 1712 he published a large map of Switzerland.
He thought the fossil “Homo diluvii testis” was a human from the Flood.
In 1811 Georges Cuvier realised that the fossil was in fact a giant salamander.
His work “Physica sacra” combines the Bible and natural science with many copper engravings.

abschnitte.text: **Johann Jakob Scheuchzer** was born in Zurich in 1672 and died there in 1733. He studied medicine and obtained his doctorate in the Netherlands. Back in Zurich he worked as a doctor, taught mathematics and looked after the city's natural history collection. He exchanged letters with many researchers all over Europe and became a member of the famous Royal Society in London.

Between about 1702 and 1711, Scheuchzer made several great **journeys in the Alps**. At that time many people still thought of the mountains as eerie and dangerous. Scheuchzer observed glaciers, plants, animals, rocks and the weather. With a **barometer**, which measures air pressure, he estimated the height of the mountains, because the higher you climb, the lower the air pressure.

On his journeys Scheuchzer also collected reports from people who claimed to have seen **dragons**. He wrote these stories down and sorted them by canton. Today we know that there are no dragons. But his collection is a valuable source for what people in the Alps believed and told each other at the time.

abschnitte.titel: The mistake of the Flood man
abschnitte.text: Scheuchzer was given a large fossil from a quarry near Öhningen on Lake Constance. He called it **Homo diluvii testis**, which means “man, witness of the Flood”. He believed it was the bones of a person who had drowned in the biblical flood. In 1811 the French researcher **Georges Cuvier** examined the fossil and showed that it was a giant salamander. In Scheuchzer's honour, the extinct species is now called Andrias scheuchzeri.

In 1712 Scheuchzer's large **map of Switzerland** appeared, which for a long time was the most accurate picture of the country. He also wrote a natural history of Switzerland in several volumes. His late main work is the **Physica sacra**, a Bible with explanations from natural history and more than 700 copper engravings. That is why it is also called the “copper Bible”.

Scheuchzer is regarded as one of the founders of Alpine research and of the natural sciences in Switzerland. Like many scholars of his time, he wanted to combine faith and the observation of nature. His famous mistake shows how science works: new investigations can correct old interpretations. The fossil of the “Flood man” is now in the Teylers Museum in Haarlem in the Netherlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or imprint of a living thing from earlier times.
An instrument for measuring air pressure, which can also be used to estimate heights.
A huge flood from a story in the Bible.
A picture printed from an engraved copper plate.

gewusst: The giant salamander that Scheuchzer thought was a human was more than a metre long.
Scheuchzer collected so many dragon stories that he could sort them by canton.
Of all names, the extinct salamander species now bears Scheuchzer's.

teile.einleitung: Solubility describes how well a substance dissolves in a liquid. When you stir sugar into warm water, it dissolves and seems to disappear, but afterwards the water tastes sweet. Some substances dissolve very well, others not at all, like oil in water.
wichtigste: Solubility tells you how much of a substance dissolves in a liquid.
Sugar and salt dissolve well in water.
Oil and sand do not dissolve in water.
A solution that cannot take in any more is called saturated.
Solids usually dissolve better in warm water.
Gases, on the other hand, dissolve better in cold water.
Water is the most important solvent on Earth.

abschnitte.text: When a substance spreads out in a liquid until you can no longer see it, this is called **dissolving**. The liquid is called the **solvent**, and the mixture is called a solution. **Solubility** tells you the most of a substance that can dissolve in a certain amount of solvent. The substance has not disappeared; it has only broken up into tiny particles. If you let the water evaporate, it appears again.

Sugar is made of tiny particles called molecules. The water particles surround these molecules and pull them one by one out of the sugar crystal. In warm water the particles move faster, so sugar dissolves faster there and in larger amounts. Stirring also helps, because fresh water keeps reaching the sugar. At 20 degrees, about 200 grams of sugar dissolve in 100 grams of water, but only about 36 grams of table salt.

If you keep adding more and more salt to a glass of water, at some point nothing more dissolves. The rest of the salt stays lying at the bottom. Then the solution is **saturated**. If a saturated solution cools down or water evaporates, crystals form again. In this way you can grow sugar or salt crystals at home.

With gases it is the other way round from sugar: they dissolve better in **cold water** than in warm water. That is why warm mineral water fizzes more and loses its fizz faster. Fish in warm lakes sometimes have too little oxygen in summer, because warm water contains less of it. Oil does not dissolve in water at all and floats on top. Chemists say “like dissolves like”, so fat dissolves in oil or petrol, but not in water.

Our body uses water as a solvent to carry nutrients in the blood. When washing up, washing-up liquid helps to spread fat out in the water. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Saltworks** obtain salt by pumping water into deep layers of salt, where it dissolves the salt. The salty brine is pumped back up, and the water is evaporated until salt is left. In caves, water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and later lets it crystallise again as **stalactites and stalagmites**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid in which another substance dissolves, for example water.
A mixture in which a substance is very finely spread out in a liquid.
So full of dissolved substance that nothing more can dissolve.
Water in which a great deal of salt is dissolved.

gewusst: So much salt is dissolved in seawater that a litre contains about 35 grams of salt.
Water dissolves so many different substances that it is often called the “universal solvent”.

teile.einleitung: Boxfish are sea fish with a hard, angular armour that makes them look like a small box. They live mainly in warm seas near coral reefs. Their unusual body shape has even inspired car engineers.
wichtigste: The boxfish has an angular shape like a box.
A hard armour surrounds its body.
It swims mainly with its fins, because its body can hardly bend.
Boxfish live in the sea near coral reefs.
Young yellow boxfish are yellow with black spots.
When in danger, the boxfish can release poison.
A car was built on the model of the boxfish.

abschnitte.text: **Boxfish** form a family of fish of their own. Their body is enclosed in a hard **armour** of bony plates that have grown together. That is why they look angular, almost like a small box. Only the eyes, mouth, fins and tail stick out of the armour. Depending on the species, they grow to about 10 to 45 centimetres long.

One of the best-known species is the **yellow boxfish**. Young animals are bright yellow with black spots and look like a small dice. As they get older, the colour becomes paler and more brownish or bluish grey. The striking colour warns predators that the fish is poisonous.

Boxfish live in warm seas, especially near **coral reefs** in the Indian and Pacific Oceans and in the Red Sea. Some species also occur in the Atlantic. They eat algae, sponges and small invertebrates on the seabed. Some species blow away the sand with a jet of water to uncover hidden prey.

When a boxfish is threatened or stressed, it releases a **poison** into the water through its skin. This poison can harm other fish nearby. In a small aquarium it can even kill the other inhabitants and the boxfish itself. That is why experts keep these fish only with great care.

Because its armour is stiff, the boxfish can hardly bend. So it swims mainly with its **fins**, which it moves like little oars. This means it is not especially fast, but it is very agile. It can turn on the spot and manoeuvre skilfully between corals.

Engineers from a German car maker studied the boxfish closely. They wanted to know how such an angular body can still glide well through the water. In 2005, on its model, they built a **concept car**, the “Bionic Car”. From the armour they learned how to build things **light and yet stable**. This is an example of biomimetics, learning from nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard protective covering around an animal's body.
An underwater landscape made from the limestone skeletons of corals.
Technology that imitates ideas from nature.
Striking colouring that shows predators that an animal is poisonous.

gewusst: With its poison, a boxfish can even kill its fellow inhabitants in an aquarium.
The car inspired by a boxfish looks more angular than most cars.
Boxfish can turn on the spot like a little helicopter.

teile.einleitung: Katherine Johnson was an American mathematician who calculated flight paths for the space agency NASA. Without her precise calculations, the first American space flights would hardly have been possible. For a long time hardly anyone knew her name, until the film “Hidden Figures” told her story.
wichtigste: Katherine Johnson lived from 1918 to 2020 and reached the age of 101.
She calculated flight paths for NASA.
When she started her work, her job was called “computer”, meaning a person who calculates.
In 1961 she calculated the path for Alan Shepard, the first American in space.
In 1962 John Glenn wanted her to check the computer calculations for his orbit of the Earth.
In 1969 she helped with calculations for the Apollo 11 Moon landing.
In 2015 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Barack Obama.
The 2016 film “Hidden Figures” tells her story.

abschnitte.text: **Katherine Johnson** was born in West Virginia in the USA in 1918. Even as a child she was extraordinarily good at maths and skipped several school years. At 18 she graduated in mathematics and French. After that she first worked as a teacher.

In 1953 Johnson started at the aeronautics research agency NACA, which became **NASA** in 1958. She worked at Langley in the state of Virginia. At that time women who carried out complicated calculations by hand were called **computers**. As an African-American, she at first had to work in a separate department, because racial segregation was the rule in many areas at the time.

Johnson calculated which **flight path** a space capsule had to follow and where it would land again. In 1961 she worked out the path for the flight of **Alan Shepard**, the first American in space. In 1962 John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth. He did not yet fully trust the new electronic computers and wanted Johnson to check the figures by hand.

abschnitte.titel: On the way to the Moon
abschnitte.text: Johnson also made important calculations for **Apollo 11**, the first Moon landing in 1969. She helped to work out how the lunar module could meet up again with the spacecraft in orbit around the Moon. Later she also worked on plans for the Space Shuttle. Altogether she worked at NASA for more than 30 years.

For many years Johnson's work was hardly known to the public. In 2015 President Barack Obama presented her with the **Presidential Medal of Freedom**, one of the highest honours in the USA. In 2016 the film **Hidden Figures** came out, telling the story of her and her colleagues. A NASA building now bears her name. She died in 2020 at the age of 101.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path that a flying object takes through the air or through space.
The space agency of the USA, founded in 1958.
The unjust separation of people by the colour of their skin, for example in schools or at work.
A circular or oval path on which something circles a heavenly body.

gewusst: John Glenn is said to have said that he would only take off once Katherine Johnson had checked the numbers.
In Johnson's time, “computer” was a job title for people.
Katherine Johnson lived to see a NASA building named after her.

teile.einleitung: Annual rings, or tree rings, are the rings you can see on a tree stump or in the cross-section of a trunk. In our climate exactly one such ring is added every year. If you read the rings, you learn the age of a tree and even what the weather was like long ago.
wichtigste: You can tell the age of a tree from its annual rings.
In our climate exactly one annual ring grows each year.
A tree stump with 50 annual rings belonged to a tree about 50 years old.
In spring the tree forms lighter wood, later in the year darker wood.
A wide ring shows a year in which the tree grew well.
With every new ring the trunk gets thicker.
Many trees in the tropical rainforest have no clear rings, because there is no cold winter there.

abschnitte.titel: How does an annual ring form?
abschnitte.text: Under the **bark** lies a thin growth layer, the **cambium**. Every year it forms new wood towards the inside and new bark towards the outside. In winter the tree takes a break. When it starts growing again in spring, a visible boundary forms, and so ring after ring is built up.

In spring the tree needs a lot of water for its new leaves. It therefore forms **earlywood** with wide, light-coloured cells. In summer and autumn **latewood** is formed, with narrow, thick-walled cells that look darker. A light and a dark band together make one annual ring.

The rings are especially easy to see on a **tree stump**. You count them from the middle to the bark, and each ring stands for one year. If a stump has 50 rings, the tree was about 50 years old. With living trees, a thin borer can be used to take a sample of wood without felling the tree.

A **wide ring** shows a good year with enough warmth and rain. A narrow ring points to drought, cold or pests. Scars in the rings can come from forest fires or lightning. In this way trees become an archive of the **climate** of past centuries.

The science that uses annual rings to date wood is called **dendrochronology**. Because the patterns of wide and narrow rings are similar within one region, they can be compared like a barcode. In Central Europe, such ring calendars go back more than 10,000 years. In Switzerland, for example, this is how the exact year in which wooden piles from pile-dwelling settlements were felled is determined.

In regions without winter, such as the tropical rainforest, many trees grow evenly all year round. That is why they often have no clear annual rings. Where there are rainy and dry seasons, rings can form according to this rhythm instead. Palm trees do not form annual rings either, because their trunk is built differently.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin growth layer under the bark that forms new wood.
Light, loose wood that the tree forms in spring.
Darker, firmer wood from summer and autumn.
A method of working out the age of wood from its annual rings.

gewusst: According to their annual rings, some bristlecone pines in California are more than 4500 years old.
Thanks to annual rings, for some pile dwellings in Switzerland we know to the exact year when their wood was felled.
Fish and mussels also form growth rings; you can read the age of fish from their scales.

teile.einleitung: In biology, consumers are living things that eat other living things. They cannot make their own food like plants do. Whether deer, fox or human, all animals are consumers.
wichtigste: Consumers depend on ready-made food; they are heterotrophic.
Primary consumers such as the roe deer eat plants.
Secondary consumers eat plant-eaters.
In the chain grass, mouse, snake, eagle owl, the eagle owl is the tertiary consumer.
Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
The bearded vulture is a scavenger that feeds mainly on bones.
In the Swiss forest, the tawny owl eats mainly mice.

abschnitte.text: The word **consumer** comes from the Latin “consumere”, which means to use up. Plants make their own food with sunlight and are therefore called producers. Consumers cannot do this and have to eat other living things. Experts call them **heterotrophic**, that is, dependent on food from others. They include all animals and humans too.

In a **food chain**, one living thing eats the next. At the start are the producers, for example grass. The mouse eats the grass and is a **primary consumer**, a first-order consumer. The snake eats the mouse and is a secondary consumer. The eagle owl eats the snake and is the tertiary consumer at the top.

Plant-eaters such as roe deer, red deer, marmots or grasshoppers are primary consumers. Meat-eaters such as the lynx, fox or tawny owl hunt other animals. **Omnivores** such as the wild boar, brown bear or human eat plants and animals. Depending on the meal, they are therefore at different levels of the chain.

A lot of energy is lost at each level of the chain, because animals move about and keep themselves warm. As a rule of thumb, only about a tenth of the energy reaches the next level. That is why there are many more mice than owls. This is often shown as a **food pyramid**, which gets narrow at the top. Long chains with more than four or five levels are therefore rare.

In the Swiss forest, the **tawny owl** hunts mainly mice at night. In the Alps lives the bearded vulture, a scavenger with a wingspan of almost three metres. It eats mainly the bones of dead chamois and ibex and drops large bones onto rocks so that they break. The bearded vulture had been wiped out in the Alps and has been reintroduced since 1991, including in the Swiss National Park.

Besides producers and consumers there is a third group, the **decomposers**. They include fungi, bacteria and many soil animals. They break down dead plants and animals and turn them back into nutrients. In this way the cycle in the ecosystem is closed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that makes its own food, such as a plant using sunlight.
Dependent on food that other living things have made.
An animal that eats plants, the first level of consumers.
An animal that eats dead animals that it has not killed itself.
A living thing that breaks down dead matter, such as a fungus or a bacterium.

gewusst: A tawny owl can eat several hundred mice a year.
The bearded vulture has very strong stomach acid, with which it can even digest bones.
When a person eats salad, they are a primary consumer, and when they eat fish, they are a higher-order consumer.

teile.einleitung: A calendar is a system with which people divide time into days, weeks, months and years. It helps us to plan birthdays, holidays and festivals. Most countries in the world, including Switzerland, use the Gregorian calendar today.
wichtigste: A year has 365 days, and in a leap year 366 days.
February is the shortest month; it has 28 days, and in a leap year 29 days.
A year corresponds roughly to the time the Earth needs to go once around the Sun.
The Gregorian calendar was introduced in 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII.
Before that, the Julian calendar of Julius Caesar was used.
There are also calendars based on the Moon, for example the Islamic calendar.

abschnitte.text: A **calendar** divides time according to natural rhythms. A day is one turn of the Earth on its axis. A month was originally linked to the Moon, which takes about 29.5 days from full moon to full moon. A year is the time in which the Earth goes once around the Sun. The word comes from the Latin calendae; that was what the Romans called the first days of a month.

Our year has twelve months with 30 or 31 days; only **February** is shorter. The Earth takes about 365 days and just under 6 hours to go round the Sun. So that the calendar does not slip, there is a **leap year** every four years with a 29 February. Whole centuries such as 1900 are not leap years, unless they can be divided by 400, like the year 2000. With this trick, the calendar is very accurate.

The Roman general **Julius Caesar** introduced the **Julian calendar** in 45 BC. It already had leap years, but it was a tiny bit too long. After many centuries it was about ten days out from the solar year. That is why Pope **Gregory XIII** had the calendar improved in 1582. 4 October 1582 was followed directly by 15 October; ten days were simply skipped.

In Switzerland, the new calendar was not adopted everywhere at the same time. The Catholic areas switched soon after 1582. Many Reformed areas hesitated because the proposal came from the Pope, and only changed around the year 1700. So it could happen that different dates applied in neighbouring villages. Some municipalities in the Grisons did not switch until the beginning of the 19th century.

Not all calendars follow the Sun. The **Islamic calendar** is a lunar calendar, and its year has only about 354 days. That is why the month of fasting, Ramadan, moves about eleven days earlier each year. The Jewish and Chinese calendars combine the Moon and the Sun. That is why Chinese New Year falls on a different date in January or February every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A year with 366 days, because February has an extra day.
The most widely used calendar today, introduced in 1582.
A calendar whose months follow the phases of the Moon.
The time the Earth needs to go once around the Sun.

gewusst: Anyone whose birthday is on 29 February can only celebrate on the right day every four years.
The name September actually means “the seventh”, because the Roman year used to begin in March.
In Russia the Julian calendar was used until 1918, which is why the October Revolution took place in November according to our calendar.

teile.einleitung: Camels are large hoofed animals that are perfectly adapted to life in deserts and dry steppes. The best known are the one-humped dromedary and the two-humped Bactrian camel. Because they carry heavy loads through the desert, they are also called “ships of the desert”.
wichtigste: The dromedary has one hump, the Bactrian camel two.
Camels store fat in their hump, not water.
If a camel goes hungry for a long time, its hump becomes floppy and smaller.
A thirsty camel drinks a great deal of water in a short time.
A dromedary can go for more than a week without drinking.
In sandstorms a camel can close its nostrils.
The camel family also includes llamas and alpacas from South America.

abschnitte.text: The **dromedary** has one hump and lives mainly in North Africa and Arabia. The **Bactrian camel** has two humps and comes from Central Asia, where the winters are very cold. Both are now known almost only as domestic animals. In the Gobi Desert there is also the wild Bactrian camel, which is very rare and critically endangered.

In their **hump**, camels store fat as an energy reserve for hard times. If a camel goes hungry for a long time, the hump becomes floppy and tips to one side. In sandstorms it can close its nostrils, and long, double eyelashes protect its eyes. Broad, soft soles on its feet stop it from sinking into the sand.

A dromedary can go for more than a week without drinking, and even longer if it eats juicy plants. Its body temperature is allowed to rise by several degrees during the day, so it has to sweat less. When it is very thirsty, it drinks more than 100 litres of water in a few minutes. Its red blood cells are oval in shape and can cope with this well.

Camels are **herbivores**. They eat grasses, leaves and even thorny shrubs that other animals avoid. Like cows, they are **ruminants**: they chew their food several times. Thanks to their tough mouth and stomach, they can also make use of salty plants.

People have kept camels as domestic animals for several thousand years. Camels carry loads and people, in the past in large **caravans** through the Sahara and along the Silk Road. They provide milk, meat, wool and leather. In some Arab countries, camel racing is a popular sport.

In Switzerland you mainly see camels in the circus, in the zoo or on a few farms that offer rides. Much more common are their South American relatives, **llamas** and **alpacas**. They are kept for their wool or accompany hikers on trekking tours in the mountains. Together with the guanaco and the vicuña, they belong to the camel family.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bump on the back in which the camel stores fat.
Animals that bring their food back up from the stomach and chew it again.
A group of travellers with pack animals who journey together through the desert.
Mammals that walk on hooves or hoof-like toes.

gewusst: Many feral dromedaries live in Australia; they were once introduced there as pack animals.
The Bactrian camel has a much thicker coat than the dromedary, so that it can survive the icy winters of Central Asia.
When walking, camels move both legs on one side of the body forward at the same time; this is called pacing.

teile.einleitung: Kurt Wüthrich is a Swiss chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. He developed a method that makes the shape of proteins visible. For this he used nuclear magnetic resonance, NMR for short.
wichtigste: Kurt Wüthrich was born in 1938 in Aarberg in the canton of Bern.
He did most of his research at ETH Zurich.
His method determines the three-dimensional structure of proteins with NMR.
In 1984 his group determined the complete structure of a protein with NMR for the first time.
In 2002 he received half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The other half went to John Fenn and Koichi Tanaka for the mass spectrometry of large biomolecules.
He also worked at the Scripps Research Institute in California.

abschnitte.text: Kurt Wüthrich was born on 4 October 1938 in the small Bernese town of **Aarberg**. He studied chemistry, physics and mathematics at the University of Bern. He gained his doctorate at the University of Basel. After that he did research in the USA for a few years before returning to Switzerland.

From 1969 Wüthrich worked at **ETH Zurich**, where he later became professor of biophysics. There he built up a well-known research group over decades. From 2001 he also did research at the **Scripps Research Institute** in La Jolla, California. So he travelled back and forth between Zurich and the USA.

NMR stands for **nuclear magnetic resonance**, a measuring method using very strong magnets and radio waves. Certain atomic nuclei, above all hydrogen nuclei, behave like tiny compass needles in a magnetic field. With radio waves you can excite them and measure their signals. From these signals you can read which atoms lie close to one another. The same technology is also used in the MRI scanner in hospital.

**Proteins** are long chains that fold into a very particular shape, and this shape decides their job in the body. In the past, the shape could only be determined if the protein was made into a crystal. Wüthrich showed that NMR can also determine the structure in a liquid, which is how proteins occur in the body. In 1984 his group achieved the first complete protein structure with this method.

For his method, Wüthrich received half of the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry in 2002. The other half was shared by John Fenn and Koichi Tanaka, who had studied large biomolecules with mass spectrometry. Wüthrich also worked out the structure of the **prion protein**, which plays a role in diseases such as BSE, mad cow disease. Today his method is used in laboratories all over the world in research on medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Nuclear magnetic resonance, a measuring method using magnets and radio waves that examines atoms inside substances.
A building block of the body that carries out many tasks.
A wrongly folded protein that can cause diseases such as BSE.
One of the most famous science prizes in the world, awarded every year in Stockholm.

gewusst: When Kurt Wüthrich received the Nobel Prize, he was 64 years old.
The magnets in NMR machines are many thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: In a calibration, you check how accurately a measuring instrument measures. You compare its reading with a very precise reference, the standard, and write down the deviation. This means you can trust all measurements, whether on the scales in a shop, on a clinical thermometer or in a research laboratory.
wichtigste: In calibration, you compare the reading of a measuring instrument with a standard and document the deviation.
If the instrument is then set correctly, this is called adjustment.
Verification is an official test required by law.
Besides the measured value, a calibration certificate must also state the measurement uncertainty.
Measuring instruments age and must therefore be recalibrated regularly.
The standard ISO/IEC 17025 sets out what calibration laboratories must be able to do.

abschnitte.text: Every measuring instrument can be slightly wrong. When **calibrating**, you use the instrument to measure a quantity whose value is known very precisely. This precisely known quantity is called a **standard**, for example an especially exact weight. You note how much the reading differs from the correct value. The instrument itself is not changed in this step.

These three words are often confused. When **adjusting**, you set the instrument so that the deviation is as small as possible. **Verification** is an official test required by law, for example for scales in shops or petrol pumps at filling stations. In Switzerland, the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern is responsible for this, together with cantonal verification offices.

The result of a calibration is recorded in a **calibration certificate**. It states what deviation was measured. Very important is the **measurement uncertainty**, because no measurement is perfectly precise. Calibration laboratories must show, according to the standard **ISO/IEC 17025**, that they work competently. In this way every measurement can be traced back through a chain of comparisons to the international units.

Thermometers are calibrated at fixed temperature points. An important fixed point is the **triple point** of water at 0.01 °C, at which ice, liquid water and water vapour exist at the same time. Scales are tested with weights; the accuracy class **E1** according to OIML refers to the most precise ones of all. Blood pressure monitors, speed cameras and laboratory pipettes are also calibrated regularly.

In chemistry, you often measure how much of a substance is in a sample. To do this, you first measure several **standards** with known amounts. From these you make a **calibration curve**, which shows how the measurement signal is related to the concentration. With this curve you can then read off the concentration of an unknown sample from its signal.

Measuring instruments change over time through **ageing**, wear, knocks or changes in temperature. That is why fixed intervals are set, for example every year. This is especially important in hospitals, in aircraft engineering and in food inspection. An instrument that measures wrongly could cause great harm there.

begriffe.erklaerung: An especially precise measuring device that serves as a comparison for other instruments.
The range in which the true value of a measurement lies with high probability.
Setting a measuring instrument so that it shows readings as correctly as possible.
The official test of measuring instruments required by law.

gewusst: Since 2019 the kilogram has no longer been defined by a metal cylinder in Paris, but by a constant of nature.
The Swiss atomic clocks that keep official time are also constantly compared with clocks in other countries.

teile.einleitung: The Cambrian explosion was a time more than 500 million years ago when a great many new forms of animal appeared within a short time. Almost all the large groups of animals that exist today appear for the first time in the fossil record then. Researchers are still puzzling over why life became so varied at exactly this time.
wichtigste: The Cambrian began around 539 million years ago.
Many new animal body plans arose within a few million years.
For the first time there were large numbers of mineralised hard parts such as shells, which fossilised well.
Before the Cambrian lived the Ediacaran biota, made up of mostly soft-bodied creatures.
The Burgess Shale in Canada and Chengjiang in China even show soft-bodied animals.
One possible reason was a rise in the amount of oxygen.
Anomalocaris was one of the largest predators of this time.

abschnitte.text: The **Cambrian** is a period of Earth's history that began around 539 million years ago and lasted about 50 million years. The Cambrian explosion took place in its early part. For Earth's history this was a short period, even though it covered many millions of years. At that time all animals lived in the **sea**; there was hardly any life on land yet.

Before the Cambrian there were mainly single-celled organisms and simple living things. The **Ediacaran biota** consisted of soft creatures, often shaped like leaves or discs. They had no hard shells and no legs. For many of them, it is still not known exactly which animals they were related to.

In the Cambrian, animals with eyes, legs, armour and spines suddenly appeared. Very common were the **trilobites**, arthropods with a three-part shell. **Anomalocaris**, with grasping limbs on its head, was one of the largest predators and probably grew up to half a metre long. **Opabinia** had five eyes and a long, trunk-like grasping arm. Early relatives of the vertebrates were also already living then.

Normally only hard parts such as bones or shells become fossils. In the **Burgess Shale** in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, however, soft bodies have also been preserved. It was discovered in 1909 by the American Charles Walcott. Even older is the **Chengjiang** site in the Chinese province of Yunnan, around 518 million years old. Thousands of tiny animals have been found there in the finest detail.

Why so many animals arose at once has not been fully explained. One important reason was probably a rise in **oxygen** in the air and the sea, because larger animals need a lot of oxygen. The development of eyes and the race between predators and prey may also have sped up evolution. With **hard parts** such as shells, the animals protected themselves, and it is exactly these parts that fossilised especially well.

Some animals were so strange that researchers at first put them together wrongly. **Hallucigenia** was at first reconstructed upside down, because its spines were thought to be legs. Anomalocaris, too, was at first thought to be several different animals. Finds like these show how alien the living world of 500 million years ago looked.

begriffe.erklaerung: A petrified remain or imprint of a living thing from earlier times.
A period of Earth's history that began around 539 million years ago.
The basic structure of the body of a group of animals.
An extinct arthropod with a three-part shell that lived in the sea.

gewusst: The name Hallucigenia means, roughly, that the animal looked like a hallucination, like something from a dream.
Ultimately, humans too are descended from early animals that lived in the sea in the Cambrian.
Trilobites lived on for around another 250 million years before they died out.

teile.einleitung: James Watt was a Scottish inventor and engineer who lived from 1736 to 1819. He improved the steam engine so much that it became the driving force of industrialisation. The unit watt, which you find on every light bulb, is named after him.
wichtigste: James Watt was a Scottish engineer and inventor.
He greatly developed the steam engine and so drove industrialisation forward.
The first steam engine came from Thomas Newcomen; Watt made it much more economical and powerful.
His most important idea was a separate condenser, which he patented in 1769.
With the businessman Matthew Boulton he built steam engines in Birmingham.
The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
He introduced horsepower as a measure for comparison.

abschnitte.text: James Watt was born in 1736 in **Greenock** in Scotland. He learned the trade of an instrument maker. At the University of **Glasgow** he repaired and built scientific instruments. There he began to take an interest in the power of steam.

In 1763 Watt was asked to repair a model of the **Newcomen steam engine**. He noticed that it wasted a great deal of coal, because the cylinder was constantly cooled and heated again. His solution was a separate **condenser**, in which the steam is cooled. This kept the cylinder hot, and the engine needed much less fuel.

From 1775 Watt worked with the businessman **Matthew Boulton** in Birmingham. Their company built hundreds of steam engines. Watt invented further improvements that turned the up-and-down movement into a **rotary movement**. This meant steam engines could drive spinning machines, mills and pumps in mines.

Steam engines made factories independent of water wheels and wind. From the late 18th century, the **Industrial Revolution** changed first England and then the whole of Europe. Later, steam engines also powered locomotives and ships. Historic **paddle steamers** still sail on Swiss lakes today, for example on Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva.
