To sell his engines, Watt compared their power with that of horses. This is how the unit **horsepower** came about. In 1882 the unit of power was named the **watt** in his honour. A kettle, for example, has about 2000 watts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that produces movement using the power of hot steam.
In a steam engine, a container in which the steam cools down and turns back into water.
The period in which machines and factories largely replaced work by hand.
The unit of power, that is, how much energy is converted per second.

gewusst: Watt did not invent the steam engine; Thomas Newcomen had already built one in 1712.
Watt also invented an early copying machine for letters.
The portraits of James Watt and Matthew Boulton appeared on a British 50-pound note.

teile.einleitung: A lab coat is a coat, usually white, that you wear when working in a laboratory. It protects skin and clothes from chemicals, dirt and germs. For many people it has become the sign of a researcher.
wichtigste: A lab coat protects skin and clothes.
Lab coats are usually white.
Many are made of cotton, because it does not melt onto the skin in a fire.
The sleeves reach down to the wrist.
In the laboratory you wear the coat fastened.
Press studs let you take the coat off quickly in an emergency.
You take it off before you leave the laboratory.

abschnitte.text: The **lab coat** is a long coat that usually reaches below the knees. It is part of the **protective equipment** in the laboratory, together with safety goggles and gloves. It is worn in chemistry labs, in biology, in hospitals and in food inspection. In school labs, too, young people often put on a coat for experiments.

In experiments, acids, alkalis or dyes can splash. The coat catches such splashes before they reach skin or clothing. In biological labs it keeps **germs** away from your own clothes. That is why you take it off before leaving the laboratory, so that nothing is carried outside. Dirty coats are washed separately or thrown away.

Many lab coats are made of **cotton** or a mixture with synthetic fibres. Cotton does burn, but it does not melt and so does not stick to the skin in a fire. For work with fire or flammable substances there are also flame-resistant coats. The long sleeves reach down to the wrist and often have tight cuffs. **Press studs** can be pulled open with one tug if the coat has to come off quickly in an emergency.

You always wear the coat fastened, otherwise it does not protect the clothes underneath. Long hair is tied back, and you wear sturdy, closed shoes. There is no eating or drinking in the laboratory. **Safety goggles** are compulsory for many experiments, because the eyes are especially sensitive.

On white fabric you can see stains and dirt at once. White has also stood for cleanliness and **hygiene** for a long time. Since the end of the 19th century, doctors have also often worn a white coat. In some areas there are also coloured coats, such as blue or green, for example in the operating theatre.

In films, comics and adverts you can often recognise researchers at once by their white coat. It has become a **symbol** of science and expert knowledge. But in many researchers' daily work it is not always needed, for example at the computer or at physics measuring instruments. It really matters where people work with chemicals, samples or living cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A room in which experts carry out experiments and examine samples.
Clothing and equipment that protect the body from dangers at work.
A fastener made of two parts that opens at once when pulled.
Measures for cleanliness so that diseases do not spread.

gewusst: Because press studs can be ripped open with one tug, a lab coat can be taken off in a second.
Doctors used to wear black clothing; the white coat only caught on with modern hygiene.
In some schools, young people get their first lab coat in chemistry lessons.

teile.einleitung: Convergent evolution means that unrelated living things develop similar features independently of each other. This happens when they live in similar surroundings and face similar challenges. So the shark and the dolphin look alike, although one is a fish and the other a mammal.
wichtigste: In convergent evolution, unrelated species develop similar features.
The shark and the dolphin have a similar shape because both are adapted to fast swimming.
Organs with the same task but a different origin are called analogous organs.
Some spurges in Africa look like cacti.
The extinct ichthyosaur looked amazingly similar to a dolphin.
The squid independently developed a lens eye like that of vertebrates.
Insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats learned to fly independently of each other.

abschnitte.text: The word **convergence** comes from the Latin “convergere” and means to come together. It refers to living things from different groups coming to look more alike in the course of evolution. The reason is natural selection: in similar surroundings, similar solutions win through. So the similarity says nothing about a close relationship.

Sharks are fish; dolphins are mammals and breathe with lungs. Even so, both have a streamlined body, a dorsal fin and a powerful tail fin. The **ichthyosaur**, a marine reptile from the time of the dinosaurs, looked almost the same too. Water slows things down a lot, which is why this torpedo shape is the best solution for fast swimmers.

Powered flight arose independently at least four times: in insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats. The wings all work in a similar way, but are built quite differently. Insect wings consist of thin membranes without bones, bird wings of feathers and arm bones. Such organs with the same task but a different origin are called **analogous organs**. Organs with the same origin but perhaps a different task, on the other hand, are called homologous.

The squid has a **lens eye** that is very similar to the human eye, although squid are molluscs. In the deserts of Africa grow some **spurges** that look like cacti, with thick, green stems and spines. Real cacti, on the other hand, come almost entirely from the Americas. Both store water in their stems because it rarely rains in deserts.

In Australia, marsupials lived separately from other mammals for a long time. Even so, lookalikes of well-known animals arose there. The **marsupial mole** digs underground and looks very like the mole, with small eyes and digging claws. The extinct thylacine was reminiscent of a wolf, and gliders sail through the air in a similar way to flying squirrels.

Convergent evolution shows how strongly the environment shapes the form of living things. For researchers, though, it is also a trap: similar appearance can be misleading about relationships. That is why today the **genome** is compared as well. Engineers learn from such solutions in nature, for example when building boats or aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Organs with the same task that arose independently of each other.
Organs with the same origin, even if they look different, such as an arm and a wing.
Living things that are better adapted survive more often and pass on their features.

gewusst: Bats and dolphins have also independently developed echolocation, with which they find their way by sound.
Crab-like body shapes have arisen independently several times among crustaceans; experts jokingly call this carcinisation.
Hummingbirds in the Americas and sunbirds in Africa look similar and both drink flower nectar, but they are not closely related.

teile.einleitung: Jacques Dubochet is a Swiss biophysicist from the canton of Vaud. In 2017 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing cryo-electron microscopy. With this method, tiny building blocks of life can be seen almost as they really are.
wichtigste: Jacques Dubochet was born in 1942 in Aigle in the canton of Vaud.
He was a professor at the University of Lausanne.
In 2017 he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
He shared the prize with Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson.
His most important contribution was freezing samples in a flash in glass-like ice.
Cryo-electron microscopy was used to work out the spike protein of the coronavirus quickly.
In his CV he wrote humorously about his dyslexia.

abschnitte.text: Jacques Dubochet was born on 8 June 1942 in **Aigle** in the canton of Vaud. At school he struggled, because he had **dyslexia**, a difficulty with reading and spelling. Later, in his CV, he wrote with humour that he had been the first officially recognised dyslexic in the canton of Vaud. Even so, he studied physics in Lausanne and later earned a doctorate in biophysics.

With an **electron microscope** you can see much smaller things than with a light microscope. But the samples have to be in a vacuum, a space with no air. Biomolecules dry out there and lose their shape. Frozen water also forms ice crystals, which disturb the pictures and damage the samples.

At the European Molecular Biology Laboratory in Heidelberg, Dubochet's team found a solution in the early 1980s. They froze thin layers of water so quickly in very cold liquid ethane that no crystals could form. The water solidified into **glass-like ice**; this is called vitrification. In this way viruses and proteins keep their natural shape.

From 1987 Dubochet was a professor at the **University of Lausanne**. For developing **cryo-electron microscopy** he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017. He shared it with the German-American Joachim Frank and the Briton Richard Henderson. Frank had developed computer methods for analysing the images, and Henderson had been the first to image a protein at high resolution with this kind of microscopy.

Today laboratories all over the world work with cryo-electron microscopy. During the Covid-19 pandemic, researchers used it to show the structure of the coronavirus's **spike protein** quickly. Such knowledge helps in developing medicines and vaccines. Dubochet lives in Morges on Lake Geneva and has been campaigning publicly for climate protection for years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A microscope that uses electrons instead of light and so makes the tiniest things visible.
A prefix from Greek that has to do with cold or ice.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.
A difficulty with reading and spelling.
An important building block of all living things.

gewusst: After the Nobel Prize, Dubochet's CV with its mention of his dyslexia became known worldwide and encouraged many children.
The prefix cryo comes from the Greek word “kryos”, which means cold or frost.
In the microscope, the frozen samples are kept at well below minus 150 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: The litre is a unit of volume, which means how much fits into a container. Milk, water, petrol and squash are measured in litres. One litre is exactly the same as a cube with edges 10 centimetres long.
wichtigste: The litre is abbreviated l.
One litre has 10 decilitres, 100 centilitres or 1000 millilitres.
One litre is exactly as much as one cubic decimetre.
A large PET bottle of mineral water holds 1.5 litres.
A full bath holds about 150 litres of water.
An ordinary drinking glass holds about 2 decilitres.
A cow in Switzerland gives about 25 litres of milk a day.

abschnitte.text: A litre is as much as fits into a cube with edges 10 centimetres long. This cube is also called a **cubic decimetre**, so 1 litre equals 1 dm³. A litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram. That is no accident: the kilogram used to be defined by the weight of a litre of water. The litre is not one of the base units, but it is approved worldwide alongside the **cubic metre**.

A litre is divided into smaller units. A **decilitre** is a tenth of a litre; in Switzerland the decilitre is very common in recipes and restaurants. A centilitre is a hundredth of a litre, and a millilitre a thousandth. A millilitre is as much as a cube with edges one centimetre long. Large amounts are measured in hectolitres: 1 hectolitre is 100 litres.

In shops you often find milk in one-litre cartons and mineral water in bottles of 1.5 litres or 5 decilitres. A drinking glass holds about 2 decilitres, and a cleaning bucket about 10 litres. A full bath holds about 150 litres. When doing sums, you can add litres together: 2 litres of squash and 3 litres of water make 5 litres. The fuel consumption of a car is also given in litres per 100 kilometres.

A dairy cow in Switzerland gives about 25 litres of milk a day. A person in Switzerland uses about 140 litres of water a day at home, mainly for the toilet, the shower and the washing machine. A swimming pool 25 metres long contains several hundred thousand litres. For very large amounts of water, for example in reservoirs, people therefore calculate in **cubic metres**. One cubic metre is 1000 litres.

The litre was introduced in France in 1795, when the metric system was created there. The name comes from an older French measure of volume called the “litron”. With the metric system, the litre spread throughout Europe. In Switzerland, old measures such as the Mass and the Saum were replaced by metric units in the 19th century. Today the litre is known almost everywhere in the world; only in the USA do people often still use **gallons** in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much space something takes up or how much fits into a container.
A tenth of a litre, abbreviated dl.
A thousandth of a litre, abbreviated ml.
A cube with edges 1 metre long; it holds 1000 litres.

gewusst: Because a small l is easily confused with the number 1, the litre may also be abbreviated with a capital L.
A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram, but a litre of olive oil weighs less, because oil is lighter than water.
Household water use in Switzerland would fill roughly one full bath per person every day.

teile.einleitung: The kelvin is the unit of temperature in the International System of Units. The kelvin scale begins at absolute zero, the lowest temperature there can possibly be. That is why it has no negative values and is used especially in science.
wichtigste: The kelvin is a unit of temperature.
0 kelvin corresponds to minus 273.15 °C, absolute zero.
20 °C is 293.15 K, and water boils at 373.15 K at normal air pressure.
A temperature difference of 1 °C is the same size as 1 K.
Kelvin is written without “degrees”, for example 300 K.
The unit is named after Lord Kelvin.
There are no negative temperatures on the kelvin scale.

abschnitte.text: The **kelvin**, with the symbol K, is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, SI. It measures temperature, that is, how warm or cold something is. In everyday life in Switzerland we use degrees Celsius, but in science people often use kelvin. No degree sign is written: 300 K is correct, not 300 °K.

The kelvin scale begins at **absolute zero**, at 0 K. This corresponds to minus 273.15 °C. Temperature has to do with the movement of the tiniest particles: the warmer something is, the more strongly they jiggle. At absolute zero the particles would have the least possible movement, and it cannot get any colder. That is why there are no negative kelvin values.

To convert Celsius into kelvin, you add 273.15. So 20 °C equals 293.15 K, and water boils at 373.15 K. A step of one degree Celsius is exactly the same size as a step of one kelvin. If the temperature rises from 15 °C to 25 °C, it has therefore risen by 10 K. That is why temperature differences in science are often given in kelvin.

The unit is named after **Lord Kelvin**, whose real name was William Thomson. He was a British physicist who lived from 1824 to 1907. He worked for many years in Glasgow in Scotland. Thomson showed that there must be a lowest possible temperature and proposed a temperature scale that starts there.

On light bulb packaging, too, there is often a figure in kelvin, the so-called **colour temperature**. Warm white light has about 2700 K, cool white daylight considerably more. The surface of the Sun is around 5800 K hot. In empty space, a background radiation of only about 2.7 K is measured.

Absolute zero can never be reached completely, only approached very closely. Researchers in laboratories cool substances down to tiny fractions of a kelvin. At such low temperatures substances show strange properties: some conduct electricity with no resistance at all; this is called **superconductivity**. Since 2019 the kelvin has been defined by a constant of nature, the Boltzmann constant.

begriffe.erklaerung: The lowest possible temperature, 0 K or minus 273.15 °C.
A unit of the International System of Units, which applies almost everywhere in the world.
A figure in kelvin that describes whether light seems warm or cool.
The property of some substances of conducting electricity without loss when very cold.

gewusst: The kelvin is the only SI base unit named after a noble title.
At around 77 K, about minus 196 °C, liquid nitrogen is ice cold.
Light bulb packaging often shows a temperature in kelvin, even though the bulb is not nearly that hot.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO₂ for short, is an invisible gas found in the air. It is produced mainly when wood, coal, oil or petrol are burned, and we also breathe it out ourselves. Plants need it to grow, but too much of it warms the Earth's climate.
wichtigste: Carbon dioxide consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
It is produced when wood, coal, oil and petrol are burned.
Humans and animals breathe out CO₂.
Plants take in CO₂ and, with sunlight, make sugar and oxygen from it.
CO₂ is a greenhouse gas and contributes to the warming of the Earth.
Frozen CO₂ is called dry ice.
The fizz in sparkling mineral water is dissolved CO₂.

abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide is a colourless and odourless gas. One **molecule** of it consists of one carbon atom (C) and two oxygen atoms (O), hence the formula CO₂. It is slightly heavier than air and therefore collects in hollows and cellars. CO₂ makes up only about 0.04 per cent of the air. Even so, this small proportion has a big effect on the climate.

CO₂ is always produced when substances containing carbon burn, such as wood, coal, natural gas or petrol. Some of these fuels are called **fossil fuels**, because they formed from the remains of ancient plants and animals. In our bodies, too, food is “burned” with oxygen, producing CO₂, which we breathe out. Volcanoes also give off CO₂. When dough or grape juice ferments, yeast produces CO₂, which makes the dough rise.

Plants take in CO₂ through small openings in their leaves. With the help of sunlight and water they make sugar from it and give off oxygen. This process is called **photosynthesis**. Forests, moors and oceans therefore store large amounts of carbon. In this way a cycle is formed between living things, the air and the sea.

CO₂ is a **greenhouse gas**: it lets sunlight through but holds back part of the heat given off by the Earth. Since the start of industrialisation, the CO₂ content of the air has risen from around 280 to over 420 parts per million (as of about 2024). The main reason is the burning of coal, oil and natural gas. As a result it is getting warmer on Earth, and in Switzerland, for example, the glaciers are melting. Switzerland has set itself the goal of emitting net zero greenhouse gases by 2050.

CO₂ is used in many ways in everyday life. As **carbonation** it makes mineral water and lemonade fizzy. Some fire extinguishers spray CO₂, because it takes the oxygen away from the fire. At minus 78 degrees CO₂ becomes solid **dry ice**, which turns directly into gas without melting and is used for cooling and for fog effects. The Zurich company Climeworks has developed plants that filter CO₂ directly out of the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat like the glass of a greenhouse.
The process by which plants use sunlight to make sugar and oxygen from CO₂ and water.
Coal, oil and natural gas, which formed millions of years ago from the remains of plants and animals.
Frozen carbon dioxide, which is very cold and turns directly into gas.

gewusst: A person breathes out roughly one kilogram of CO₂ a day.
Dry ice does not melt into a liquid but turns directly into gas.
The bubbles that make bread and cakes light when baking are often CO₂.

teile.einleitung: Ida Pfeiffer was a traveller and writer from Vienna. In the 19th century she travelled around the world twice as a woman on her own, something hardly anyone thought possible at the time. Her travel books were translated into many languages.
wichtigste: Ida Pfeiffer was born in Vienna in 1797 and died there in 1858.
She began her first great journey at about 44 years old.
She travelled around the world alone twice.
In 1845 she visited Iceland and Scandinavia.
With her travel books she earned the money for new journeys.
She collected insects, plants and other natural objects for museums.
She is regarded as one of the first women to go on research journeys alone.

abschnitte.text: Ida Pfeiffer was born on 14 October 1797 in **Vienna**; her maiden name was Reyer. She grew up with several brothers, liked to wear boys' clothes as a child and wanted to see the world from an early age. Later she married a lawyer named Pfeiffer and brought up two sons. Only when the sons were grown up could she make her dream of travelling come true.

In 1842, at about 44 years old, Ida Pfeiffer set off on her first great journey. She travelled via Constantinople, today's Istanbul, to the **Holy Land** and to Egypt. Her diary was published as a book and became a success. In 1845 she travelled to the cold north, to **Iceland** and Scandinavia.

From 1846 to 1848 she travelled around the world for the first time, visiting Brazil, Chile, Tahiti, China, India and Persia, among other places. From 1851 to 1855 came her second **journey around the world**, which took her to South Africa, to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and to America. She travelled very cheaply, often on simple ships, on foot or on horseback. She often lived with local families along the way.

Ida Pfeiffer wrote a **travel book** about every journey. With the money from the sales she paid for the next journey. She also collected **insects**, plants, shells and rocks and sold them to museums, for example in Vienna and London. Some of the animal species she brought back had been unknown to science until then.

In 1857 Ida Pfeiffer travelled to **Madagascar**. There she fell seriously ill, probably with malaria. She returned to Vienna and died there on 27 October 1858. Famous researchers such as Alexander von Humboldt valued her work, and the Geographical Society in Berlin made her an honorary member.

begriffe.erklaerung: A book in which someone tells of their journeys and experiences.
A journey on which you want to get to know and study foreign countries, people and nature more closely.
A dangerous disease that is passed on by mosquitoes in warm countries.
A person whom a society honours for special achievements.

gewusst: Ida Pfeiffer had hardly any money and therefore travelled much more simply than most researchers of her time.
Her books were translated into several languages, including English and French.
Ida Pfeiffer covered tens of thousands of kilometres on her journeys, all without aeroplanes or cars.

teile.einleitung: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with at least one other substance, usually of two or more metals. Mixing them produces a material with new properties, which is, for example, harder or rusts less. Bronze, brass and steel are well-known alloys.
wichtigste: An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals.
Sometimes a non-metal such as carbon is also mixed in.
Alloys have different properties from the pure metals.
Bronze is made of copper and tin.
Brass is made of copper and zinc.
Steel is an alloy of iron with a little carbon.
Swiss coins are also made of alloys.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is made when you melt a metal and mix other substances into it. Usually these are other metals, sometimes non-metals such as carbon. When it cools, the mixture becomes solid again. The result looks like a metal and has typical metal properties. But it behaves differently from each of its single parts.

Pure metals are often too soft or rust easily. Pure gold, for example, can almost be bent with a fingernail. When you mix metals, they usually become **harder** and stronger. Some alloys hardly rust or melt at a low temperature, like the solder used for soldering electronics. In this way the right material can be made for every purpose.

**Bronze** is an alloy of copper and a little tin and one of the oldest in the world. It is much harder than pure copper. Because bronze was so important for tools, weapons and jewellery, a whole era is named after it, the **Bronze Age**. In central Europe, including Switzerland, it lasted from about 2200 to 800 BC. Bells and statues are still cast in bronze today.

**Steel** consists of iron and a little carbon and is the most important material for bridges, cars and machines. If you add chromium and nickel, you get rust-free **stainless steel**, from which many saucepans and much cutlery are made. Brass, made of copper and zinc, shines golden yellow and is used for door handles and brass instruments such as trumpets. Light aluminium alloys are needed for aircraft and bike frames. Gold jewellery is almost always an alloy too: 18-carat gold, for example, contains 75 per cent gold.

The Swiss franc coins and the 10 and 20 centime coins are made of an alloy of copper and nickel. The gold-coloured 5 centime coin is made of aluminium bronze. In the Swiss **watch industry**, special alloys are used for cases, springs and gear wheels. Some watch companies have even developed their own gold alloys. So alloys also play a big role in a typically Swiss craft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal and at least one other substance, usually another metal.
A hard alloy of copper and tin.
An alloy of iron and a little carbon.
Steel that hardly rusts thanks to additions such as chromium.

gewusst: Pure gold is so soft that jewellery made from it would quickly get scratched and bent.
Some alloys, called shape-memory alloys, return to their original shape when warmed after being bent.

teile.einleitung: An insect hotel is a nesting aid in which wild bees and other insects find space for their young. It is usually made of wood, hollow plant stems and other natural materials. You can put it up in the garden or on the balcony and so watch nature from very close up.
wichtigste: An insect hotel serves as a nesting place for insects.
Wild bees are the most common guests.
It is often filled with hollow plant stems and wooden blocks with small holes.
It belongs in a sunny spot.
A small roof protects it from damp.
Flowering plants are needed nearby so that the bees find food.
It is best to put up an insect hotel before spring.

abschnitte.text: An **insect hotel** is an artificial **nesting aid** for insects. In nature, many insects nest in old tree trunks, cracks in walls or hollow stems. Such places have become rare in tidy gardens and towns. An insect hotel partly replaces them. The insects lay their eggs in it, and the young develop safely in the tubes.

The most common guests are **wild bees**, for example the **red mason bee** or leafcutter bees. Wild bees are peaceful and almost never sting. Potter wasps and digger wasps also like to use the tubes. There are more than 600 species of wild bee in Switzerland. Most of them, however, nest in the ground and not in insect hotels.

You fill a wooden frame with **hollow plant stems** such as reed or bamboo. Into blocks of hardwood you drill **small holes** with a diameter of about 2 to 10 millimetres. The holes should be smooth and closed at the back, so that the insects do not injure their wings. A small **roof** protects the hotel from rain, because damp makes the young go mouldy. Pine cones and straw look pretty, but wild bees hardly use them.

An insect hotel belongs in a **sunny**, sheltered spot, ideally facing south or south-east. It should stand firmly and not sway in the wind. It is best to put it up before spring, because that is when the first bees hatch. Very important are **flowering plants** nearby, because without food even the finest hotel is no use. Wild bees often fly only a few hundred metres.

Wild bees pollinate many wild and crop plants, for example fruit trees. Many species are endangered in Switzerland because habitats and flower meadows are disappearing. An insect hotel alone will not save the wild bees, but it helps and draws attention to them. Even more important are native flowers, patches of bare ground and a bit of untidiness in the garden. If you watch an insect hotel in spring, you can see bees sealing tubes with clay or bits of leaf.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial place where animals can raise their young.
A wild species of bee that usually lives alone rather than in a colony.
The transfer of pollen so that plants can produce fruit and seeds.
The eggs and young of insects.

gewusst: The red mason bee seals its nesting tubes with clay, like a tiny bricklayer.
Leafcutter bees cut round pieces out of leaves and use them to line their nesting tubes.
Most wild bees live for only a few weeks as flying bees.

teile.einleitung: John Snow was an English doctor who lived from 1813 to 1858. Using a map, he proved that the dangerous disease cholera is spread through polluted drinking water. That is why he is regarded as one of the founders of epidemiology, the science of how diseases spread.
wichtigste: John Snow was born in York in England in 1813.
In his time most people believed in the miasma theory, the idea that bad air makes people ill.
Snow suspected that cholera is spread through water contaminated with human waste.
In 1854 he identified the pump in Broad Street in London as the source of an outbreak.
With a map of the deaths he showed the connection.
He had the pump handle removed so that nobody could fetch water any more.
Snow was also a pioneer of anaesthesia.

abschnitte.text: John Snow was born on 15 March 1813 in **York**, the son of a labourer. As a teenager he was apprenticed to a doctor. Later he worked as a doctor in **London**, at that time a huge and very dirty city. He lived modestly, drank no alcohol and ate no meat. Snow died in 1858 at only 45.

**Cholera** is a disease of the gut that causes severe diarrhoea and dries the body out. Untreated, it can kill within hours. It spreads mainly through water contaminated with human waste. In the 19th century there were several great waves of cholera in Europe. At the time most experts believed in the **miasma theory**, according to which foul air brings the disease.

In late summer 1854, hundreds of people died of cholera within a few days in the London district of **Soho**. Snow marked all the deaths on a street map. The dots clustered around the water pump in **Broad Street**. He persuaded the authorities to remove the **pump handle**. It was striking that the workers of a nearby brewery hardly fell ill, because they drank beer or had water from their own well.

Snow also compared two London water companies that supplied households in the same streets. One company took its water from the **Thames** further upstream, where it was cleaner. The other drew it where the city's sewage was already flowing in. Far more people died of cholera among the customers of the second company. This comparison was a strong argument for his theory.

Snow was also an expert in **anaesthesia**. He researched how to dose ether and **chloroform** safely, so that patients feel no pain during operations. He developed his own devices for this. Even Queen Victoria had him anaesthetise her.

Snow's ideas only became accepted after his death. The Italian anatomist **Filippo Pacini** had already described the pathogen in 1854, but hardly anyone took notice. Only Robert Koch finally proved the bacterium in 1884. After that, cities such as London built sewers and waterworks. Today there is a replica of the famous pump in London, and Snow's map is regarded as a milestone of **epidemiology**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies how diseases spread in the population.
Poisonous, foul air that people used to think caused diseases.
Numbing or putting someone to sleep so that they feel no pain during an operation.
A tiny living thing, for example a bacterium, that causes a disease.

gewusst: In front of a London pub in today's Broadwick Street there is a replica of the pump, but without a handle.
Snow worked with the vicar Henry Whitehead, who at first doubted Snow's theory and later supported him.

teile.einleitung: A laboratory is a room in which researchers do experiments, examine samples and discover new things. It has special equipment such as microscopes, test tubes and scales. The word comes from the Latin “laborare”, which means “to work”.
wichtigste: A laboratory is a workroom for experiments and tests.
There are laboratories for chemistry, biology, medicine, physics and much more.
Typical equipment includes test tubes, pipettes, Bunsen burners and microscopes.
Strict safety rules apply in the laboratory.
Lab coats, safety goggles and gloves protect the people working there.
Many new medicines are developed in laboratories.
One of the largest research laboratories in the world, CERN, is near Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A **laboratory**, or lab, is a room specially equipped for experiments and measurements. Work there is precise, clean and follows fixed rules. Researchers ask a question, plan an **experiment** and write down all the results. Then others check whether they get the same result. This is how reliable knowledge is built up.

In a chemistry lab you find **test tubes**, beakers and conical flasks made of heat-resistant glass. With pipettes you can measure tiny amounts of liquid accurately. The **Bunsen burner**, named after the chemist Robert Bunsen, produces a hot gas flame. Biology and medical labs have microscopes, centrifuges and fridges for samples. Today many labs also have computers and robots that check thousands of samples automatically.

In the laboratory people often work with fire, acids or germs that cause disease. That is why everyone wears a **lab coat**, safety goggles and often gloves. Dangerous fumes are sucked away in a fume cupboard so that nobody breathes them in. Eating and drinking are forbidden in the laboratory. Hazard symbols on bottles show whether a substance is, for example, poisonous or flammable.

There are many kinds of laboratory. In a medical lab, for example, blood samples are examined so that doctors can identify an illness. In a food lab, tests check whether food is clean and safe. At school there is often a science room where pupils do their own experiments. Computer chips even need **clean rooms**, where there is hardly a speck of dust in the air.

Near Geneva lies **CERN**, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, which was founded in 1954. There, thousands of researchers from all over the world study the smallest particles. In Aargau there is the Paul Scherrer Institute, the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. In Basel, pharmaceutical companies run large laboratories where medicines are developed. ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne also have many research labs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned test used to check a question.
A narrow glass tube in which small amounts of substances are mixed or heated.
A gas burner that produces a hot, adjustable flame in the laboratory.
A room with especially clean air, with almost no dust.

gewusst: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989 so that researchers could share their results more easily.
The discovery of penicillin began in 1928 when Alexander Fleming noticed a mouldy dish of bacteria in his laboratory.

teile.einleitung: The lotus effect describes how some plant leaves keep themselves clean. Water forms round beads, rolls off and takes the dirt with it. The effect is named after the lotus plant, whose leaves always look clean even in a muddy pond.
wichtigste: On a lotus leaf, water beads up and takes dirt with it.
This is called self-cleaning.
The surface of the leaf has tiny bumps and is coated with wax.
A drop rests on the tips of the bumps above trapped cushions of air.
Nasturtiums also show a strong lotus effect.
If the fine structures are rubbed away, the effect is lost.
The lotus effect is used in bionics for paints and coatings.

abschnitte.text: The **lotus plant** grows in water, mainly in Asia, and has large round leaves above the water's surface. When rain falls on them, round drops form and roll off straight away. As they do so, they take dust and dirt with them, and the leaf cleans itself. This **self-cleaning** is called the lotus effect.

Under an electron microscope you can see that the lotus leaf is covered with **tiny bumps**. These bumps are also coated with even finer **wax crystals**; scientists speak of **micro- and nanostructures**. A drop of water touches only the tips and rests on a cushion of trapped air. This state is called the Cassie-Baxter state. Dirt particles hardly stick either, and they cling to the drop instead of to the leaf.

How strongly a surface repels water is shown by the **contact angle** between the drop and the surface. If it is below 90 degrees, the surface counts as **hydrophilic**, and water wets it well. On the lotus leaf the angle is greater than 150 degrees, and the drop is almost a sphere. Such surfaces are called **superhydrophobic**. If the water fills the hollows instead, this is called the Wenzel state, and the drop sticks more strongly.

In Swiss gardens, the **nasturtium** shows a very strong lotus effect, and cabbage leaves also let water bead off well. The **pond skater** can walk on water thanks to water-repellent hairs on its legs. A floating fern holds a layer of air on its leaves under water with what is called the **Salvinia effect**. In the rose petal effect, drops stay stuck to the petal despite a large contact angle.

The German botanist **Wilhelm Barthlott** studied the effect from the 1970s at the University of Bonn and gave it its name. Following this model, there are now **facade paints** from which rain washes off the dirt. Roof tiles, textiles and glass are also coated in this way. Because the fine structures are delicate, the effect is lost if the surface is rubbed hard.

You can watch the lotus effect at home. Sprinkle a little dust or cocoa powder on a nasturtium leaf and then drip some water onto it. The drops roll off and collect the powder. If you rub the leaf with your finger, the water beads off less well at that spot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A surface stays clean because water takes the dirt away with it.
Water-repellent: water forms round drops.
Water-loving: water spreads out flat.
The angle that a drop makes with the surface it is lying on.

gewusst: In Asia, because of its clean leaves, the lotus flower is a symbol of purity in several religions.
In Japan there are yoghurt lids with a water-repellent coating modelled on the lotus leaf, to which hardly any yoghurt sticks.

teile.einleitung: Toads are amphibians with a sturdy body, short legs and warty skin. Many people find them creepy, but they are harmless and very useful snail hunters. In Switzerland the common toad is the best-known species.
wichtigste: Like frogs and newts, toads are amphibians.
Their skin is usually drier and bumpier than that of frogs.
The bumps on the skin are glands that can release a defensive poison.
If you touch a toad you do not get warts, because warts are caused by viruses.
Common toads like to eat snails, insects, worms and spiders.
In spring many toads migrate to the waters where they spawn.
Small fences along roads protect the migrating toads from traffic.

abschnitte.text: Toads have a stocky body, a broad snout and rather short hind legs. That is why they hop less than frogs and prefer to walk slowly. Their skin is dry and covered with many bumps, which are **skin glands**. Behind the eyes there are two large swellings, the **parotoid glands**. The eyes of the common toad glow copper-red to golden.

When a toad is attacked, its glands give off a milky, bitter slime. It contains poisons called **bufotoxins**. For people the poison is harmless after normal touching, but you should wash your hands afterwards. Dogs that take a toad in their mouth can become ill. The idea that toads give you warts is an old mistake, because warts are caused by **viruses**.

For most of the year toads live on land, for example in woods, gardens, meadows and cellars. During the day they hide under stones, leaves or wood and go hunting at dusk. They eat snails, beetles, woodlice, worms and spiders. This makes them welcome helpers in the vegetable garden. They spend the winter in **hibernation** in frost-free hiding places.

In spring, when the nights become milder and damp, common toads migrate to the pond where they themselves hatched. This **toad migration** often crosses roads, where many animals are run over. Volunteers therefore put up low fences that the toads walk along until they fall into buckets. In the morning, helpers carry the buckets safely across the road. Some roads also have permanent **toad tunnels**.

In the pond, common toads lay long strings of spawn among the water plants. Small black **tadpoles** hatch from them and breathe in the water with gills. After a few weeks they grow legs, the tail disappears, and they turn into tiny toads. In summer the young toads leave the pond in their thousands.

The common toad, the natterjack toad and the green toad live in Switzerland. The **natterjack toad** has a yellow stripe on its back and needs small, warm pools, for example in gravel pits. Because many wetlands have disappeared, the natterjack toad and the green toad are considered endangered. All amphibians are protected in Switzerland, and you are not allowed to catch or kill them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live first in water and later mostly on land, for example frogs, toads and newts.
The larva of frogs and toads, which lives in water and has a tail.
Eggs of amphibians or fish that are laid in water.
Poisons from the skin glands of toads.

gewusst: Toads often return to exactly the same water in which they grew up as tadpoles.
The cane toad was released in Australia in 1935 and has become a huge pest there.
Toads do not drink with their mouths but take in water through their skin.

teile.einleitung: Lidar is a measuring method that scans the surroundings with laser light and creates exact three-dimensional pictures from this. With lidar you can even measure the ground through forests. This is how researchers have discovered hidden ruins of ancient cultures that were concealed under the jungle.
wichtigste: Lidar stands for “Light Detection and Ranging”.
A lidar device sends out laser pulses and measures how long the light takes to reach the target and come back.
All the measuring points together are called a point cloud.
For large areas, lidar data are usually collected from aircraft or helicopters.
Some pulses reach the ground through gaps in the leaves, so measurements can be made even under forest.
From the ground points, a digital terrain model without vegetation and buildings is calculated.
In 2018, lidar revealed tens of thousands of unknown Maya structures in northern Guatemala.

abschnitte.text: Lidar is the abbreviation for **Light Detection and Ranging**, roughly “detecting and measuring distance with light”. It works much like radar, only with laser light instead of radio waves. A device sends out very short **laser pulses**, often hundreds of thousands a second. From these, an exact 3D image of land, buildings or trees is created.

Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres a second. The device measures the time it takes for a laser pulse to be reflected by an object and come back. From this **travel time** it calculates the distance. Together with the exact position, which is found by satellite navigation, each hit gives a point in space. All the points together make a **point cloud**.

When measuring from aircraft or helicopters, many pulses hit the tops of trees. But some get through gaps in the leaves to the **ground**. A computer filters out the ground points and calculates a **digital terrain model**, which shows the Earth's surface without trees and houses. With **hillshading**, meaning artificial light and shadow, even fine shapes in the land become visible.

In 2018 a large lidar campaign in northern **Guatemala** discovered tens of thousands of previously unknown Maya structures, including houses, roads and fortifications. In **Cambodia**, extensive medieval urban landscapes around the temple complex of Angkor were mapped with lidar. In Swiss forests, lidar data often reveal burial mounds, earthworks and old sunken lanes. In this way archaeological sites are found without digging.

The Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**, has measured the whole of Switzerland with lidar from the air. This produces very accurate elevation models of the country, which anyone can look at online. They help in planning roads, in protecting against natural hazards such as debris flows and in monitoring glaciers. Foresters also use the data to work out the height and density of forests.

Many self-driving cars and robots use lidar to detect obstacles around them. Some smartphones and tablets have small lidar sensors that can be used to measure rooms. Lidar is also used in research on clouds and air pollution. The technology is getting smaller and cheaper all the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Concentrated, very precise light of a single colour.
A huge collection of measuring points that together make a 3D image.
A computer model of the Earth's surface without trees and buildings.
A way of showing land with artificial light and shadow so that its shapes look three-dimensional.

gewusst: A lidar aircraft can record hundreds of thousands of measuring points a second.
With lidar, traces of settlements have been discovered in Swiss forests that had been hidden under leaves and moss for centuries.
On the Apollo missions a laser was already used to measure the height above the Moon's surface.

teile.einleitung: The last ice age was a long, cold period of Earth's history that began about 115,000 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. At that time, huge glaciers lay over northern Europe, North America and the Alps. Much of the Swiss Central Plateau was also buried under thick ice.
wichtigste: The last ice age ended about 11,700 years ago.
In the Alpine region it is called the Würm glaciation, after a river in Bavaria.
A large part of the Swiss Central Plateau was covered by glacier ice.
The Rhône Glacier carried rock from Valais as far as the area around Solothurn.
Large boulders carried along by the ice are called erratic boulders.
The sea level was about 120 metres lower than today.
Woolly mammoths also lived in Switzerland at that time.

abschnitte.text: Over the last 2.6 million years or so, **cold periods** and **warm periods** have alternated on Earth several times. During the cold periods, huge ice sheets and glaciers grew. The last cold period lasted from about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago. In the Alpine region it is called the **Würm glaciation** after the River Würm in Bavaria, and in northern Germany the Weichselian glaciation. Today we live in a warm period, the Holocene.

At the height of the glaciation, about 20,000 years ago, the Alpine glaciers flowed far out into the Central Plateau. The **Rhône Glacier** reached from Valais over Lake Geneva to the area of Solothurn and Wangen an der Aare. The Reuss Glacier and the Linth Glacier also pushed far to the north. Only the highest peaks stuck out of the ice. When the glaciers retreated, they left behind lakes such as Lake Zurich, Lake Lucerne and Lake Biel.

The glaciers carried boulders over long distances; these are called **erratic boulders**. In the Central Plateau there are many erratics made of granite from Valais, which clearly do not come from the area. At the edges of the glaciers, hills of rubble formed, the **moraines**. Many valleys were also scoured out by the ice and therefore have a typical U shape.

In the cold steppe in front of the glaciers lived **woolly mammoths**, woolly rhinoceroses, reindeer, wild horses and cave bears. In Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich, many mammoth bones were found, which can be seen in a small museum. The animals had thick fur and fat reserves against the cold. Towards the end of the ice age many of these large animals died out.

Because so much water was locked up as ice on land, the sea level was about **120 metres** lower than today. Many areas that are sea today were dry land. Between Asia and North America, the land bridge **Beringia** at the Bering Strait lay exposed. People and animals reached America across it, and Great Britain was also joined to the European mainland.

During the last ice age, first the Neanderthals and later also modern humans lived in Europe. They hunted reindeer and wild horses and lived in caves or in tents made of hides. Famous cave paintings come from this time, such as those in the cave of Lascaux in France. In Switzerland, tools and skilful carvings by ice-age hunters were found in the **Kesslerloch** cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long time with a cold climate and large glaciers, also called an ice age.
A warmer period between two cold periods.
A large boulder that a glacier has carried far from where it came from.
A ridge or hill of rubble left behind by a glacier.
A land bridge between Asia and North America that lay dry during the ice age.

gewusst: At the height of the ice age, a layer of ice several hundred metres thick lay over the area of today's city of Bern.
Because Great Britain was joined to the mainland, you could then walk from France to England without getting your feet wet.
Many erratic boulders in the Central Plateau used to be broken up for building material; today some are protected.

teile.einleitung: A coral reef is a huge structure in the sea built by tiny animals: corals. Its colourful hiding places teem with fish, crabs, snails and starfish. Coral reefs are among the habitats with the most species on the whole of Earth.
wichtigste: Coral reefs are built by stony corals, which form a limestone skeleton.
They grow best in warm, clear and shallow tropical seawater.
The largest coral reef in the world is the Great Barrier Reef off Australia.
Tiny algae live inside the corals and supply them with food.
If the water gets too warm, the corals lose their algae and turn white.
A reef grows very slowly, often only a few millimetres to centimetres a year.
Because so many animal species live there, reefs are also called the rainforests of the sea.

abschnitte.text: A reef consists of millions of small **coral polyps**, which are related to jellyfish. Each polyp is only a few millimetres in size and sits in a cup of limestone. When a polyp dies, its limestone skeleton remains, and new polyps build on top of it. In this way, over thousands of years, a mighty structure of **limestone** forms.

Tiny algae called **zooxanthellae** live in the tissue of the corals. They use sunlight to make sugar, which they share with the coral. In return, the coral gives them protection and nutrients. Such cooperation for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**. The algae also give the corals their bright colours.

Reef-building corals need warm water of about 20 to 29 degrees Celsius. The water must be clear so that enough light reaches the algae, which is why reefs usually grow only at shallow depths. They are found mainly in the Indian Ocean, the Pacific, the Red Sea and the Caribbean. Depending on their shape, a distinction is made between **fringing reefs** close to the coast, barrier reefs further out and ring-shaped **atolls**.

Countless animals find shelter in the cracks and caves of a reef. The orange and white **clownfish** lives among the poisonous tentacles of sea anemones, which do not harm it. Parrotfish nibble at the corals, moray eels lurk in holes, and sea turtles look for food. Although reefs cover only a tiny part of the seabed, a large proportion of all marine animal species live there.

If the sea gets too warm, the corals expel their algae and turn white. This **coral bleaching** is dangerous, because without algae the corals starve and can die. Because of climate change, such marine heatwaves are happening more and more often. Pollution, overfishing and acidic seawater also harm the reefs.

Today there are of course no coral reefs in Switzerland. But around 150 million years ago, in the **Jurassic period**, the area of today's Jura lay under a warm, shallow sea. At that time coral reefs grew there, and their fossilised remains can be found in the limestone today. So anyone hiking in the Jura is sometimes walking over ancient reefs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small animal with tentacles that forms a coral together with many others.
Tiny algae that live in corals and supply them with food.
Two living things living together in a way that benefits both.
A ring-shaped coral reef with a lagoon in the middle.
The whitening of corals when they lose their algae because the water is too warm.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is over 2000 kilometres long and so big that it can be seen from space.
Corals look like plants or stones, but they are animals.
Some parrotfish nibble corals and excrete fine white sand, which ends up on beaches.

teile.einleitung: The Keeling Curve is a graph that shows how much carbon dioxide (CO2) there is in the air. It is based on measurements that have been taken on the volcano Mauna Loa in Hawaii since 1958. The curve has been rising steadily since the measurements began and is one of the most important pieces of evidence for human-made climate change.
wichtigste: The Keeling Curve is named after the American researcher Charles David Keeling.
The measurements began in 1958 on the volcano Mauna Loa in Hawaii.
At the start, the CO2 level was around 315 ppm.
By now the annual average has passed 420 ppm (as of 2025).
The unit ppm means parts per million.
The yearly rise and fall is caused by the growing and dying back of plants in the northern hemisphere.
The curve reaches its lowest point each year in late summer to early autumn.

abschnitte.text: **Charles David Keeling** was an American chemist and climate researcher who lived from 1928 to 2005. He worked at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography in California. Keeling developed very precise instruments for measuring carbon dioxide in the air. After his death his son Ralph Keeling continued the measurements.

Since **1958** the CO2 content of the air has been measured on the volcano **Mauna Loa** in Hawaii. The measuring station is at a height of around 3400 metres, in the middle of the Pacific. There the air is far away from cities and factories and well mixed. That is why the values show well what is happening to the air of the whole Earth.

When the measurements began, the CO2 level was about 315 **ppm**. Since then it has risen every year, and the annual average is now over 420 ppm (as of 2025). Before industrialisation it was only about 280 ppm. The increase comes mainly from burning coal, oil and natural gas.

The curve does not rise in a straight line, but has a small wave every year. In spring and summer many plants grow in the northern hemisphere and take in CO2 during **photosynthesis**. That is why the CO2 level reaches its lowest point in late summer to early autumn. In autumn and winter leaves and plants rot, CO2 is released, and the value rises again until about May.

**Carbon dioxide** is a greenhouse gas. It holds heat in the atmosphere, rather like the glass of a greenhouse. The more CO2 there is in the air, the warmer the Earth becomes on average. The Keeling Curve was one of the first series of measurements to show clearly that humans are changing the make-up of the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas made of carbon and oxygen, chemically CO2, which is produced by burning.
Parts per million, that is, how many particles of a substance there are for every million particles of air.
A gas in the air that holds back heat and warms the Earth.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar from CO2 and water.

gewusst: The measurements on Mauna Loa have been running almost without interruption since 1958.
The waves in the curve show how the Earth's plants breathe in and out over the course of the year.
Today's CO2 level is higher than ever before in human history.

teile.einleitung: Compost is dark, crumbly soil made from kitchen and garden waste. Countless small living things turn vegetable peelings, leaves and grass cuttings into valuable fertiliser. In this way waste becomes food for new plants again.
wichtigste: Compost forms when tiny living things break down plant remains.
Compost imitates the cycle in the forest floor.
If you compost, you produce less rubbish.
Without a garden, you can compost in your flat with a wormery.
Several neighbours can share a neighbourhood compost heap.
Eggshells may go on the compost, preferably crushed.
Diseased plants do not belong on the compost, because the disease can spread.

abschnitte.text: Compost is a mixture of decomposed plant remains that looks and smells like loose forest soil. It is made from vegetable peelings, coffee grounds, leaves, grass cuttings and small twigs. Experts call the breakdown **rotting** or **decomposition**. Finished compost is a natural **fertiliser** that makes the soil loose and fertile.

Billions of **bacteria** and fungi that can only be seen under a microscope live in compost. In addition there are earthworms, woodlice, millipedes and springtails, which break the waste into smaller pieces. At first the inside of a large heap can get really hot, often over 50 degrees. Later **compost worms** and other soil animals take over the work. After about six months to a year the compost is ready.

In the forest nobody clears away the leaves, and yet the ground does not get buried. The soil creatures break down leaves and branches and turn them into humus. This releases **nutrients** such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which the trees take up again. Garden compost imitates exactly this **cycle**. In this way nothing is lost.

Good compost needs air, moisture and a good mix of wet and dry waste. It should be as damp as a wrung-out sponge. In continuous rain you cover the heap so that it does not get too wet and start to rot badly. Turning it now and then brings **oxygen** into it. Meat, bones, cooked leftovers and diseased plants do not belong in it.

If you do not have a garden, you can set up a **wormery** on the balcony or in the kitchen. In it, compost worms eat the waste and leave behind fine worm humus. Many Swiss towns also have a **neighbourhood compost heap** that neighbours share. Many municipalities also collect green waste separately and process it in large composting plants or biogas plants.

About a third of household rubbish consists of organic waste. If this is composted, less **rubbish** has to be burned. If you use compost in the garden, you need less artificial fertiliser and no peat from moors. Compost also stores water in the soil and so protects plants from drought.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow breakdown of plant remains by living things, with air present.
A dark, fertile layer of soil made from broken-down plant and animal remains.
A small red worm that eats waste especially quickly and lives in wormeries.
Plant waste from the kitchen and garden that is collected separately.

gewusst: More living things live in a handful of compost than there are people on Earth.
A large compost heap can get so warm inside that it steams on cold mornings.
Compost worms can eat roughly their own weight every day.

teile.einleitung: Smart materials are materials that react to their surroundings by themselves. For example, they change their shape, colour or hardness when it gets warmer, when light falls on them or when electricity flows. That is why they are also called intelligent materials.
wichtigste: Smart materials react to stimuli such as heat, light, pressure, electricity or magnetic fields.
Shape memory alloys return to their original shape when heated, thanks to the martensite-austenite transformation.
Piezoelectric materials produce an electrical voltage when you squeeze them.
The piezoelectric effect was discovered by the brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie.
Electrochromic glass changes its tint when an electrical voltage is applied.
Photochromic glass darkens by itself in sunlight, for example in spectacle lenses.
Empa uses an iron-based shape memory alloy to pre-stress and strengthen concrete structures afterwards.

abschnitte.text: Ordinary materials such as wood or steel usually stay as they are. **Smart materials**, on the other hand, react to a **stimulus** from their surroundings. Such stimuli can be heat, light, pressure, electrical voltage or a magnetic field. The material then changes one of its properties, for example its shape, colour or toughness. They are not really clever, but they behave as if they were thinking along.

A **shape memory alloy** can remember its original shape. If you bend a wire made of it and then heat it, it springs back into its old shape. The reason is a change in the crystal lattice, the **martensite-austenite transformation**. The best-known alloy is nitinol, made of nickel and titanium. Some of these alloys show **superelasticity**: they can be greatly deformed and spring back by themselves when released, which is used, for example, for brace wires and spectacle frames.

**Piezoelectric** materials produce an electrical voltage when you squeeze them. Conversely, they change shape slightly when a voltage is applied. This effect was discovered by the brothers **Jacques and Pierre Curie** in 1880. In everyday life it is found in gas lighters, which strike a spark when pressed. Quartz watches and ultrasound machines also use piezoelectric crystals.

**Photochromic glass** darkens by itself in sunlight and becomes clear again in the shade. It is familiar from self-tinting spectacle lenses. **Electrochromic glass** changes its tint when an electrical voltage is applied. This lets windows be darkened at the press of a button, for example in some aircraft and office buildings. This saves energy, because rooms heat up less.

A **magnetorheological fluid** contains tiny iron particles. In a magnetic field these particles line up into chains, and the fluid becomes thick or even solid. This makes it possible, for example, to make shock absorbers in cars harder or softer in a flash. In Switzerland, the research institute **Empa** in Dübendorf has developed an iron-based shape memory alloy. It can be used to pre-stress and strengthen concrete structures such as bridges afterwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance from which things are made.
A mixture of a metal with other substances, for example bronze.
Electrical voltage that is produced when certain crystals are squeezed.
Very great deformability that reverses by itself when released.
The Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology.

gewusst: When you click a gas lighter, a small hammer strikes a crystal, and the voltage produced creates the spark.
Pierre Curie, one of the discoverers of piezoelectricity, later received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Marie Curie.

teile.einleitung: Isotope analysis is a method with which researchers can read teeth, bones and other materials like a diary. It reveals what a person or animal ate and where they grew up. In this way it was found out, for example, where the Iceman, Ötzi, spent his childhood.
wichtigste: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Stable isotopes such as C-13 and N-15 do not decay, unlike radioactive C-14.
Tooth enamel forms in childhood and is not rebuilt afterwards.
Bones tend to reflect the last years of life.
A high N-15 value in bone collagen shows a lot of animal protein in the diet.
Oxygen isotopes provide clues about drinking water and climate.
Isotope analyses showed that the Iceman grew up south of the main ridge of the Alps.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny **atoms**. Atoms of one element, for example carbon, always have the same number of protons, but sometimes different numbers of neutrons. These versions are called **isotopes**. Carbon, for example, exists as C-12, C-13 and C-14. C-12 and C-13 are **stable** and do not decay, while C-14 is radioactive and slowly decays.

abschnitte.titel: Teeth and bones as an archive
abschnitte.text: What we eat and drink is built into our body, including the isotopes. **Tooth enamel** forms in childhood and is not rebuilt afterwards. So it stores information about the first years of life. **Bones**, on the other hand, are constantly renewed and tend to reflect the last years of life. By comparing the two, you can see whether someone moved during their life.

A high value of the nitrogen isotope **N-15** in bone collagen shows a lot of animal protein in the diet. The ratio of C-13 to C-12 reveals whether someone ate so-called C4 plants such as **millet** or maize. High C-13 and high N-15 values together point to a lot of fish from the sea. In this way archaeologists can tell whether people were mainly farmers, hunters or fishers. Collagen is a protein that is well preserved in bone.

**Oxygen isotopes** in teeth and bones give clues about the drinking water and so about the climate where someone lived. Strontium isotopes also reveal something about the rock on which the plants grew. A famous example is the **Iceman**, known as Ötzi, who was found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991. He lived more than 5000 years ago. Isotope analyses showed that he grew up south of the main ridge of the Alps, in what is now South Tyrol.

The measurement needs only a small sample, such as a tiny piece of tooth or bone. A **mass spectrometer** separates the isotopes by their weight and counts them. The differences are very small, but the instruments are extremely precise. Isotope analyses also help outside archaeology. They can be used, for example, to check whether honey, wine or asparagus really come from the region stated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A version of an element with a different number of neutrons.
A tiny building block of which all substances are made.
The hard outer layer of the teeth.
A protein that makes bones strong and at the same time slightly elastic.
A measuring instrument that sorts particles by their weight and counts them.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
Isotopes can also be used to find out where an animal such as a mammoth travelled during its life.

teile.einleitung: A compass is a device whose needle always points north. With it you can find out which direction you are going in, even without the Sun, the stars or mobile reception. For almost a thousand years it has helped sailors, hikers and explorers to find the right way.
wichtigste: The needle of a compass points north.
The compass needle is a small magnet.
It aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field.
The magnetic North Pole is not exactly at the geographic North Pole.
The compass was invented in China.
With a compass and a map you can find your way in open country.
Many smartphones today also have a built-in digital compass.

abschnitte.text: A **compass** usually consists of a case with a freely rotating **magnetic needle**. The tip of the needle that points north is often coloured red. A scale with the points of the compass, north, east, south and west, is printed on the case. If you know where north is, you also know all the other directions. In many compasses the needle sits in liquid so that it stays steadier.

The Earth itself is like a giant magnet and has an invisible **magnetic field**. The small magnetic needle of the compass aligns itself with this field. It points to the magnetic North Pole, which lies near the geographic North Pole in the Arctic. Because the two poles are not in the same place, there is a small difference, the **magnetic declination**. In Switzerland this difference is very small today. Iron or magnets nearby can disturb the compass.

The first compasses existed in **China**, where lodestone was known early on. Around the 11th century, Chinese sailors used the compass for navigation. By about the year 1200 it was also known in Europe. The compass was essential for the great voyages of discovery across the oceans. Later came gyrocompasses, which work without a magnet and are used on large ships.

abschnitte.titel: Finding your way in open country
abschnitte.text: Together with a map, you can find your way with a compass. To do this, you turn the map so that its north points in the same direction as the compass needle; this is called **orienting the map**. In Switzerland, **orienteering** is a popular sport in which you have to find checkpoints in the forest with a map and compass. Scouts, mountaineers and soldiers also learn how to use a compass. The company Recta from Biel made well-known compasses for a long time.

Today most smartphones have a built-in **digital compass**. A tiny sensor in them measures the Earth's magnetic field. Map apps use it to show which direction you are facing. Even so, many people take a real compass with them on mountain tours. That is because it needs no electricity and still works when the battery is flat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small magnetic needle that aligns itself with the Earth's magnetic field.
The invisible magnetic field that surrounds the whole Earth.
The small difference between magnetic north and geographic north.
Turning a map so that its north matches the real direction of north.

gewusst: The magnetic North Pole moves many kilometres every year.
Some animals, such as migratory birds and sea turtles, can also sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.

teile.einleitung: A climate model is a huge computer program that recalculates the Earth's climate. It uses the laws of physics to describe how air, water, ice and land influence each other. In this way researchers can estimate how the climate might change in the future, for example if more CO2 gets into the air.
wichtigste: A global climate model divides the Earth into a three-dimensional grid of cells.
Processes smaller than a grid cell are described in a simplified way through parameterisation.
Earth system models also calculate biological and chemical cycles.
Downscaling is used to refine global results for a region such as Switzerland.
A model is considered more reliable if it can recalculate the past climate well.
In the CMIP project, climate models from all over the world are compared according to the same rules.
In 2021 Syukuro Manabe received part of the Nobel Prize in Physics for early climate models.

abschnitte.text: A **climate model** is a simplified copy of the Earth in a computer. It contains equations for wind, temperature, moisture, ocean currents and ice. Unlike a weather forecast, it does not predict the weather on a particular day. Instead it shows how the average weather develops over decades. This needs very powerful **supercomputers**.

For the calculation, the Earth is covered as if with a net. The air and the sea are divided into many layers one above the other, creating a three-dimensional **grid** of cells. For each cell, the computer calculates temperature, wind and moisture step by step. Small things such as individual clouds or thunderstorms are smaller than a cell. They are described in a simplified way through **parameterisation**.

A central term is **radiative forcing**, which is given in watts per square metre. It describes how strongly, for example, greenhouse gases change the Earth's energy balance. **Climate sensitivity** tells you how much the Earth warms when the CO2 content of the air doubles. Many models show a warming of about 2.5 to 4 °C for this.

A model must show that it can recalculate the past correctly. You start it, for example, in the year 1850 and compare the results with real measurements. In the international **CMIP** project, institutes from many countries run the same tasks. The results feed into the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the **IPCC**. Because different models give slightly different results, a range is usually given.

A global model is too coarse for the Alps, because valleys and mountains can hardly be made out in it. With **downscaling**, the results are refined for a region. This is how the Swiss climate scenarios of MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich are produced. They show, for example, that summers in Switzerland are likely to become hotter and drier and winters to have less snow. Calculations are done at the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre **CSCS** in Lugano, among other places.

The first simple climate models were created in the 1960s. The Japanese-American researcher **Syukuro Manabe** showed early on that more CO2 warms the Earth. For this, in 2021, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with Klaus Hasselmann and Giorgio Parisi. Today's **Earth system models** also calculate plants, ocean chemistry and the carbon cycle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified description of processes that are too small to be calculated directly.
The warming of the Earth when the CO2 content of the air doubles.
Refining coarse model results for a smaller region.
A possible future based on certain assumptions, for example about future CO2 emissions.

gewusst: Some climate models consist of more than a million lines of program code.
Even Manabe's simple models from the 1960s predicted today's warming astonishingly well.

teile.einleitung: IDSIA is a research institute for artificial intelligence in Lugano in the canton of Ticino. Methods were developed here that are now found in smartphones, translation programs and speech recognition. This makes the small Swiss institute one of the most important places in the history of AI.
wichtigste: IDSIA stands for Istituto Dalle Molle di studi sull'intelligenza artificiale.
The institute is named after the entrepreneur and patron Angelo Dalle Molle.
Today it is affiliated to the Università della Svizzera italiana (USI) and the University of Applied Sciences SUPSI.
Jürgen Schmidhuber worked at IDSIA as scientific director.
In 1997 Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber published the fundamental article on LSTM.
Before the rise of transformers, LSTM networks were widely used in speech recognition on smartphones.
In 2011 a network developed at IDSIA recognised traffic signs better than humans.

abschnitte.text: **IDSIA** is a research institute for artificial intelligence in **Lugano**. The name is Italian, because Italian is spoken in Ticino. In full it is called Istituto Dalle Molle di studi sull'intelligenza artificiale, the Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence Studies. It was founded in 1988. Today it belongs to the Università della Svizzera italiana (**USI**) and the University of Applied Sciences and Arts of Southern Switzerland (**SUPSI**).

The institute is named after **Angelo Dalle Molle**, an Italian entrepreneur and patron. A patron is someone who supports art or science with their money. Dalle Molle had become rich with a herbal liqueur. He set up a foundation that was to support research for the good of people. IDSIA was also created with its money.

IDSIA is especially famous for **LSTM**, short for Long Short-Term Memory. This is a kind of artificial neural network with a kind of memory. It can remember important information for a longer time, for example the beginning of a sentence when the end comes. The fundamental article was published by **Sepp Hochreiter** and **Jürgen Schmidhuber** in 1997. Schmidhuber worked for a long time as scientific director of IDSIA.

Before the rise of the so-called transformers, LSTM networks were used very widely. They were found in **speech recognition** on smartphones, for example when you dictate something to your phone. Automatic translation programs also used them. This meant that ideas from Lugano were used on billions of devices. Today large language models are mostly based on transformers, but LSTM is still found in many applications.

Researchers at IDSIA trained **convolutional networks**, a kind of neural network for images, on fast graphics cards. In 2011 such a network won a competition for recognising **traffic signs**. It even made fewer mistakes than humans. Abilities like this are important, for example, for self-driving cars. Graphics cards were originally built for computer games, but today they are one of the main tools of AI research.

begriffe.erklaerung: Computer programs that solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.
A computer program that learns roughly on the model of nerve cells in the brain.
A neural network with a built-in memory for sequences such as language.
A person who supports art or science with money.

gewusst: The LSTM idea first appeared in Sepp Hochreiter's diploma thesis at the Technical University of Munich.
A small institute in Ticino supplied technology that was used in billions of mobile phones worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, inventor and researcher of the Renaissance. He painted the famous Mona Lisa and filled thousands of pages with drawings of machines, plants and the human body. That is why many people call him a universal genius.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci lived from 1452 to 1519.
He was born near the small town of Vinci in Italy.
He painted the Mona Lisa and the mural The Last Supper.
He was not only a painter but also an inventor and researcher.
He dreamed of flying and drew flying machines.
To draw people better, he studied muscles and bones.
His drawing Vitruvian Man is world-famous.
He often wrote his notes in mirror writing.

abschnitte.text: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near **Vinci** in Tuscany, hence his name: Leonardo from Vinci. As a young man he went to **Florence** to train with the artist Andrea del Verrocchio. There he learned painting, sculpture and a lot about technology. He lived in the **Renaissance**, a time when art and science flourished in Europe.

The **Mona Lisa** shows a woman with a mysterious smile and hangs today in the Louvre in Paris. It is probably the best-known painting in the world. In Milan, Leonardo painted the huge mural **The Last Supper** in a monastery. Leonardo worked very slowly and thoroughly, so he finished only a few paintings completely.

Leonardo wanted to know exactly how the human body is built. He studied muscles, bones and organs and drew them very accurately. His **anatomy** drawings were far ahead of their time. Also famous is the **Vitruvian Man**, a man with outstretched arms and legs in a circle and a square, which shows the proportions of the body.

Leonardo watched birds and bats to understand how they fly. He drew flying machines with flapping wings, a parachute and a kind of **aerial screw** that is reminiscent of a helicopter. Most of these machines were not built in his time. But his ideas show how far ahead he was thinking.

Leonardo always carried notebooks with him and wrote from right to left in **mirror writing**. In them you find plans for bridges, canals, weapons, diving suits and machines. He also studied water, light, plants and rocks. Today about 7000 pages of his notes still survive.
