For a long time Leonardo worked in Milan for Duke **Ludovico Sforza**. Later he lived again in Florence and in Rome. In the end the French king Francis I brought him to France. Leonardo died on 2 May 1519 in Amboise on the Loire.

begriffe.erklaerung: The period from the 14th to the 16th century, when art and science flourished anew in Europe; the word means rebirth.
A person who achieves great things in very many fields.
The science of how the body is built.
Writing that can only be read normally in a mirror.

gewusst: The Mona Lisa is only about 77 centimetres high and 53 centimetres wide, so smaller than many people think.
In 1911 the Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre and was only found again in Florence two years later.
Leonardo was left-handed, which made his mirror writing easier.

teile.einleitung: The hook-and-loop fastener, often called Velcro, is a fastener made of two strips that stick to each other when pressed together. It was invented by the Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral after burrs had got stuck in his dog's fur on a walk. Today hook-and-loop fasteners are found on shoes, bags, jackets and even in space.
wichtigste: The hook-and-loop fastener was invented by the Swiss Georges de Mestral.
He got the idea when burrs got stuck in his dog's fur.
He looked at the burrs very closely under a microscope.
One side of the strip has many small hooks, the other many small loops.
In 1951 de Mestral applied for a patent for the hook-and-loop fastener in Switzerland.
The name “Velcro” contains the French word “velours”, which means velvet.
In space, hook-and-loop strips stop things from floating away.

abschnitte.text: **Georges de Mestral** was an engineer from western Switzerland who lived from 1907 to 1990. After a hunting trip with his dog in the 1940s, lots of **burrs** were stuck in the dog's fur and on his clothes. Instead of just being annoyed, he wanted to know why they stuck so well. He put them under a **microscope** and discovered countless tiny hooks.

A hook-and-loop fastener consists of two strips. One has many small, stiff **hooks**. The other is covered with soft **loops**. When you press the strips together, the hooks catch in the loops. When you rip them apart, the hooks bend open for a moment and come loose, which makes the typical rasping sound.

The hook-and-loop fastener is a classic example of **biomimetics**, learning from nature. The fruits of the burdock have hooked tips so that they get caught in the fur of animals. In this way the seeds are spread far and wide. De Mestral transferred this principle to a technical product.

It took several years before de Mestral found a suitable material. The synthetic fibre **nylon** worked best. In 1951 he applied for a patent for his invention in Switzerland. He formed the brand name **Velcro** from the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and in space
abschnitte.text: Many children's shoes have hook-and-loop fasteners, because they can be closed quickly without laces. They are also found on jackets, rucksacks, blood pressure cuffs and sports pads. In space travel, hook-and-loop strips help to fix objects to the walls so that they do not **float away** in weightlessness. A hook-and-loop fastener can be opened and closed many thousands of times.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fruit of a plant such as burdock, which sticks to fur and clothing with small hooks.
Technology that imitates ideas from nature.
The right to be the only one to use an invention for a certain time.
A synthetic fibre that is very tear-resistant.

gewusst: The name “Velcro” is made up of the French words for velvet and hook.
The hook-and-loop fastener is a Swiss invention inspired by a dog.
The rasping sound comes from thousands of hooks coming loose at the same time when it is opened.

teile.einleitung: Kitchen scales are a measuring device used to weigh ingredients for cooking and baking. They usually show the weight in grams. If you weigh accurately, your cakes and bread turn out better.
wichtigste: You weigh ingredients with kitchen scales.
They usually show the weight in grams.
The “Tare” button sets the display to zero.
The scales must stand on a level, firm surface.
Old scales with two pans are called balance scales.
For your own body weight you need bathroom scales.

abschnitte.text: Kitchen scales measure how heavy flour, sugar, butter or vegetables are. Most show the weight in **grams**; 1000 grams make one kilogram. Many household scales can weigh up to about 5 kilograms and are accurate to one gram. Some can also show millilitres for water or milk.

Older kitchen scales work with a **spring** that is squeezed by the weight and moves a pointer. Today's digital scales have a **load cell** with a piece of metal that bends very slightly under the load. Electronics measure this bending and convert it into grams. The number then appears on a display.

If you want to weigh flour in a bowl, the weight of the bowl gets in the way. So you put the empty bowl on the scales and press the **Tare** button. The display jumps to zero, and after that you only see the weight of the ingredient. If the bowl weighs 300 grams and the scales show 800 grams without tare, there are 500 grams of flour in it. Tare originally meant the weight of the packaging.

A recipe asks for 200 grams of sugar, for example. If 150 grams are already in the bowl, 50 grams are still missing. Accurate weighing is important in baking, because even small differences can change the dough. So that the scales measure correctly, they stand on a level, firm surface and not on a cloth.

As long as over 4000 years ago, people in ancient Egypt used **balance scales**. They have a beam with two pans. You put the goods in one pan and weights in the other until both hang at the same height. Later spring scales were added, and from the 1980s electronic scales became widespread.

With **bathroom scales** you measure your own body weight. Letter scales weigh post, and precision scales in pharmacies or laboratories measure to a thousandth of a gram. At the butcher's or in shops, scales must be officially checked. In Switzerland this is the job of the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of weight; 1000 grams make one kilogram.
The weight of the packaging or bowl, which is taken away from the display.
A part in digital scales that measures the weight electrically.
Scales with a beam and two pans, where you compare against weights.

gewusst: A litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram, so you can also weigh water instead of measuring it.
Scales actually measure the force with which an object presses down, and convert it into grams.
On the Moon, spring scales would show only about a sixth of the weight.

teile.einleitung: Karl Alexander Müller was a Swiss physicist who lived from 1927 to 2023. Together with the German Georg Bednorz, he discovered high-temperature superconductivity in 1986 at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich. Just one year later, the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it.
wichtigste: Karl Alexander Müller was born in Basel in 1927.
He worked for many years at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon.
In 1986, with Georg Bednorz, he discovered high-temperature superconductivity in ceramic materials.
In superconductivity, electric current flows without resistance.
The material studied was a copper oxide ceramic, a so-called cuprate.
It became superconducting at around 35 kelvin.
In 1987 Müller and Bednorz were already awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

abschnitte.text: Karl Alexander Müller was born on 20 April 1927 in **Basel**. He studied physics at **ETH Zurich** and wrote his doctoral thesis there. From 1963 he did research at the **IBM** laboratory in Rüschlikon on Lake Zurich. Alongside this he taught at the University of Zurich. He died in January 2023 at the age of 95.

In a normal cable, the electrons bump into the atoms, so energy is lost as heat. In **superconductivity**, current flows with no resistance at all, that is, without any loss. But this only happens when a material is cooled below a certain **critical temperature**. For a long time superconductivity was known only at extremely low temperatures close to absolute zero. Superconductors can also make magnets float.

Müller and his younger colleague **Georg Bednorz** from Germany looked in an unusual place. They studied **ceramics** made of copper oxide, which normally hardly conduct electricity. In 1986 they found a material that became superconducting at around 35 kelvin, about minus 238 °C. This was considerably warmer than for any superconductor known before. After that, many researchers worldwide threw themselves into studying these new **cuprates**.

abschnitte.titel: A Nobel Prize in record time
abschnitte.text: As early as 1987, only about a year after publication, Müller and Bednorz received the **Nobel Prize in Physics**. The prize is very rarely awarded so quickly. In the same year, other researchers found cuprates with a critical temperature above 77 kelvin. These can be cooled with **liquid nitrogen**, which is cheap and easy to obtain.

Today high-temperature superconductors are used in special **power cables**, strong magnets and sensitive measuring instruments. They could carry electricity over long distances with almost no loss. Exactly how superconductivity works in cuprates is still not fully understood. Müller's discovery made the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon world-famous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that conducts electricity with no resistance at all below a certain temperature.
A unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero, at minus 273.15 °C.
A hard, fired material, as familiar from crockery.
The property of a substance that slows down the flow of current.

gewusst: In the same IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon, the scanning tunnelling microscope had been invented a few years earlier, and it also won a Nobel Prize.
Müller and Bednorz first tested materials that most experts thought were completely unsuitable.

teile.einleitung: A line graph is a chart in which measurements are plotted as points and joined with a line. This lets you see at a glance how something changes over time. Temperature charts for fever, share price charts and temperature curves are well-known examples.
wichtigste: A line graph is especially good at showing a change over time.
Time is usually shown on the horizontal axis.
If the line rises, the values are increasing.
A horizontal line means that the values stay the same.
A steep line shows a fast change.
If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences look much bigger.
A line graph is ideal for the temperature over the course of a day.

abschnitte.text: A line graph has two **axes**: a horizontal one and a vertical one. The horizontal axis usually shows time, for example hours, months or years. The vertical axis shows the quantity measured, such as degrees Celsius or francs. For each measurement you plot a **data point** and join the points with a line. A good chart also has a title and labelled axes with units.

If the line rises from left to right, the values get bigger; if it falls, they get smaller. The steeper the line, the faster something is changing. A horizontal line means no change. If a graph shows 200 bike helmets sold in January and 260 in February, sales have risen by 60. The highest and lowest points of a line are called the **maximum** and **minimum**.

Weather reports use line graphs to show how warm it will get over a day or a week. Doctors draw temperature charts to see whether a fever is going down. In business, lines show how share prices develop. In a **climate graph**, the temperature is often shown as a line and the rainfall as bars. You can also draw several lines in the same graph, for example the temperatures of Zurich and Lugano for comparison.

Graphs can be misleading even when the numbers are not wrong. If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences suddenly look huge. A squashed or stretched **scale** also strongly changes the impression a curve gives. So whenever you read a graph, you should first look at the axes and their labels. Then you can tell whether a change really is dramatic.

The Scot **William Playfair** is considered the inventor of the line graph. In 1786 he published a book in which he showed England's trade with lines over the years. Before that, such figures were usually just listed in long tables. Today spreadsheet programs such as Excel create a line graph in a few clicks. Even so, children learn to draw graphs by hand at school so that they understand how they work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line with a scale from which you read off the values.
A single measurement plotted on the graph.
The highest value in a series of data.
A chart that shows values as bars of different heights.

gewusst: Swiss weather services measure the temperature every ten minutes at many stations, which produces very accurate curves.
As well as the line graph, William Playfair also invented the bar chart and the pie chart.
A line graph is not good for things that have no order, for example the favourite colours of a class.

teile.einleitung: A live vaccine contains living but greatly weakened germs. They do not make you properly ill, but they teach the immune system to recognise and fight off the real germ. Well-known examples are the vaccinations against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox.
wichtigste: Live vaccines contain living, weakened germs.
The combined vaccination against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) is a live vaccine.
There is also a live vaccine against chickenpox.
People with a severely weakened immune system are usually advised against live vaccines.
Traditionally, germs are weakened by passing them many times through cell cultures or other hosts.
In 1885 Louis Pasteur vaccinated the boy Joseph Meister against rabies.
In 1951 Max Theiler received the Nobel Prize for a live vaccine against yellow fever.
BCG protects young children from severe forms of tuberculosis.

abschnitte.text: A **vaccine** prepares the body for a disease without you having to go through it properly. In a **live vaccine**, the viruses or bacteria are still alive and can multiply a little in the body. But they are so greatly weakened that they cause mild symptoms at most. There are also inactivated vaccines, which contain only killed germs or parts of them.

The **immune system** recognises the weakened germs as foreign and makes defensive substances, the **antibodies**, as well as memory cells. If the real germ comes later, the body recognises it at once and can fight it quickly. Because the germs multiply a little, the protection is usually especially strong and long-lasting. So one or two doses are often enough.

Traditionally, the germs are grown many times in cell cultures or in other animals. This is called **passaging**. In the process the germs change so that they are hardly dangerous to humans any more. This is how, for example, the yellow fever vaccine 17D was made, for which Max Theiler received the Nobel Prize in 1951. Today researchers can also change germs on purpose in their genetic material.

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner protected people from dangerous smallpox with harmless **cowpox**. The Frenchman Louis Pasteur developed weakened vaccines, and in 1885 he successfully vaccinated nine-year-old Joseph Meister against rabies. In 1921 the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis, named after Calmette and Guérin, was used for the first time in France. In the 1950s and 1960s Albert Sabin developed an oral polio vaccine with live viruses.

Live vaccines include the MMR vaccine against **measles**, mumps and rubella, as well as the vaccine against chickenpox. In Switzerland the MMR vaccine is recommended in two doses in early childhood. People are also vaccinated with a live vaccine against yellow fever, which occurs in tropical countries. For babies there is an oral vaccine against rotaviruses, which cause diarrhoea.

People with a severely weakened immune system should usually not receive live vaccines. In them, even the weakened germs could cause illness. These include, for example, people receiving chemotherapy for cancer. They are protected when as many people as possible around them are vaccinated, which is called **herd protection**. Families discuss with their doctor whether a vaccination is suitable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that prepares the body for a disease.
A germ that has been changed so that it hardly makes you ill any more.
The body's defensive substances, which recognise and fight germs.
The body's defence system against germs.
Protection for unvaccinated people, because the disease can hardly spread when many people are vaccinated.

gewusst: The word vaccine comes from the Latin “vacca” for cow, because of Jenner's cowpox.
Thanks to worldwide vaccination, smallpox has officially been wiped out since 1980.
Joseph Meister later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute in Paris.

teile.einleitung: A monastery library is the book collection of a monastery. In the Middle Ages, monasteries were the most important places where books were copied and kept. One of the most famous monastery libraries in the world is the Abbey Library in St Gallen.
wichtigste: In the Middle Ages, monks copied books by hand.
They usually wrote with a bird's quill on parchment made from animal skin.
Large, artistically decorated first letters are called initials.
In some libraries, books were chained up to protect them from theft.
The Abbey Library of St Gallen is one of the oldest libraries in the world.
It holds the Abrogans, the oldest surviving book in the German language.
Above the entrance, the word “pharmacy of the soul” is written in Greek.

abschnitte.text: In a **monastery**, monks or nuns live together according to fixed rules. Their life included prayer, work and learning, which is why they needed books. In the **monastery library** they collected religious writings, but also works on medicine, history and mathematics, and texts by ancient poets. Many old texts have only survived because monks copied them.

Before the invention of printing around 1450, every book was written by hand. This was done in the **scriptorium**, the writing room of the monastery. The monks wrote with a cut **bird's quill** and ink on **parchment**, which was made from the skin of calves, sheep or goats. A large book needed the skins of many animals and often months or years of work.

Many manuscripts are splendidly decorated. Large, artistically painted first letters are called **initials**, and sometimes they were even decorated with gold. Because books were very valuable, in some libraries they were fixed to the reading desks with **chains**. That way nobody could simply take them away.

abschnitte.titel: The Abbey Library of St Gallen
abschnitte.text: The monastery of St Gallen was founded in the 8th century, and its library is one of the oldest in the world. The magnificent Baroque hall was built in the 18th century. Above the entrance it says “Psyches Iatreion” in Greek, meaning **pharmacy of the soul**. Since 1983 the Abbey District of St Gallen has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Abbey Library owns around 2100 manuscripts, many of them over a thousand years old. They include the **Abrogans**, a Latin-German dictionary from the 8th century that is considered the oldest surviving book in the German language. Also famous is the **Plan of St Gall** from the 9th century, a drawing of an ideal monastery complex. The monasteries of Einsiedeln and Engelberg also have important libraries.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where monks or nuns live together according to religious rules.
A writing material made from treated animal skin.
The writing room in a medieval monastery.
A book written by hand.
A large, decorated first letter at the beginning of a text.

gewusst: In the Baroque hall of the Abbey Library of St Gallen, visitors have to wear felt slippers to protect the valuable wooden floor.
The Abbey Library of St Gallen even holds a real Egyptian mummy.
The book gets the name Abrogans from its first word, a Latin word for humble.

teile.einleitung: Insulin is a vital hormone that regulates the amount of sugar in the blood. It is made in the pancreas and helps the body's cells to take in sugar. Its discovery in 1921 saved the lives of millions of people with diabetes.
wichtigste: Insulin is made in the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
It lowers blood sugar by helping cells to take in sugar.
In 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best at the University of Toronto obtained an effective extract for the first time.
In 1922 a person was treated with insulin for the first time.
In 1923 Banting received the Nobel Prize together with John Macleod.
The discoverers handed the patent to their university for a symbolic dollar.
Today human insulin is made mainly with genetically modified microorganisms.

abschnitte.text: When we eat, sugar in the form of **glucose** gets into the blood. Insulin works like a key that opens the body's cells to this sugar. In this way muscles and organs get energy, and the **blood sugar** level falls again. Its opposite number is the hormone glucagon, which raises blood sugar.

Insulin is made in the **pancreas**, which lies behind the stomach. There are small groups of cells there, the **islets of Langerhans**, named after the researcher Paul Langerhans. In them the beta cells produce insulin. An insulin molecule consists of 51 amino acids in two chains.

In **diabetes**, the blood sugar level is permanently too high. In type 1 diabetes, the body's own immune system destroys the beta cells, and the body no longer makes insulin. Those affected, often children and young people, have to inject insulin or wear an insulin pump. In type 2 diabetes, insulin works less well; here exercise, diet and tablets often help.

In summer 1921, **Frederick Banting** and the student **Charles Best** carried out crucial experiments at the University of Toronto. They obtained an extract from the pancreas that lowered blood sugar. The chemist James Collip purified it, and in January 1922 a boy with diabetes was treated for the first time. Banting and the head of the laboratory, John Macleod, received the Nobel Prize in 1923 and shared the prize money with Best and Collip.

In the past, insulin was obtained from the pancreas of cattle and pigs. Frederick Sanger was the first to work out the complete sequence of amino acids in insulin and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1958. Today genetically modified bacteria or yeasts produce **human insulin**, which is exactly the same as the human kind. This means there is enough insulin for everyone who needs it.

Many people with diabetes use an **insulin pen**, which looks like a thick ballpoint pen. Others wear a small pump and a sensor that measures their sugar level continuously. Hundreds of thousands of people with diabetes live in Switzerland. Every year on 14 November, Frederick Banting's birthday, is **World Diabetes Day**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance in the body that passes on messages to organs via the blood.
The amount of sugar dissolved in the blood.
An organ behind the stomach that produces digestive juices and hormones such as insulin.
A disease in which the blood sugar level is permanently too high.

gewusst: Banting said that insulin belonged to the world and not to him, so nobody should get rich from it.
The first patient, 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, lived for many years after the treatment.
In 1982 insulin was the first genetically engineered medicine to be approved.

teile.einleitung: The AI Act is a law of the European Union that regulates how artificial intelligence may be developed and used. It is the world's first comprehensive AI law and came into force on 1 August 2024. The more dangerous an AI application can be for people, the stricter the rules.
wichtigste: The EU's AI Act came into force on 1 August 2024.
It regulates artificial intelligence using a risk-based approach.
Rating people's social behaviour, so-called social scoring, is banned.
AI for selecting job applications counts as a high-risk application.
Deepfakes must be labelled as artificially generated.
For banned AI practices, fines of up to 35 million euros or 7 per cent of worldwide turnover can be imposed.
The law also applies to companies outside the EU if their AI is used in the EU.
In 2025 Switzerland chose its own path with the Council of Europe's AI Convention.

abschnitte.text: **Artificial intelligence**, AI for short, means computer programs that can write texts, recognise pictures or suggest decisions. The EU's **AI Act** lays down which rules apply to such programs. It is meant to protect people from dangers and at the same time make new inventions possible. The European Parliament and the EU member states adopted it in 2024.

The law follows a **risk-based approach**. AI with **unacceptable risk** is banned, for example rating people's social behaviour, so-called social scoring. **High-risk AI**, such as programs for selecting job applications, in medicine or in schools, must meet strict requirements. For AI with limited risk, mainly transparency obligations apply, and for most simple applications such as spam filters there are hardly any rules.

People should know when they are dealing with an AI. That is why chatbots must be recognisable as such. Artificially generated pictures, videos or voices, so-called **deepfakes**, must be labelled as such. Additional rules apply to very large AI models that can be used for many purposes.

The law came into force on 1 August 2024, but its rules apply in stages. The bans have applied since February 2025. The rules for large AI models have applied since August 2025, and many other obligations follow from 2026 or later. Anyone who breaks the bans can expect **fines** of up to 35 million euros or 7 per cent of worldwide turnover.

Switzerland is not a member of the EU, so the law does not apply here directly. Swiss companies, however, must comply with it if they offer their AI in the EU or if it is used there. In 2025 the Federal Council decided to implement the **Council of Europe's AI Convention**. To do this, existing Swiss laws are to be adapted in targeted ways, instead of creating one big AI law of its own.

begriffe.erklaerung: Computer programs that solve tasks that would otherwise need human thinking.
In the EU, a law that applies directly in all member states.
An artificially generated picture, video or sound recording that seems real.
Rating people with points according to their behaviour, which is banned in the EU.
The possibility that something causes harm.

gewusst: The AI Act is regarded as the world's first comprehensive AI law.
Companies from Switzerland or the USA must also follow the rules if their AI is used in the EU.
Under the law, a simple spam filter in an email program counts as AI with minimal risk.

teile.einleitung: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. It is a huge gas planet with no solid ground, surrounded by colourful bands of cloud and enormous storms. With its many moons, it is almost like a small solar system of its own.
wichtigste: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system.
It is the fifth planet counting from the Sun.
Jupiter consists mainly of hydrogen and helium and has no solid surface.
It is more than 300 times as heavy as the Earth.
A day on Jupiter lasts just under 10 hours.
The Great Red Spot is a huge storm into which the Earth would fit.
Jupiter has more than 90 known moons.

abschnitte.text: Jupiter has a diameter of about 143,000 kilometres, about eleven times that of the Earth. It is a **gas planet** and consists mainly of hydrogen and helium, much like the Sun. Further in, the gas becomes liquid because of the enormous pressure. Right at the centre, researchers suspect there is a core of rock and ice. Jupiter is heavier than all the other planets put together, in fact more than twice as heavy.

abschnitte.titel: Its place in the solar system
abschnitte.text: On average Jupiter is about 778 million kilometres from the Sun, around five times as far as the Earth. It takes almost 12 Earth years to go once around the Sun. But it spins very fast on its own axis: a **Jupiter day** lasts just under 10 hours. Because it spins so quickly, it is slightly flattened at the poles. After Venus and the Moon, Jupiter is often the brightest object in the night sky.

Jupiter's atmosphere is divided into light and dark **bands of cloud** that flow in different directions. Winds there blow at several hundred kilometres per hour. The most famous storm is the **Great Red Spot**, a storm that is bigger than the Earth. It has been observed for almost 200 years, but it is slowly getting smaller. There are also huge flashes of lightning and auroras on Jupiter.

Jupiter has more than 90 known moons, and new ones keep being discovered. The four largest are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. They were discovered in 1610 by Galileo Galilei with a simple telescope and are therefore called the **Galilean moons**. Ganymede is the largest moon in the whole solar system and even bigger than the planet Mercury. There are active volcanoes on Io, and beneath the ice of Europa there is probably an ocean of water.

The first space probes flew past Jupiter in the 1970s, for example Pioneer 10 and the two Voyager probes. In 1979 Voyager 1 discovered Jupiter's faint **rings**. Since 2016 NASA's **Juno** probe has been orbiting the planet and studying its interior. The European probe JUICE was launched in 2023 and is to explore the icy moons. The University of Bern helped to build a measuring instrument for JUICE.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planet made mainly of gas, with no solid ground you could stand on.
A huge, reddish storm on Jupiter that has been raging for a very long time.
Jupiter's four largest moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, discovered by Galileo Galilei.
An unmanned craft sent into space to explore planets and moons.

gewusst: More than 1000 Earths would fit inside Jupiter.
Jupiter is named after the father of the Roman gods, whom the Greeks called Zeus.
With its strong gravity, Jupiter deflects many comets and asteroids and so influences the whole solar system.

teile.einleitung: When growing crystals, you let crystals grow on purpose. This works even in the kitchen with sugar and water, but also in large factories. There, crystals are made for computer chips, watches and lasers.
wichtigste: Crystals have smooth faces and straight edges.
For sugar crystals you only need sugar and water.
More sugar dissolves in hot water than in cold water.
The crystals grow well on a thread or a wooden skewer.
The glass should stand still and not be shaken.
Beautiful crystals take several days.
Rock candy is made of large sugar crystals.
Natural rock crystals are found in the Swiss Alps.

abschnitte.text: A **crystal** is a solid substance in which the tiniest particles are arranged in a very regular way. You can imagine it like neatly stacked building blocks. That is why crystals have smooth faces, straight edges and often a typical shape. Table salt forms small cubes, snowflakes form six-pointed stars and quartz forms six-sided columns.

You dissolve as much sugar in hot water as will go in, because warm water can take up more sugar. Then you hang a thread or a wooden skewer in the glass. As the water cools and evaporates, it can no longer hold all the sugar. The sugar settles on the thread, and crystals grow. After several days to about two weeks, beautiful, large crystals form, as in **rock candy**.

A solution that contains more dissolved substance than it can really hold is called **supersaturated**. Crystals grow especially well from it. Keeping it still is important: if you shake the glass, you get many small crystals instead of a few large ones. A small starter crystal, the **seed crystal**, helps the growth. Similar experiments work with table salt, alum or copper sulphate, but copper sulphate is poisonous and should only be handled by adults.

In industry, huge and very pure crystals are grown. The most important example is **silicon**, from which computer chips and solar cells are made. In the Czochralski process, a crystal is slowly pulled upwards out of molten silicon. This produces rods that can be over a metre long. They are cut into wafer-thin slices.

As early as around 1900, the Frenchman Auguste Verneuil managed to make artificial rubies. Such synthetic rubies are still used today as jewel bearings in mechanical watches, including Swiss watches. In quartz watches, a small grown quartz crystal vibrates very evenly and keeps the beat. Sapphire glass for watch faces is also grown artificially.

In clefts in the Swiss Alps, **rock crystals**, which are clear quartz crystals, have been growing for millions of years. They formed from hot, mineral-rich water in the rock. People who search for crystals in the mountains are called **Strahler** in Switzerland. The Gotthard area and the Grimsel area are especially famous for crystal finds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid body with regularly arranged particles and smooth faces.
A liquid in which a substance such as sugar is spread out invisibly.
A solution that contains more dissolved substance than it can really hold.
A small starter crystal on which a larger crystal goes on growing.
A person who searches the Alps for rock crystals and other minerals.

gewusst: Almost every computer chip in the world comes from a grown silicon crystal.
People in the past thought rock crystal was frozen ice that never melts, which is where the Greek word krystallos for ice comes from.
Mechanical watches often contain about 20 to 30 tiny artificial rubies.

teile.einleitung: Food additives are substances added to food on purpose so that it keeps longer, looks better or has a particular texture. On packaging you can often recognise them by their E numbers. Many of them also occur in nature, for example in fruit or seaweed.
wichtigste: E numbers stand for permitted additives.
E 300 is ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C.
E 330 is citric acid.
An emulsifier such as lecithin joins fat and water.
Agar-agar is obtained from red seaweed.
Pectin from apples or citrus peel makes jam set.
Antioxidants stop fats from going rancid.
Preservatives such as sorbic acid slow down moulds and yeasts.

abschnitte.text: An **additive** is added to a food on purpose during production. It is meant, for example, to make it keep longer, to improve its colour or to give it a creamy texture. Salt, sugar or spices, on the other hand, count as normal ingredients. Every additive must be tested and approved before it can be used.

Approved additives have an **E number**; the E stands for Europe. The numbers are sorted into groups: E 100 to E 199 are mostly colourings, E 200 to E 299 preservatives and E 300 to E 399 mainly antioxidants and acidity regulators. From E 400 there are, among others, thickeners and gelling agents. Switzerland largely follows this system. The responsible authority is the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office, the FSVO.

**E 300** is ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C; it protects fruit juices, for example, from turning brown. **E 330** is citric acid, which is found in lemons and gives many drinks a sour taste. E 322 is lecithin, which is often obtained from soya or sunflowers. These substances sound strange, but they are natural parts of many plants.

Fat and water do not normally mix, as you can see with oil in water. An **emulsifier** such as lecithin holds the two together, for example in chocolate, margarine or mayonnaise. **Pectin** comes from apples or citrus peel and makes jam set. Agar-agar is obtained from red seaweed and is a plant-based alternative to gelatine.

Food goes bad when moulds, yeasts or bacteria grow. **Preservatives** such as sorbic acid, E 200, slow down this growth, for example in bread, cheese or sauces. Antioxidants protect fats from the oxygen in the air so that they do not go rancid and smell bad. Cooling, drying or bottling also make food keep, without any additives at all.

All additives must be listed in the **list of ingredients** on the packaging, either by name or by E number. If you want to know what is in a food, you can look up the numbers. Approved substances are considered safe in the permitted amounts, but some people are sensitive to particular substances. Fresh, little-processed foods usually contain hardly any additives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A code for a food additive approved in Europe.
A substance that joins fat and water into an even mixture.
A substance that makes food keep longer by slowing down germs.
A substance that protects food from being changed by oxygen.
A substance that makes liquids firm and wobbly like jelly.

gewusst: Even vitamin C from oranges gets an E number as an additive, namely E 300.
Agar-agar gels so strongly that just a little powder can make a whole litre of liquid set.
Thousands of years ago people were already preserving meat and fish with salt and smoke.

teile.einleitung: A conflict of interest exists when a person's own interests could influence their judgement. In research this can happen, for example, when a company pays for a study whose result benefits it. That is why researchers disclose such conflicts, so that others can judge the results correctly.
wichtigste: A conflict of interest exists when your own interests could influence your judgement.
Academic journals require authors to disclose their conflicts of interest.
A reviewer who is asked to assess an article by her direct competitor should turn down the task or report it.
For decades the tobacco industry funded studies to play down the health risks of smoking.
On average, industry-funded drug studies more often turn out favourably for the funder.
A close friendship can also be a conflict of interest, even though no money is involved.
Disclosing a conflict of interest is not proof of bad research; it only shows a possible risk.

abschnitte.text: We speak of a **conflict of interest** when someone has to make a judgement but could at the same time gain something from it. A simple example: a referee officiates at a match in which his own son is playing. Even if he referees completely fairly, others might doubt him. In research it is usually about money, career or personal relationships. So a conflict of interest does not mean that someone is cheating, but that there is a **risk of bias**.

The most common are **financial conflicts of interest**. A researcher might, for example, receive money from a company whose medicine she is studying, or own shares in that company. But there are also **non-financial** conflicts. These include a close friendship with the authors of an article or strong rivalry with them. The wish to see your own favourite theory confirmed can also influence your judgement.

Academic journals require authors to **disclose** their conflicts of interest. That is why at the end of many articles there is a section saying who paid for the study and what connections exist. Reviewers in **peer review** must also be honest. If a reviewer is asked to assess an article by her direct competitor, she should turn down the task or report the conflict. In this way the review stays as fair as possible.

For decades the **tobacco industry** funded studies that were meant to play down the health risks of smoking. As a result, effective measures against smoking were delayed for a long time. In the 1960s the **sugar industry** paid for a review that presented fat rather than sugar as the main risk for heart disease. This only became known decades later through old documents. Studies also show that, on average, industry-funded drug studies more often turn out favourably for the funder.

Conflicts of interest do not only exist in science. In Switzerland, members of the federal parliament must declare their **interests** in a public register. It shows, for example, on which boards of directors or associations they serve. Judges and members of public authorities must also **recuse** themselves when they are personally affected. Openness helps people to trust decisions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A situation in which your own advantages could influence your judgement.
Publicly stating connections and sources of money.
An expert who checks and assesses a piece of work.
When someone does not take part in a decision because they may be biased.
A one-sided deviation from the truth, often unintended.

gewusst: Internal documents of the tobacco industry later became public through court cases and now fill huge online archives.
Many researchers write a statement even when they have no conflicts of interest.

teile.einleitung: The impact factor is a figure that shows how often articles in a scientific journal are cited on average. Many people see it as a measure of a journal's reputation. But it is controversial, especially when it is used to judge individual researchers.
wichtigste: The idea of the impact factor comes from Eugene Garfield.
It measures the average number of citations per article from the two previous years.
Impact factors are published every year in the Journal Citation Reports.
A few highly cited articles shape the average, so it is not suitable for judging individual researchers.
Citation habits differ greatly from subject to subject.
The DORA declaration of 2012 calls for research not to be assessed by the impact factor of the journal.
The h-index is another figure, which relates to individual researchers.

abschnitte.text: Researchers publish their results in **academic journals**. When others mention this work in their own articles, this is called a **citation**. The impact factor counts how often the articles in a journal are cited on average. The idea came from the American information scientist **Eugene Garfield** in the 1950s. He wanted to help libraries decide which journals to buy.

For a particular year, you count all the citations that articles from the **two previous years** received in that year. You divide this number by the number of articles from the two previous years. An example: a journal published 200 articles in two years, which were cited 900 times in the following year. 900 divided by 200 gives an impact factor of **4.5**. The values appear every year in the **Journal Citation Reports** database.

The impact factor is an average. Often a few very highly cited articles shape the value, while many others are hardly cited at all. That is why it says little about a single article or a single researcher. In addition, subjects are hard to compare because **citation habits** are very different. In medicine people cite much more than, for example, in mathematics.

In 2012 the **San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment**, **DORA** for short, was drawn up in San Francisco. It calls for research to be judged by its content and not by the impact factor of the journal. Many universities and research funders have signed it, including the Swiss National Science Foundation. Critics fear that the pressure for high figures holds back good research. Some journals even tried to raise their value with tricks.

For individual researchers there is the **h-index**, which the physicist Jorge Hirsch proposed in 2005. An h-index of h means: you have h articles that have each been cited at least h times. Example: a researcher has 5 articles with 12, 8, 5, 3 and 1 citations. Three articles have at least 3 citations, but there are not four articles with at least 4, so her h-index is 3. This figure has weaknesses too; for example, it puts young researchers at a disadvantage.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reference in an article to another scientific work.
A journal in which researchers publish their results.
The sum of all values divided by how many there are.
A figure that combines the number and citations of a person's articles.

gewusst: Originally the impact factor was only meant to help libraries buy journals.
A single extremely often cited article can push up the impact factor of a small journal sharply for two years.

teile.einleitung: Ceramics are hard materials that are shaped from clay or other mineral substances and then fired in a kiln. Cups, plates, bricks and flowerpots are made of ceramic. It is one of humanity's oldest inventions and is even used in space travel and medicine today.
wichtigste: Classic ceramics are made mainly from clay.
Firing in a kiln makes the shaped clay permanently hard.
Ceramic is typically hard but brittle.
The glass-like layer on ceramics is called a glaze.
Porcelain was invented in China; one of its main ingredients is the white clay kaolin.
In 1710 the first European porcelain factory was founded in Meissen.
Bricks and the heat shield tiles of the Space Shuttle are also made of ceramic.

abschnitte.text: The word **ceramics** comes from the Greek “keramos”, which means potter's clay. Ceramic is made by shaping a soft mass, drying it and firing it at high heat. The most important raw material is **clay**, a fine soil that is easy to shape when moist. It is typical of ceramic that it is hard and heat-resistant, but **brittle**. That is why a cup that falls on the floor breaks instead of bending.

First the clay is kneaded and shaped, by hand, on a **potter's wheel** or in moulds. Then the piece has to dry slowly. During **firing** in a kiln, at about 900 to over 1400 °C depending on the ceramic, the minerals change and bond firmly together. Many pieces are also given a **glaze**, a glass-like layer that shines and makes the vessel watertight.

There are many kinds of ceramic. **Earthenware**, such as flowerpots, is porous and lets water through. Stoneware is denser and harder. **Porcelain** is especially fine, white and sometimes slightly translucent. It is made from **kaolin**, feldspar and quartz and fired at a very high temperature.

Fired clay figures have existed for more than 25,000 years. Clay vessels for cooking and storage came later and became important all over the world. **China** invented porcelain, which was long regarded as a precious secret. In Europe, Johann Friedrich Böttger was the first to succeed in making porcelain, and in 1710 the first European porcelain factory was founded in **Meissen**.

Many building materials are also ceramics, such as **bricks**, roof tiles and wall tiles. In Switzerland, tiled stoves are an old tradition, and in the Emmental the colourful Heimberg and Langnau pottery is well known. Washbasins and toilets are made of sanitary ceramics. Dentists use ceramic for crowns because it is hard and looks like a real tooth.

Modern **technical ceramics** are extremely heat-resistant and hard. Most of the heat shield tiles of the **Space Shuttle** were made of ceramic and protected it when it re-entered the atmosphere. Ceramic is also found in spark plugs, the brake discs of sports cars and electronic components. Some ceramics even conduct electricity without resistance at low temperatures.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fine soil that can be shaped when moist, the main raw material for ceramics.
A thin, glass-like layer on ceramic that shines and seals.
A very pure, white clay that is used for porcelain.
A material is brittle if it breaks under stress instead of changing shape.

gewusst: In English, porcelain is called “china” because it originally came from China.
A porcelain kiln can get hotter than some liquid lava.

teile.einleitung: Left-handedness means that a person is more skilful with the left hand than with the right. Left-handers prefer to write, draw, throw and cut with their left hand. About one in ten people in the world is left-handed.
wichtigste: A left-hander is someone who is more skilful with the left hand.
About 10 to 15 per cent of all people are left-handed.
Experts advise letting a left-handed child write with the left hand.
There are special scissors, fountain pens and other aids for left-handers.
International Left-Handers Day is on 13 August.
Someone who uses both hands equally well is ambidextrous.
There are also left-footed people, who are more skilful with the left foot.

abschnitte.text: Most people have one hand they prefer; this is called **handedness**. For left-handers this is the left hand, for right-handers the right. Handedness shows even in small children and can usually be clearly seen by nursery school age. Someone who uses both hands about equally well is called **ambidextrous**. In a similar way, there are people who prefer to kick a ball with their left foot, the left-footed.

abschnitte.titel: What the brain has to do with it
abschnitte.text: The brain consists of a left half and a right half. The nerves cross over, so the **right half of the brain** mainly controls the left side of the body. In left-handers, control of the hand is distributed differently from that in right-handers. Why someone becomes left-handed is not fully understood, but heredity plays a part. That is why some families have a striking number of left-handers.

In the past, the left hand was considered wrong in many countries, and children were forced at school to write with their right hand. This **forced switching** could lead to problems, for example difficulty concentrating or messy handwriting. Today we know that left-handedness is completely normal. Experts therefore advise letting children write with their stronger hand.

Many everyday objects are made for right-handers, such as scissors, tin openers or computer mice. For left-handers there are **left-handed scissors**, where the blades are the other way round so that you can see the cutting line. When writing in ink, the left hand passes over the fresh writing and can smudge it. Quick-drying ink, a special **left-handed fountain pen** and a sheet of paper placed at a slant help with this.

In some sports left-handers have an advantage, for example in tennis, fencing, table tennis or handball. Their opponents are mostly used to right-handers and have to adjust. The ball or the blade comes from an unfamiliar direction. That is why left-handers are often more common in top-level sport than in the rest of the population.

Since 1976, International Left-Handers Day has been celebrated every year on **13 August**. It is meant to draw attention to the fact that the world is often set up for right-handers. In many languages, words for right have a good meaning; in English, too, “right” also means correct. Today more and more schools and companies make sure that left-handers can manage well too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The preference for one hand that you use more skilfully.
Describes a person who can use both hands about equally well.
The former practice of forcing left-handers to write with their right hand.
Describes a person who is more skilful with the left foot.

gewusst: Some animals also have a favourite paw or favourite side, for example cats and parrots.
On left-handed scissors the blades are swapped, otherwise the upper blade would block the view of the cutting line.
The Latin word for left, sinister, also means ominous, which shows how left-handers used to be seen.

teile.einleitung: Octopuses are sea animals with eight arms that belong to the molluscs. They have no bones, can change their colour in a flash and are considered the cleverest invertebrates. Around 300 species live in all the world's seas.
wichtigste: Octopuses have eight arms covered with suckers.
They are cephalopods and are related to snails and mussels.
Because they have no bones, they fit through very narrow gaps.
When in danger, they squirt out a cloud of ink.
They camouflage themselves by changing their colour and even the texture of their skin.
They break up their prey with a hard beak.
Octopuses are very good at learning and can, for example, open a jar with a lid.
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.

abschnitte.text: An octopus consists of a soft, sack-shaped body, the **mantle**, and eight arms. On the underside of the arms are many **suckers**, with which it holds on, feels and even tastes. In the middle between the arms is the mouth with a hard, parrot-like beak. The only hard part of the body is this beak. That is why an octopus can squeeze through any hole that its beak fits through.

Octopuses live in all the world's oceans, from shallow water on rocky coasts to the deep sea. They like to hide in caves, rock crevices or empty shells. The **common octopus** lives in the Mediterranean and on Europe's Atlantic coast. There are no octopuses in Swiss lakes, because they need salt water.

Octopuses are predators and hunt mainly at night. They eat crabs, mussels, snails and fish. They grab their prey with their arms and crack it with their **beak**. Some species drill holes in shells and paralyse their prey with poison from their saliva.

In an octopus's skin there are thousands of tiny colour cells, the **chromatophores**. The octopus can enlarge or shrink them in fractions of a second and so change its colour. Some octopuses even make their skin rough like a stone or imitate other animals. If that does not help, the octopus squirts out **ink** and escapes by jet propulsion, pressing water out of its body.

Octopuses have a large brain, but a large part of their nerve cells sits in their arms. Each arm can therefore feel and grip partly on its own. In experiments, octopuses learned to open screw-top jars, find their way through mazes and tell people apart. Some octopuses carry coconut shells around with them and use them as a hiding place.

Most octopuses live only one to two years. The biggest is the **giant Pacific octopus**, whose arms can reach several metres. The blue-ringed octopus from the area around Australia, by contrast, is only the size of a golf ball. But it is one of the most poisonous sea creatures and very dangerous for humans.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of molluscs whose arms sit directly on the head, for example octopuses and squid.
A round hollow on the arms with which the octopus can attach itself by suction.
Tiny colour cells in the skin with which octopuses change their colour.
A way of moving in which water is pressed out hard towards the back, so that the animal shoots forwards.

gewusst: Octopuses have three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, one through the rest of the body.
Octopus blood is blue because the oxygen is bound to a substance containing copper.
An octopus can taste with its suckers what it is touching.

teile.einleitung: The Kibble balance is a highly precise measuring instrument with which a mass can be determined using a constant of nature. It helped to redefine the kilogram in 2019. Since then, no prototype piece of metal has been needed to know how heavy a kilogram is.
wichtigste: A Kibble balance determines a mass using the Planck constant.
It used to be called a watt balance.
It is named after the British physicist Bryan Kibble.
It works in two modes, the weighing mode and the moving mode.
Its basic principle is described by the equation U · I = m · g · v.
The local acceleration due to gravity g must be measured very precisely at the site.
The measurement is usually made in a vacuum to avoid disturbances from the air.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been defined by the Planck constant.

abschnitte.text: From 1889 to 2019 a kilogram was exactly as heavy as a small cylinder made of platinum and iridium. This **International Prototype Kilogram** is kept in a safe near Paris. Comparisons showed, however, that it changed by tiny amounts relative to its copies. That is why researchers looked for a definition that never changes and can be reproduced anywhere in the world.

abschnitte.titel: What does the Kibble balance measure?
abschnitte.text: The **Kibble balance** compares a mass with electrical quantities. Using quantum effects, these electrical quantities can be traced back very precisely to the **Planck constant** h, a constant of nature. In this way a mass can be determined from a constant of nature instead of from a piece of metal. The instrument used to be called a **watt balance**, because it compares mechanical and electrical power.

In **weighing mode**, the mass lies on the balance, and a coil in a magnetic field pushes against it with current until everything is in balance. In **moving mode**, the same coil is moved through the magnetic field at a constant speed and the voltage produced is measured. Together the two measurements give the equation U · I = m · g · v. Here U stands for voltage, I for current, m for mass, g for the acceleration due to gravity and v for speed.

Because g appears in the equation, the **acceleration due to gravity** must be measured very precisely at the site. It is not the same everywhere on Earth, but depends, for example, on the altitude and on the rock underground. The measurement usually takes place in a **vacuum**, so that buoyancy and air movements do not interfere. Vibrations and changes in temperature must also be kept as small as possible.

The British physicist **Bryan Kibble** proposed the method in 1975. After his death in 2016, the instrument was renamed in his honour. Before the kilogram could be redefined, independent measurements of h had to agree with very small uncertainty. In 2018 the member states decided on the redefinition, which has applied since 20 May 2019. The Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern is also working on a Kibble balance of its own.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that tells you how heavy and inert a body is, measured in kilograms.
A value in physics that never changes, anywhere.
A very small constant of nature, h, from quantum physics.
How quickly an object speeds up as it falls, about 9.81 metres per second squared on Earth.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.

gewusst: The old prototype kilogram was so valuable that it was kept under three glass bells in a safe.
A Kibble balance is much bigger than kitchen scales and often fills a whole laboratory room.
Since 2019, no object has been the basis of any SI unit.

teile.einleitung: The problem of induction is a famous question in philosophy: are we allowed to conclude a general rule from many observations? We are sure that the sun will rise tomorrow, because it always has so far. But the Scottish philosopher David Hume showed that this cannot be proved logically.
wichtigste: Induction means concluding a general rule from many individual cases.
With the example of the sunrise, Hume wanted to show that such expectations cannot be proved logically.
In 1748 Hume set out the problem in an easy-to-read way in the work “An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding”.
According to Hume, our trust in inductive conclusions is based on habit.
Justifying induction by saying it has worked so far is itself inductive and therefore circular.
Bertrand Russell illustrated the problem with a chicken that is fed every day and one day is slaughtered.
Mathematical induction is not affected, because it is a deductive method of proof.

abschnitte.text: In **induction**, you conclude a general rule from observed individual cases. An example: the sun has risen every morning, so it will rise tomorrow too. In everyday life and in science we rely on such conclusions all the time. But nothing about the future follows with logical necessity from the past. This very gap is called the **problem of induction**.

The Scottish philosopher **David Hume** lived from 1711 to 1776. He first described the problem in his “Treatise of Human Nature”. In 1748 he set it out more briefly and in a way that was easier to read in **“An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding”**. Hume thought that our trust in induction is based on **habit**. Because we have experienced something often, we expect it again, without being able to prove it.

abschnitte.titel: A circle with no way out
abschnitte.text: You could say: induction has always worked well so far, so it will go on working. But this justification is itself an inductive conclusion. So you are assuming what you want to prove. Such a justification is called **circular**, a circular argument. That is why the problem is still considered very hard to solve today.

The British philosopher **Bertrand Russell** told of a chicken that is fed every day and therefore trusts the farmer. One day, however, it is slaughtered. With the **raven paradox**, Carl Gustav Hempel presented another difficulty: logically speaking, every green apple seems to confirm the sentence “All ravens are black”. Nelson Goodman invented the made-up word **“grue”**, which means green up to a certain point in time and blue after that. All the green emeralds seen so far fit “green” just as well as “grue”.

For a long time people in Europe believed that all swans were white, until black swans were discovered in Australia. The philosopher **Karl Popper** concluded from this that general laws can never be finally proved, but they can be refuted. Science therefore tests theories and keeps them as long as they have not been refuted. **Mathematical induction** is not affected by the problem. Despite its name, it is a strictly deductive method of proof.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conclusion from many individual cases to a general rule.
A logical conclusion from a general rule to an individual case.
A justification that already assumes what it is supposed to prove.
A statement that seems contradictory or absurd, even though it appears logical.

gewusst: Today the expression “black swan” stands for a completely unexpected event.
Russell's chicken is sometimes told as a turkey that is slaughtered shortly before a holiday.

teile.einleitung: Innosuisse is the Swiss Innovation Agency. It helps to turn good ideas from research into new products and services. To do this, it brings universities and companies together and supports young firms.
wichtigste: Innosuisse is the Swiss Innovation Agency, based in Bern.
On 1 January 2018 it replaced the Commission for Technology and Innovation (CTI).
Legally, Innosuisse is a public-law institution of the Swiss government.
In innovation projects, a research institution and an implementation partner work together.
In classic innovation projects, the funding goes to the research partner, not to the company.
Innosuisse supports start-ups especially with coaching.
With an innovation cheque, an SME can do a preliminary check of an idea with a research partner.

abschnitte.text: An **innovation** is a new idea that is actually used, for example a new device or a better process. Innosuisse promotes such innovations on behalf of the Swiss government. It is a **public-law institution** based in Bern. This means it belongs to the state but works fairly independently.

Before Innosuisse there was the **Commission for Technology and Innovation**, CTI for short. It had already been promoting cooperation between universities and business for decades. On 1 January 2018 it was replaced by Innosuisse. This gave funding a new, more independent form.

In a typical **innovation project**, two partners work together. A research institution, such as a university of applied sciences or ETH, supplies the knowledge. An **implementation partner**, usually a company, wants to bring the idea to market later. Innosuisse pays for the work of the research partner, while the company itself bears part of the costs.

A **start-up** is a young company with a new business idea. Innosuisse offers courses and experienced **coaches** who advise founders. Many start-ups are **spin-offs**, that is, companies founded to make use of a university's research results. Examples come from medical technology, robotics or energy technology.

Small and medium-sized enterprises, SMEs for short, often have no research department of their own. With an **innovation cheque**, they can do a first preliminary check of their idea with a research partner. In this way they find out whether a bigger project would be worthwhile. This lowers the barrier to working with a university.

Switzerland has hardly any raw materials; its most important capital is knowledge. That is why it is important for ideas from universities to find their way into business. In international rankings of innovative strength, Switzerland has been near the top for years. Alongside the **Swiss National Science Foundation**, which mainly funds basic research, Innosuisse is one of the most important funding bodies of the Swiss government.

begriffe.erklaerung: A new idea or invention that is actually used.
A young company with a new, often technical business idea.
A company founded out of a university in order to make use of research.
Small and medium-sized enterprises, that is, companies with up to 250 employees.

gewusst: The name Innosuisse is made up of innovation and Suisse, the French word for Switzerland.
In projects with companies, Innosuisse gives the money not to the company but to the university.
Many well-known Swiss high-tech companies started out as a small university spin-off.

teile.einleitung: The kilogram is the unit used to say how heavy something is. It is abbreviated kg, and one kilogram is 1000 grams. It is one of the seven base units on which the International System of Units is built.
wichtigste: One kilogram is 1000 grams.
The abbreviation for kilogram is kg.
Kilograms are used to say how heavy something is, or more precisely its mass.
A litre of water weighs roughly one kilogram.
1000 kilograms make one tonne.
Until 2019 the kilogram was defined by a metal cylinder near Paris.
Today it is determined by a constant of nature, the Planck constant.

abschnitte.text: The **kilogram** is the unit of mass in the International System of Units, **SI** for short. The prefix “kilo” comes from Greek and means thousand. That is why one kilogram is exactly 1000 grams. In everyday life people often just say “a kilo”.

A litre of water weighs roughly 1 kilogram, and a packet of flour or sugar usually does too. A 7-year-old child weighs about 23 kilograms. Three bags each holding 5 kilograms of potatoes weigh 15 kilograms altogether. An elephant even weighs several thousand kilograms, that is, several **tonnes**.

Originally, in France in 1795, it was laid down that a kilogram is as heavy as a litre of water. From 1889 a small cylinder made of platinum and iridium served as the standard, the **International Prototype Kilogram**. It is only about 39 millimetres high and is kept in a safe in Sèvres near Paris. Many countries received precise copies of it so that they could check their scales.

Over time it was found that the prototype kilogram and its copies differed by tiny amounts. That is why, since 20 May 2019, the kilogram has been determined by a **constant of nature**, the Planck constant. With very precise instruments such as the **Kibble balance**, it can be realised with the same accuracy anywhere in the world. In Switzerland, the Federal Institute of Metrology METAS in Bern-Wabern makes sure that units of measurement are correct.

Strictly speaking, the kilogram measures **mass**, that is, how much matter there is in a body. Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls on a body. On the Moon, a kilogram of apples would have exactly the same mass but would feel much lighter. In shops it is important that scales are verified, so that everyone gets exactly what they pay for.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter there is in an object, measured in kilograms.
A fixed quantity used to measure something, for example the metre or the kilogram.
1000 kilograms.
To test and confirm officially that a measuring instrument measures correctly.

gewusst: The kilogram is the only SI base unit whose name already contains a prefix.
On the Moon, scales would show only about a sixth for a kilogram of apples, because they measure the pull of gravity.
A blue whale can weigh more than 100,000 kilograms and is regarded as one of the heaviest animals that have ever lived.

teile.einleitung: Short-term memory is the part of memory that holds information for only a short time. You use it, for example, to remember a phone number until you have typed it in. It is small and forgetful, but essential for thinking.
wichtigste: Without repetition, short-term memory holds information for only about 15 to 30 seconds.
According to George Miller, it can hold about seven items, plus or minus two.
In chunking, you group information into larger units.
Working memory holds information and works on it at the same time, for example in mental arithmetic.
The hippocampus is important for getting content into long-term memory.
After brain surgery in 1953, Henry Molaison could no longer permanently remember new experiences.
Spaced repetition helps most to keep what you have learned for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Memory works in several stages. First, sense impressions land in the sensory store for fractions of a second. What we pay attention to goes into **short-term memory**, where it disappears again after about 15 to 30 seconds unless it is repeated. Only part of it reaches **long-term memory**, where it can stay for years. The researchers Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin described this stage model in 1968.

In 1956 the American psychologist **George Miller** found that people can hold about seven items at once, plus or minus two. These can be digits, letters or words. More recent research suggests that it is often only about four items. That is why a long row of numbers is so easily forgotten.

You can remember more if you group information into packages. This is called **chunking**, from the English word “chunk”. The digits 1, 2, 9, 1 are easier to remember as the year 1291, the year the Swiss Confederation was founded. That is also why phone numbers are written in groups. A chess expert can remember whole positions because he sees them as familiar patterns.

In mental arithmetic you have to hold numbers in your head and calculate with them at the same time. This combination is called **working memory**. The British researchers Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch described it in more detail in 1974. It has one part for language and sounds and one for pictures and places. You also need it when reading a long sentence, so as not to forget the beginning.

In 1953 the American **Henry Molaison** had brain surgery because of severe epileptic seizures. The doctors also removed large parts of both **hippocampi**. After that he could no longer permanently remember new experiences, even though his short-term memory worked. He became famous under the initials H. M., and through him it was discovered that short-term and long-term memory are separate systems.

When someone reads a list to you, you often remember the last words well, because they are still in your short-term memory. The first words also often stick, because you have repeated them more often. To keep knowledge for a long time, **spaced repetition** helps, which means learning several times with gaps of days in between. Testing yourself, for example with flashcards or quiz questions, works better than just reading again. Getting enough sleep also helps, because the brain strengthens what you have learned while you sleep.

begriffe.erklaerung: A store that holds a small amount of information for seconds.
A store in which knowledge and memories can stay for years.
Grouping single items into larger, meaningful packages.
The part of memory that holds information and works on it at the same time.
An area of the brain that helps to store new memories permanently.

gewusst: The hippocampus is called that because its shape is reminiscent of a seahorse, hippokampos in Greek.
If you quietly repeat a piece of information to yourself, you can hold it in short-term memory for much longer.
Henry Molaison helped research for over 50 years, even though he greeted the researchers like strangers every time they met.

teile.einleitung: Carbon fibres are wafer-thin threads made almost entirely of carbon. Embedded in plastic, they make a material that is lighter than aluminium and yet extremely strong. It is found in racing bikes, aircraft, sports equipment and even in the Swiss solar aircraft Solar Impulse 2.
wichtigste: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic is abbreviated to CFRP.
Most carbon fibres are made from polyacrylonitrile.
The starting fibres are transformed by strong heating without oxygen.
A single fibre is about 7 micrometres thick.
Carbon fibres are very strong and light at the same time.
Unlike glass fibres, they conduct electricity.
In the Boeing 787, composite materials make up around 50 per cent of the structural mass.

abschnitte.text: A **carbon fibre** is a very thin thread of almost pure carbon. A single fibre is only about 7 **micrometres** thick, around ten times thinner than a human hair. Thousands of such fibres are combined into bundles and fabrics. On its own the fabric is soft like cloth. Only with plastic does it become a hard material.

Most fibres are made from the plastic **polyacrylonitrile**, PAN for short. These fibres are first pretreated in air and then heated to very high temperatures **without oxygen**. In the process almost all the other elements disappear, and carbon is left. Production needs a lot of energy, which is why carbon fibres are expensive.

Carbon fibres are very **strong** and **stiff**, but light at the same time. A component made of CFRP can be much lighter than one made of steel with the same strength. Unlike glass fibres, they **conduct** electricity. They do not rust, but can splinter if hit hard. The black, fabric-like pattern on the surface is typical.

Because every kilo counts, carbon fibres are in great demand in **aircraft construction**. In the Boeing 787, around 50 per cent of the structural mass consists of composite materials. The Swiss solar aircraft **Solar Impulse 2** had a structure made of carbon fibre composite and flew round the Earth in 2015 and 2016 using only solar power. Racing bikes, ski poles, tennis rackets, Formula 1 cars and the rotor blades of wind turbines are built with it too.

As early as around 1880, **Thomas Edison** used carbonised fibres of bamboo or cotton as filaments in his light bulbs. These fibres, however, were not strong. High-strength carbon fibres were only developed from the 1950s and 1960s onwards. Since then they have become ever cheaper and more widely used.

Components made of CFRP are difficult to **recycle**, because the fibres and the plastic are firmly bonded. Researchers are looking for methods to recover the fibres. Working with it produces fine dust, against which you have to protect yourself. In addition, repairs are more complicated than with metal.

begriffe.erklaerung: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic, a light and strong composite material.
A material made of two or more substances which together have better properties.
A thousandth of a millimetre.
A plastic from which most carbon fibres are made.

gewusst: Many professional racing bikes with carbon fibre frames weigh only around 7 kilograms.
The wingspan of Solar Impulse 2 was larger than that of a jumbo jet, but the aircraft weighed only about as much as a car.

teile.einleitung: A vaccine is a substance that prepares the body for a disease before you catch it. It trains the immune system with harmless parts or weakened forms of a pathogen. Vaccinations are among the most important inventions in medicine.
wichtigste: A vaccination trains the immune system with harmless parts of a pathogen.
Memory cells make sure that the immune system remembers a pathogen for a long time.
A live vaccine, for example against measles, contains weakened pathogens.
An inactivated vaccine contains killed pathogens or parts of them.
An adjuvant is an additive that strengthens the immune response.
A booster vaccination strengthens protection that is wearing off.
In Switzerland, the FOPH and the Federal Commission for Vaccination publish the Swiss vaccination schedule.

abschnitte.text: Our **immune system** protects the body from pathogens such as viruses and bacteria. A vaccine shows it a harmless part or a weakened form of a pathogen. The immune system then forms **antibodies** and special defence cells. In addition, **memory cells** are created, which often remember the pathogen for years. If the real pathogen comes later, the body can react immediately and strongly.

A **live vaccine** contains weakened pathogens that can hardly multiply any more, for example against measles, mumps and rubella. An **inactivated vaccine** contains killed pathogens or only parts of them, for example against tetanus or polio. Newer vaccines contain building instructions for part of a pathogen, for example the **mRNA vaccines** that were used against Covid-19 from 2020. Some vaccines contain an **adjuvant**. This additive strengthens the immune response.

In 1796 the English doctor **Edward Jenner** carried out a famous experiment. He gave a boy harmless cowpox and showed that the boy was then protected from dangerous smallpox. This is where the word vaccine comes from, from the Latin vacca for cow. Later Louis Pasteur developed a vaccine against rabies. Thanks to worldwide vaccination, smallpox was eradicated, which the World Health Organization announced in 1980.

In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health (**FOPH**) and the Federal Commission for Vaccination publish the **Swiss vaccination schedule**. It recommends which vaccinations make sense at which age. Children receive many vaccinations as babies. To keep the protection going, a **booster** is sometimes needed. Vaccination is voluntary in Switzerland, but the vaccinations in the schedule are recommended.

After a vaccination, **redness and pain at the injection site** are common and harmless. Sometimes you feel tired for one or two days or have a slight temperature. This shows that the immune system is working. Serious side effects are very rare and are closely monitored. When many people are vaccinated, this also protects those who cannot be vaccinated; this is called **herd protection**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body's defence system against pathogens.
Proteins that recognise and mark pathogens so that they can be fought.
A defence cell that remembers a particular pathogen for a long time.
An additive in a vaccine that strengthens the immune response.
Protection for everyone, because a pathogen can hardly spread when many people are vaccinated.

gewusst: The word vaccine comes from the Latin word for cow.
Smallpox is the first human disease to have been eradicated worldwide by vaccination.
Some vaccines are grown in hens' eggs.

teile.einleitung: Insects are small animals with six legs and a body made of three parts. They are the most species-rich group of animals on Earth, from the ant to the butterfly. Without insects, many plants would not bear fruit.
wichtigste: An insect such as an ant has six legs.
The body consists of a head, a thorax and an abdomen.
Insects have a hard exoskeleton made of chitin.
Most insects have antennae and two pairs of wings.
More than a million insect species have been described, more than all other animal species put together.
Many insects change from an egg via a larva into the finished animal.
Bees and other insects pollinate a large share of our crop plants.

abschnitte.text: An insect's body has three parts: the **head**, the **thorax** and the **abdomen**. On the head are the antennae, the mouthparts and often large compound eyes. Attached to the thorax are the six legs and usually four wings. Instead of bones, insects have a hard **exoskeleton** made of chitin, which protects them like a suit of armour.
