Researchers have so far described more than a million insect species, and there are probably many more. Among the largest groups are **beetles**, butterflies and moths, flies, and bees, wasps and ants. Insects live almost everywhere: in forests, deserts, lakes and even in the high mountains. Only in the open sea are there hardly any.

Many insects completely change their shape during their lives; this is called **metamorphosis**. A butterfly lays eggs, and caterpillars hatch from them. The caterpillar eats, grows and turns into a pupa. Inside the **pupa** its body is rebuilt until a butterfly emerges.

Bees, bumblebees and hoverflies carry pollen from flower to flower; this is called **pollination**. Without them there would be far fewer apples, cherries and strawberries. Insects also break down leaves and dead animals and are food for birds, bats and fish. Some insects, such as mosquitoes, can also spread diseases.

Tens of thousands of insect species live in Switzerland. Well-known examples are the Rosalia longicorn, a blue-coloured beetle, the red wood ant and many butterflies on mountain meadows. But many species are threatened because habitats are disappearing and **pesticides** are being used. Flower meadows, hedges and bee hotels in the garden help insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hard shell on the outside of the body that supports and protects insects instead of bones.
The transformation of an animal, for example from a caterpillar into a butterfly.
An eye made of many small individual eyes, typical of insects.
When pollen reaches another flower so that fruits and seeds can grow.

gewusst: Spiders are not insects, because they have eight legs.
Ants can carry many times their own body weight.
Insects have existed for more than 400 million years, long before the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: A fridge is a household appliance that keeps food cool so that it stays fresh for longer. It does not make cold but pumps heat from the inside to the outside. Today there is a fridge in almost every kitchen in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Germs grow more slowly in the fridge, so food stays fresh for longer.
A temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius is recommended.
The compressor squeezes the gaseous refrigerant.
The evaporating refrigerant takes up the heat inside.
At the back, the fridge gives off the heat to the kitchen.
Carl von Linde built an important refrigerating machine around 1876.
With the fridge door open, the kitchen gets warmer overall, not cooler.

abschnitte.text: In the cold, **germs** such as bacteria and moulds multiply much more slowly. That is why milk, meat, cheese and vegetables stay fresh for longer in the fridge. For the household fridge, a temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius is recommended. In the **freezer** it is much colder, usually about minus 18 degrees, so that ice cream stays hard.

Inside the fridge, a **refrigerant** flows round a closed circuit of pipes. Inside the fridge it evaporates and takes up heat as it does so, much as sweat cools the skin when it evaporates. The **compressor** sucks in the gas and squeezes it, which makes it hot. In the grid at the back it gives off its heat to the kitchen and becomes liquid again, then the cycle starts all over.

It is not equally cold everywhere in the fridge. The **vegetable drawer** is usually right at the bottom; it is a little damper and less cold there. Meat and fish belong on the coldest shelf, usually just above the vegetable drawer. Hot food, such as a pan of freshly cooked soup, should first be left to cool before you put it in.

In the past, food was kept in a cool **cellar** or put in ice boxes filled with blocks of ice. In winter people sawed ice out of lakes for this and stored it in ice houses. The German engineer **Carl von Linde** built an important refrigerating machine around 1876, which was first used in breweries. Electric fridges for households spread from the 1920s in America and later in Europe too.

Fridges used to contain refrigerants that damaged the protective **ozone layer**; today more environmentally friendly substances are used. If you leave the door open for a long time, cold air escapes and the fridge uses more electricity. You also cannot cool a kitchen with the door open, because the fridge gives off more heat at the back than the cold it lets out at the front. The energy label shows when you buy one how economical an appliance is.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance in the fridge that takes up heat and gives it off again.
A pump that squeezes the gaseous refrigerant together.
The part inside where the refrigerant evaporates and takes up heat.
Tiny living things such as bacteria that make food go bad.

gewusst: A heat pump for heating works on the same principle as a fridge, only used the other way round.
Albert Einstein, together with Leo Szilard, applied for a patent for a fridge with no moving parts.
When the fridge hums, the compressor is running.

teile.einleitung: Classical conditioning is a form of learning in which a living thing links two stimuli together. It became famous through the Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov, whose dogs produced saliva at the mere sound of a signal. This kind of learning also happens in humans, often without them noticing.
wichtigste: In classical conditioning, you learn to link two stimuli together.
An unconditioned stimulus triggers a reaction even without learning.
With dogs, Ivan Pavlov showed how a neutral stimulus can become a trigger.
When a learned reaction disappears, this is called extinction.
When an extinguished reaction reappears after a break, this is called spontaneous recovery.
When similar stimuli trigger the same reaction, this is called stimulus generalisation.
John B. Watson founded the school of behaviourism.
Disgust at a food after a stomach upset is called taste aversion.

abschnitte.text: Around 1900 the Russian researcher **Ivan Pavlov** was studying digestion in dogs. He noticed that the dogs produced saliva even before they were given food. So before feeding them, he always sounded a signal, such as a tone. After a while the dogs produced saliva at the tone alone. Pavlov received the Nobel Prize in 1904 for his research on digestion.

Food is an **unconditioned stimulus**: it triggers a reaction without learning, namely the flow of saliva. The tone is at first a **neutral stimulus**, which has no effect. If it is often presented together with the food, it becomes a **conditioned stimulus**. It now triggers a learned, conditioned reaction on its own.

If the tone sounds for a long time without food, the flow of saliva becomes weaker and disappears. This is called **extinction**. After a break, however, the reaction can suddenly reappear; this is called **spontaneous recovery**. So the link has not been completely forgotten, only suppressed.

If an animal also reacts to tones that are similar to the learned tone, this is called **stimulus generalisation**. If, on the other hand, it learns to react only to one particular tone, this is called **stimulus discrimination**. Both are useful in everyday life. Someone who has once been stung by a wasp might also be careful around bees.

The American psychologist **John B. Watson** founded **behaviourism**, which studies only observable behaviour. In 1920, in an experiment, he taught a small child, “Little Albert”, to be afraid of a white rat. To do this, a loud, frightening noise sounded every time Albert saw the rat. Today this experiment is considered ethically unacceptable and would be forbidden.

We often come across classical conditioning. Many people get nervous as soon as they hear the sound of the drill at the dentist's. Advertising links products with cheerful music or beautiful pictures so that we connect good feelings with them. And anyone who fell ill after a particular food often feels disgusted by it for a long time; this is called **taste aversion**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that a living thing perceives, for example a sound or a smell.
The response of the body or of behaviour to a stimulus.
Learning by linking stimuli, or behaviour and consequences.
A school of psychology that studies only observable behaviour.

gewusst: Pavlov did not receive the Nobel Prize for conditioning but for his research on digestion.
A taste aversion can arise after just a single bad experience.
Pets are conditioned too, when they come running at the rustle of the food packet.

teile.einleitung: In an experiment, a control group is the comparison group that does not receive the treatment being tested. Only through this comparison can you find out whether an effect really comes from the treatment or is just chance. Control groups are therefore a cornerstone of good science, from medicine to the cress experiment in the classroom.
wichtigste: A control group is a comparison group without the treatment being tested.
The group that receives the treatment is called the experimental group.
Without a control group, you cannot tell a real effect from chance.
Participants should be assigned to the groups at random.
In trials of medicines, the control group is often given a dummy medicine.
In a double-blind study, neither the participants nor the researchers know who belongs to which group.
In 1747 the ship's doctor James Lind compared groups of sailors to find a remedy for scurvy.

abschnitte.text: In an experiment you want to know whether something has an effect, for example a fertiliser or a medicine. To do this you form two groups that differ, as far as possible, in only one respect. The **experimental group** gets the treatment, the **control group** does not. At the end you compare the results of both groups. Only the difference shows what the treatment has achieved.

A class sows **cress** in two dishes. One dish gets fertiliser, the other does not; otherwise both are treated the same. The dish **without fertiliser** is the control group. If the fertilised cress grows clearly better, this suggests the fertiliser has an effect. Without the second dish you would not know how well the cress would have grown anyway.

People sometimes feel better just because they expect a treatment; this is called the **placebo effect**. That is why, in trials of medicines, the control group is often given a **dummy medicine** without an active substance that looks exactly the same. In a **double-blind study**, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is getting the real medicine. In this way expectations cannot distort the result.

Participants should be assigned to the groups **at random**, for example by drawing lots or by computer. This is called **randomisation**. If the researchers chose themselves, they might unconsciously put healthier people into one group. Thanks to chance, both groups are on average made up in the same way. Such studies are considered especially reliable in medicine.

An early example comes from the Scottish ship's doctor **James Lind**. In 1747, on board a warship, he treated sailors with **scurvy**, a dangerous deficiency disease, in small groups with different remedies. Only the men who were given oranges and lemons recovered quickly. Today we know that scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group in an experiment that receives the treatment being tested.
A dummy medicine without an active substance.
Assigning participants to groups at random.
A study in which neither the participants nor the researchers know who is getting which treatment.

gewusst: A placebo can even work when patients know that it is not a real medicine.
British sailors were later given citrus fruit, which is why they got the nickname “Limeys” in English.

teile.einleitung: The Ig Nobel Prize is a fun prize for unusual research. It is awarded for work that first makes people laugh and then makes them think. The name is a pun on the English word ignoble, which means something like unworthy.
wichtigste: The Ig Nobel Prize is awarded for research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think.
It has been awarded since 1991.
It is organised by the magazine Annals of Improbable Research.
Traditionally the prizes are handed over by real Nobel Prize winners.
Andre Geim received both an Ig Nobel Prize and a real Nobel Prize.
The prize money is a banknote for 10 trillion Zimbabwean dollars.
Traditionally, the audience throws paper aeroplanes onto the stage at the ceremony.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Ig Nobel Prize?
abschnitte.text: The Ig Nobel Prize is a **parody** of the famous Nobel Prize. Every year about ten prizes are awarded in subjects such as physics, biology, medicine or peace. Real pieces of research are honoured that sound crazy but often have a serious core. The motto is: first laugh, then think.

The prize was founded in 1991 by Marc Abrahams. He is the editor of the magazine **Annals of Improbable Research**. The magazine collects strange and funny scientific studies. For many years the ceremony took place in the Sanders Theatre at **Harvard University** in the USA; since 2020 it has been shown online.

The prizes are handed over by real **Nobel Prize winners**. The audience throws paper aeroplanes onto the stage. If a speech goes on too long, a little girl called Miss Sweetie Poo keeps calling out: Please stop, I'm bored. The prize money is a banknote for 10 trillion **Zimbabwean dollars**, which is practically worthless.

In 2000 Andre Geim and Michael Berry received the Ig Nobel Prize for Physics for making a live frog levitate with strong magnets. Ten years later Geim received the real **Nobel Prize in Physics** for his work on graphene. He is so far the only person to have both awards. This shows that unusual ideas and great research go well together.

In 2017 a prize went to a study that investigated whether cats can be both solid and liquid. In 2019 research was rewarded on why wombats produce cube-shaped droppings. Behind such questions there is often real **physics**, for example about how substances flow or about shapes in nature. That is why many prize winners are pleased about the award.

The Ig Nobel Prize shows that science is allowed to be funny. It makes research interesting for many people who otherwise hardly deal with it. At the same time it encourages **critical thinking**, because not every study makes sense. Sometimes questionable decisions by politicians or companies are also mocked with the prize.

begriffe.erklaerung: A funny imitation of something well known.
A world-famous prize for outstanding achievements, for example in physics, chemistry or medicine.
A loss of the value of money, in which money is worth less and less.
A scientific investigation into a particular question.

gewusst: The banknotes for 10 trillion Zimbabwean dollars come from a time of extreme inflation in Zimbabwe.
Many prize winners travel to the ceremony at their own expense, because they find the award funny.
In 1991 an Ig Nobel Prize went to Josiah Carberry, an invented professor who does not exist at all.

teile.einleitung: An invasive species is an animal, plant or fungus that people have brought into a foreign area and that spreads strongly there. In doing so it often pushes out native species or causes damage. There are many such newcomers in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Invasive species were brought into new areas by people, deliberately or by accident.
In Europe, plants brought in after the cut-off year 1492 count as neophytes.
In Switzerland, Himalayan balsam overgrows the banks of streams and rivers and flings its seeds several metres.
Common ragweed (Ambrosia) must be controlled because of its highly allergenic pollen.
The Asian hornet has been spreading in Switzerland since 2017 and hunts honeybees.
Since the 2010s the quagga mussel has been spreading in large lakes such as Lake Geneva and Lake Constance.
The cane toad was introduced to Australia in 1935 against sugar cane pests and became invasive itself.

abschnitte.text: Many animals and plants came to new areas with people, for example with ships, garden plants or deliveries of goods. Plants brought in after **1492** are called **neophytes**, and animals are called **neozoa**. The year 1492 was chosen because that was when Columbus reached America and worldwide trade increased greatly. Most newcomers are harmless. Only those that spread strongly and harm nature, health or the economy are called **invasive**.

**Himalayan balsam** comes from the Himalayas and has pink flowers. It overgrows the banks of streams and rivers and, when touched, flings its seeds several metres. **Common ragweed**, also called Ambrosia, comes from North America and has highly allergenic pollen, so it must be controlled in Switzerland. The Asian **knotweeds** even grow through asphalt and walls. Under the Release Ordinance, any handling of them is forbidden, except to control them.

The **Asian hornet** has been spreading in Switzerland since 2017 and especially likes to hunt honeybees. Since the 2010s the **quagga mussel** has been colonising large lakes such as Lake Geneva and Lake Constance. It clogs water pipes and changes the food chain in the lake. North American crayfish such as the **signal crayfish** carry crayfish plague, from which native noble crayfish die. The Asian tiger mosquito has also settled in Ticino.

In 1935 the **cane toad** was brought from America to Australia. It was supposed to fight beetles that were damaging the sugar cane. That hardly worked, but the toad multiplied explosively. Its skin is poisonous, and many native animals die if they eat a cane toad. Today millions of these toads live in large parts of northern Australia.

abschnitte.titel: What can be done about it
abschnitte.text: Worldwide, invasive species are among the greatest threats to **biodiversity**, the variety of life. Most important is that they are not brought in in the first place. That is why boats should be cleaned thoroughly before being taken to another lake. In the garden you should plant native plants instead of invasive ornamental ones. If you find an Asian hornet or a nest, you can report the find to the authorities.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant brought by people into a new area after 1492.
An animal brought by people into a new area.
Spreading strongly and causing harm in the process.
The variety of all living things and habitats.
A substance that triggers an allergy in some people.

gewusst: The seed capsules of Himalayan balsam burst open at the slightest touch.
The larvae of the quagga mussel are tiny and can get into new lakes unnoticed in the water carried by boats.
Not every non-native species is bad; the potato, for example, also came from America.

teile.einleitung: A pie chart is a round diagram that shows how a whole is divided into parts. Each part is a slice of the pie, and the bigger the share, the bigger the slice. That is why it is called a pie chart.
wichtigste: A pie chart shows shares of a whole.
A whole circle has 360 degrees.
All the parts together make 100 per cent.
A share of 25 per cent corresponds to an angle of 90 degrees.
A share of 10 per cent corresponds to 36 degrees.
An angle of 120 degrees corresponds to one third.
In everyday language it is also called a cake chart in German.

abschnitte.text: A pie chart is a circle divided into several **sectors**. Each sector stands for a part of the whole, for example a party in an election or a flavour of ice cream. The sectors are usually drawn in different colours and labelled with a **key**. Together all the parts always make 100 per cent.

abschnitte.titel: How to work out the angles
abschnitte.text: A full circle has 360 degrees, and that corresponds to 100 per cent. So one per cent corresponds to 3.6 degrees. For 25 per cent you multiply 25 by 3.6 and get 90 degrees, a right angle. For 10 per cent it is 36 degrees. A sector of 120 degrees is one third of the circle, because 360 divided by 3 is 120.

In a class of 30 children, 6 come to school by bike. That is one fifth of the class, so 20 per cent. The angle for it is 360 divided by 30, times 6, which is 72 degrees. Using a **set square** or a protractor, you then draw the sector from the centre.

Pie charts are especially good for showing **shares**, for example how pocket money is divided up. They work best with only a few parts, about two to six. With many small slices it becomes confusing, and slices of similar size are hard to compare. For changes over time a line graph is better, and for comparisons a **bar chart**.

The Scottish engineer **William Playfair** is considered the inventor of the pie chart. He published one of the first pie charts in 1801. Playfair also invented the bar chart and the line graph. Later the nurse Florence Nightingale also became famous for using a kind of pie chart to show what soldiers died of in the Crimean War.

Pie charts can be found in newspapers, school books and presentations. After votes and elections in Switzerland, for example, they show how the seats are shared out or the share of yes votes. With spreadsheet programs on a computer they can be made in a few seconds. A version with a hole in the middle is called a **doughnut chart**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of a circle between two radii, like a slice of cake.
A unit for measuring angles; a full circle has 360 degrees.
A share out of a hundred, so 50 per cent is half.
An explanation next to a chart showing which colour means what.

gewusst: The idea that a circle has 360 degrees goes back to the Babylonians, who counted in sixties.
A semicircle of 180 degrees always stands for exactly 50 per cent.
Many graphics experts advise against three-dimensional pie charts, because the slices at the front look bigger than they are.

teile.einleitung: A coprolite is fossilised dung from prehistoric animals. The name comes from Greek: “kopros” means dung and “lithos” means stone. For researchers, coprolites are real treasure chests, because they reveal what animals ate millions of years ago.
wichtigste: Coprolites are fossilised dung.
They are trace fossils.
The English geologist William Buckland introduced the term in 1829.
Coprolites tell you what an animal ate.
Bone remains in a coprolite show that it came from a meat-eater.
Even the eggs of parasites can be found in them.
Coprolites are rarer than bones, because dung usually breaks down quickly.

abschnitte.text: A **coprolite** is an animal's dung that has turned to stone over a very long time. In the process, the original substances were gradually replaced by minerals. Coprolites count as **trace fossils**, because they do not come from the body itself but are traces of its life. Fossilised footprints and feeding marks also belong to this group.

The term coprolite was introduced by the English geologist **William Buckland** in 1829. He studied strange stones from the cliffs near Lyme Regis in southern England. The fossil collector **Mary Anning** had noticed that such stones often lay in the belly area of ichthyosaur skeletons. Buckland realised that they were fossilised dung and found fish scales and pieces of bone in them.

From coprolites, researchers learn what an animal ate. If a coprolite contains **bone remains**, it comes from a meat-eater. Plant remains or pollen point to a plant-eater. Sometimes even the eggs of **parasites** are found, that is, of worms that lived in the animals' gut.

In 1995 a huge coprolite more than 40 centimetres long was found in Saskatchewan in Canada. It is attributed to the large predatory dinosaur **Tyrannosaurus**. It contains many crushed pieces of bone from another dinosaur. This shows that Tyrannosaurus could bite through its prey, bones and all.

Dung usually breaks down quickly, because it is soft and is decomposed by bacteria, fungi and insects. Only if it was quickly covered by mud or sand could it become fossilised. That is why coprolites are found much more rarely than bones. Some coprolites are so prettily coloured that they are cut and polished and sold as jewellery or collectors' items.

begriffe.erklaerung: Remains or traces of living things from earlier times that have turned to stone.
A fossilised trace of a living thing, such as a footprint, a burrow or dung.
A living thing that lives in or on another and feeds on it.
A scientist who studies rocks and the history of the Earth.

gewusst: There is also fossilised or dried-out dung from prehistoric people, and archaeologists can tell from it what was eaten at the time.
Coprolites no longer smell, because by now they are made of stone.
Mary Anning, the fossil collector from Lyme Regis, is now considered one of the most important pioneers of palaeontology.

teile.einleitung: Julius Maggi was a Swiss entrepreneur who lived from 1846 to 1912. He invented instant soups, the liquid Maggi seasoning and the stock cube. His products are still found in almost every kitchen today.
wichtigste: Julius Maggi lived from 1846 to 1912 and came from Frauenfeld in Thurgau.
He built his factory in Kemptthal in the canton of Zurich.
He wanted to develop cheap and nourishing food for factory workers' families.
His first instant soups were made mainly from pulse flour.
The liquid Maggi seasoning came onto the market in 1886.
In 1908 the company brought out the stock cube.
Since 1947 the Maggi brand has belonged to the Nestlé group.

abschnitte.text: **Julius Maggi** was born in Frauenfeld in 1846. His father was a miller who had come to Switzerland from Italy. Julius later took over a **mill** in Kemptthal in the canton of Zurich. Because the milling business was difficult, he looked for new products. He died in Küsnacht in 1912.

In the 19th century many women and men worked long hours in **factories**. There was little time left for cooking, and many families ate badly. The factory inspector Fridolin Schuler and the Swiss Society for the Common Good therefore looked for a cheap, healthy food. In response, from 1884 Maggi developed soup flours made from **pulses** such as peas and beans, which contain a lot of protein.

In 1886 the liquid **Maggi seasoning** came onto the market. It gives soups and sauces a strong, savoury flavour. The bottle is brown and has a yellow and red label that still looks almost the same today. The garden plant **lovage** smells so similar that it is often called “Maggi herb” in German, even though it is not in the seasoning at all.

In 1908 the company brought out the **stock cube**. You dissolve it in hot water and immediately have a broth. This saved time and made stock affordable for many people. Products like this are called ready meals or convenience food.

abschnitte.titel: From family firm to global group
abschnitte.text: The company grew quickly and also built factories abroad, for example in Singen in Germany. Maggi relied early on advertising and had its own advertising department. In 1947 the company merged with **Nestlé**. Today Nestlé sells Maggi products in a great many countries around the world.

In Kemptthal, where the Maggi factory used to stand, a new site has been created with companies, shops and leisure facilities. Maggi is regarded as one of the best-known Swiss inventors in the field of food. His idea of making healthy food quick and cheap changed cooking in Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: The seeds of plants such as peas, beans and lentils, which grow in a pod.
A liquid or powder that gives food more flavour.
A strong broth, for example made from vegetables or meat.
A kitchen herb that smells similar to Maggi seasoning.

gewusst: In German, lovage is called “Maggi herb”, even though there is no lovage at all in Maggi seasoning.
The shape and colour of the Maggi bottle have hardly changed in more than a hundred years.
Julius Maggi started out as a miller and became the inventor of instant soups.
